attributes.title: 明石

field_history_en.value: Akashi has been known from ancient times as a place of scenic beauty. In Man'yōshū, there are nine poems dedicated to Akashi, beginning with the following poem by Kakinomoto no Hitomaro: “Over a long road, from barbarian lands at the far reach of the heavens, I have come, yearning. And now the Straits of Akashi open on the island, Yamato” (Translation by Levy). Akashi no ura (bay) (Nōin Utamakura, Waka Shogakushō), Akashi no seto (strait) (Waka Shogakushō), Akashi no mon (gate) (Godaishū, Yakumo Mishō), Akashi no hama (seashore) (Godaishū, Yakumo Mishō), Akashi no kata (inlet) (Yakumo Mishō) and others later developed into utamakura, making Akashi one of the most representative poetic locations. Furthermore, Hikaru Genji, encountering a rainstorm during his exile in Suma, was visited by Akashi no Nyūdō (Akashi Priest), who invited him to relocate to Akashi. The image associated with the Akashi chapter of Genji Monogatari, where Genji meets Akashi no Kimi, the daughter of Akashi no Nyūdō, also had considerable influence on future generations.

field_history_ja.value: 古くから景勝地として知られ、『万葉集』には柿本人麻呂の「天離る夷の長道ゆ恋ひ来れば明石の門より大和島見ゆ」をはじめ明石に関する歌が九首収められる。のち明石浦（能因歌枕・和歌初学抄）、明石瀬戸（和歌初学抄）・明石門（五代集・八雲御抄）・明石浜（同上）、明石潟（八雲御抄）などが歌枕となるなど、代表的な歌枕の一つであるといえよう。また、須磨の謫居で暴風雨に遭った光源氏が明石入道に迎えられて明石に移り、入道の娘明石の君を知るという『源氏物語』明石巻に描かれるイメージも後代に大きな影響を与えた。

attributes.title: 逢坂

field_history_en.value: The barrier of Ausaka was erected in 646 (Taika 2). Around 795 (Enryaku 14), after the capital had been transferred to Heian, it was discontinued for a while (Nihon Kiryaku). Later, in 857 (Ten'an 1), it was reestablished (Montoku Jitsuroku). From the time of Man'yōshū, love poems employing images of border crossing and separation or making word plays on the keyword afu (meet) were composed, and gradually “crossing Ausaka barrier” evolved into a specialized term used in love poems. We find it in many poems meaning that a man and a woman whose love is prohibited cross a borderline and come together. Other motifs that have been employed include seki no shimizu (“the clear waters at the barrier”), as in “Reflected in the clear waters of Ausaka barrier, are they leading the horses at full moon?” (Shūishū, autumn, Tsurayuki). Another is ausaka no yūtsukedori (“the rooster of Ausaka Barrier”).

field_history_ja.value: 逢坂の関は大化二年（646）に設置され、延暦十四年（795）平安遷都の頃に一時廃止され（日本紀略）、その後天安元年（857）に再び設置された（文徳実録）。『万葉集』の時代から越境・別離のイメージや「逢ふ」を掛けた恋の歌も詠まれていたが、次第に恋の歌のテクニカル・タームと化し、「逢坂の関」を越える、すなわち許されない男女が一線を越えて結ばれるといった詠まれ方が多みられる。また、「逢坂の関の清水にかげ見えて今や引くらむ望月の駒」（拾遺集・秋・貫之）に代表される「関の清水」や、「逢坂の木綿つけ鳥」などもよく詠まれる景物である。

field_topography_en.value: An important transportation route, the Tōkaidō, passes through here, connecting Ōmi and Kyōto. In the narrow sense, Mt. Ausaka (pronounced Ōsaka) is a mountain 325 meters above sea level located in the southwest of Ōtsu City north of today’s National Route One highway. In the broad sense, it refers to the general area at the south foot of the mountain (the region at the border between southwest Ōtsu City and Yamashina Ward in Kyōto City). The name Ausaka was used historically to refer to the border region between Ōmi and Yamashina along the Tōkaidō road. Because of the strategic importance of the Ausaka mountain pass, Ausaka no Seki (Ausaka Barrier) was established in ancient times for military reasons and became a tax collection point during the Middle Ages. Because of the barrier, it was also called Sekiyama [seki means “barrier” or “gate,” yama “mountain”]. Ausaka Barrier is one of the “three great barriers” in Japan, together with Suzuka and Fuwa.

field_topography_ja.value: 近江と京都を結ぶ交通の要衝で東海道が通る。逢坂山は、狭義には大津市街南西部、国道一号の北側に位置する標高三二五メートルの山をいうが、広義には同山の南麓一帯（大津市南西部と京都市山科区の境付近）をさし、歴史的には街道沿いの近江と山城との国境を逢坂と総称して用いられた。いわゆる逢坂越の交通の要所であり、古代には軍事上の目的から逢坂関が置かれ、中世には同関で関銭が徴収された。関が設置されたため、関山ともよばれた。逢坂関は鈴鹿・不破とともに三関の一つに数えられる。

attributes.title: 生田

field_history_en.value: Ikuta is listed as an utamakura in Nōin Utamakura, Waka Shogakushō, Yakumo Mishō and so on, and it has been well known since ancient times. It also often became the stage for battles. In 1184 (Juei 3), during the war between the Minamoto and Heike, the Heike military forces set up a fortress in Ichinotani, and Ikuta Forest served as a front defense gate (Heike Monogatari book 9). The generals’ encampments were lined up between Ichinotani and Ikuta Forest. In 1338 (Kenmu 5), the Shikoku forces of the Ashikaga landed in the vicinity of the Ikuta Forest and took up their position in order to hinder the Nitta and Kusunoki forces fleeing towards Kyōto (Baishōron).

field_history_ja.value: 「能因歌枕」「和歌初学抄」「八雲御抄」などに歌枕として記載されるなど、古くから著名であった。しばしば合戦の舞台ともなり、源平合戦中の寿永三年（1184）には平家の軍勢は一ノ谷に城郭を構え生田森を大手の木戸口としており（『平家物語』巻九）、一ノ谷と生田森の間には各将の陣屋が並んだとされる。さらに、建武五年（1338）には足利方の四国勢が京都方面へと逃れる新田・楠木軍を妨げるために生田森の辺より上陸して陣取ったとされる。（『梅松論』）

field_topography_en.value: A place name in Chūō Ward of Kōbe City (Hyōgo Prefecture) where Ikuta Shrine is located. It is a strategic point for traffic on the San'yōdō, a road leading west along the coast of the Seto Inland Sea. Ikuta Shrine and the surrounding Ikuta Forest are well known. The Ikuta Forest was vast in ancient times, but today, because of the development and urbanization of the nearby area, it has been reduced to a small area inside the boundaries of Ikuta Shrine. The Ikuta River flows through the eastern part of Kōbe City and pours into Ōsaka Bay. This is the setting for the legend of Unai-otome in Man'yōshū and the legend of Ikutagawa in chapter 147 of Yamato Monogatari.

field_topography_ja.value: 兵庫県神戸市中央区の地名で、生田神社の所在地。山陽道の交通の要衝にあり、生田神社およびその周辺に広がる生田森が著名。生田森は古くは広大であったが、現在は周辺地の開発や都市化により大部分が失われ、生田神社境内地として小区画となっている。また、生田川は神戸市の東部を流れ大阪湾に注ぐ川であり、『万葉集』の菟原処女や『大和物語』百四十七段の生田川伝説の舞台となった。

attributes.title: 伊勢

field_history_en.value: Ise was one of the 15 provinces along the Tōkaidō. Serving as the site of Kōtai Jingū (the inner shrine of Ise Shrine) since ancient times, it became a province through the Taika Reform. After being controlled by the Taira, Kitabatake and Oda families, in the Edo period it was divided into six domains (han). In Yamada, which was under the direct control of the shōgun, a magistrate was established. After the abolition of feudal domains and the establishment of prefectures, it became Anotsu, Watarai Prefecture and finally a part of Mie Prefecture in 1876 (Meiji 9). With the popularization of the Ise pilgrimage, which began in the Kamakura period and reached its peak in the middle of the Edo period, the town originally built in front of the torii (Shintō gate) flourished. In Man'yōshū, Ise is collocated with words like “province” (kuni), “sea” (umi), “reed” (hamaogi), and so on. In the second half of the seventh century, the system of shrine princesses (saiō) was established, and this gave rise to tales in verse form (utagatari). Especially famous among them are the story of Kari no Tsukai in Ise Monogatari and the story of imperial consort Akikonomu Chūgū and Rokujō Miyasundokoro (Lady Rokujō) travelling to Ise in the “Sacred Tree” (Sakagi) chapter of Genji Monogatari. From the middle of the Heian period, love poems became prevalent. In the Edo period, the connection with Ise Shrine came to be emphasized in poetry under the influence of the popularity of the Ise pilgrimage.

field_history_ja.value: 東海道十五か国の一つ。古くから皇大神宮の鎮座地として開け、大化改新で一国となる。以後、平、北畠、織田の支配を経て江戸時代は六藩に分かれ、幕府の直轄地山田には奉行が置かれた。廃藩置県後、安濃津、度会県となり、明治九年（一八七六）合併して三重県となる。鎌倉時代に始まり江戸中期に最盛期を迎えた庶民の神宮参詣の風習が普及すると、その鳥居前町としても発展した。『万葉集』では「国」「海」「浜荻」などと連語として用いられ、7世紀後半に斎王制度が確立すると、それにまつわる歌語りが生じた。中でも著名なのは『伊勢物語』の「狩の使ひ」一連の段と、『源氏物語』賢木巻の秋好中宮と六条御息所の伊勢下向であろう。平安中期では恋歌が中心となるが、江戸期の伊勢参り流行の影響で神宮との結びつきが強くなる。

field_topography_en.value: Ise is at the center of Mie Prefecture and is the location of Ise Shrine. It lies at the base of the Shima Peninsula, facing Ise Bay to the north. From the east to the south, a mountainous area extends about 500 meters above sea level, including Asamagatake, Shimaji-yama and Kamigatake. The town developed in the delta of the Miyagawa and Isuzugawa rivers. From ancient times, several transportation routes were constructed and prospered, with the Ise Kaidō road leading to the imperial Ise Shrine at their center. Ise has profoundly influenced Japanese literature, starting with mythology.

field_topography_ja.value: 三重県中部、伊勢神宮の所在地。志摩半島の基部にあって、北は伊勢湾に面し、東から南へ朝熊ヶ岳、島路山、神岳を含む標高500メートル前後の山地が展開する。市街地は宮川と五十鈴川の間の山麓デルタに発達する。古くから神宮に至る伊勢街道を中心に多くの街道が整備され栄え、神話伝説をはじめ日本の文学に深く関わった。

attributes.title: 宇治

field_history_en.value: On the right bank of the Uji River, settlements have existed since ancient times. In the Heian period, the left river bank developed as an area of villas for the court nobility. In the year 646, the first bridge was built. Uji was located about 20 km south of the Heian court, and was on the way to Chōkoku-ji Temple where Kannon was venerated. Emperors paid imperial visits to the villas of Minamoto no Tōru, Fujiwara no Kaneie, Fujiwara no Michinaga and others. Poetry meetings, parties and competitions were also held. In the mid 11th century, the residence of a son of Michinaga’s, Yorimichi, was reconstructed as a temple (Byōdō-in), and in the year 1052, the Phoenix Hall (Hōō-dō) was constructed. In the 12th century, Uji became the main vacation site of the Fujiwara clan. In the year 1180, at the height of the Genpei War, Prince Mochihito and Minamoto no Yorimasa were attacked by the Heike forces at Uji Bridge. Yorimasa committed suicide on the Byōdō-in temple grounds, while Prince Mochihito was taken and killed by the Heike. In the 13th century, Uji became a location for tea plantations and Ashikaga Yoshimitsu became the main patron of tea and tea plantations (the seven famous plantations of Uji of the 16th century). The first Buddhist temple was built in Uji in the 8th century. The temples served as excursion sites for Emperor Kōnin, Emperor Kazan and Emperor Shirakawa. Manpuku-ji, the head temple of the Ōbaku Zen sect, was built by Ingen in 1661.

field_history_ja.value: 宇治川右岸は早い時期から集落が密集し、平安時代になると左岸は貴族の別荘地として発展した。646年に初めて橋が架けられた。平安京から約20㎞ほど離れた場所にあり、観音信仰の聖地である長谷寺（ちょうこくじ）へと向かう途中にある。源融や藤原兼家、藤原道長などの別荘には帝が行幸したり、詩会や歌会などが行われていた。11世紀中頃、道長の息子・頼通の邸宅が寺（平等院）として再建され、1052年には鳳凰堂が建立された。12世紀には藤原家の主要な別荘地となった。源平合戦の最中の1180年には、宇治橋で平家によって以仁王と源頼政が襲撃された。13世紀になると、茶の栽培地となり、足利義満が茶・茶園（16世紀の宇治七名園）の主なパトロンとなった。初めて仏教の寺が建立されたのは8世紀で、光仁天皇・花山天皇・白河天皇の別荘とされた。黄檗宗の寺院・万福寺が1661年に隠元によって建立された。

field_topography_en.value: In the earliest works which mention it, “Uji” was written as follows: 宇遅 in Kojiki (712), 宇治in Harima Fudoki (715), 菟道 in Nihon Shoki (720), and 菟道 , 氏 , and 是  (which is a variant character for 氏) in Man'yōshū (ca. 760). There was a ferry landing on the banks of the Uji River as Uji was a focal point for the traffic on the Hokuriku-dō road of the Nara period (and later the Nara Kaidō road), as well as for traffic from Yamato (Heijō-kyō) to Yamashiro Province. Furthermore, the Uji River itself was an important transportation route connecting Lake Biwa and Naniwa Bay.

attributes.title: 大井川、大堰川

field_history_en.value: The Ōi-gawa and Katsura-gawa flow through Kadono District in Yamashiro Province, which is why they were also called Kadono-gawa in ancient times. The history of the river reaches back to former times. In the Hata-uchi no honkei-chō, which is cited in the Seiji yōryaku, it is mentioned that the Hata-clan built the Kadano ōi (a small weir). It is said that they built the weir to irrigate the area and make it cultivable. After the transfer of the capital in the Heian period, many pilgrimages were made to the weir, making it a place of scenic beauty. From the end of the ninth century the area was often used as a sightseeing spot after Emperor Saga established the Saga-in Temple in this area. Umezu flourished as a river port for unloading timber from the Tanba region, which was an important source for timber. Even in the Middle Ages the river was of great value as a waterway for bringing abundant timber from the Tanba region to Kyōto. Yamaguni no shō in the upper reaches was a famous production site for this timber. In the early modern period in 1606 (Keichō 11) the Hozu-gawa was corrected by Suminokura Ryōi to make the passage between Funai District and Kyōto possible, and since the western Takase-gawa was cut through near the Arashiyama Togetsu-kyō (bridge), the Ōi-gawa was used even more. The area around the river basin also prospered as a lumbering area. Arashi-yama, at the upper reaches of the river is well known as a meisho (famous place) of the Tokugawa period.

field_history_ja.value: 大堰川と桂川は山城国葛野郡を流れるところから古く葛野川ともいった。この川の歴史への登場は古く『政事要略』所引の『秦氏本系帳』には秦氏が葛野大堰を作ったと記されており、堰堤を築いて一帯を灌漑して耕作可能地としたという。平安遷都以後、大堰への行幸は盛んであり、当時から景勝の地であった。嵯峨天皇によってこの地域に嵯峨院が築かれたことをきっかけに、九世紀末からは遊覧の地としてしばしば利用されてくる。また、木材出荷地である丹波地方から木材を荷上げする河港として梅津なども栄えた。中世になってからも京都に丹波地方の豊富な木材をもたらす水運として価値は大きく、上流の山国荘はその生産地として有名であった。近世に至って慶長十一年（一六〇六）に角倉了以が保津川を改修して船井郡と京都との間を通船可能とし、また嵐山渡月橋付近から西高瀬川が開鑿されてからはさらに大堰川の利用度は高くなり、流域付近も材木業地帯として栄えた。

field_topography_en.value: The river flows in a southern direction through the western part of Kyōto City. Its name is also written with the characters “大堰川”. The river is part of the Katsura River, Ōi-gawa is referring to the upper reaches of the Katsura river starting from the Kameoka Basin in Kyōto Prefecture. It originates near Mount Daihi (Daihizan) in the Tanbasan region. Downstream from the Kameoka basin the river is called Hozu-gawa, and from near Togetsukyō (bridge) in Kyōto City it is called Katsura-gawa and it flows into Yodo-gawa.

field_topography_en.value: A general term for the upper reaches of the Saho River north of today’s Nara city center and northeast of the ancient capital of Heijō-kyō. The Saho River originates at Mt. Saho and Mt. Kasuga in the hills north of the Hōren-chō and Hokkeji-chō areas of Nara City. It then traverses the Saho area to the west, turns south at Hokke-ji Temple, passes through Yamato Kōriyama City, merges with the Hase River and eventually flows into the Yamato River. In the Nara period, Saho was a residential area for court nobles. It is on the route of the pilgrimages to Kasuga Taisha Shrine and Hase-dera Temple.

attributes.title: 白川

field_history_en.value: Originally, the Shirakawa flowed north of Kyōto City’s Sanjō Street in a westward direction and united with the Kamo River. By the time of the Shin Aratame Rakuyo Narabini Rakugai no Ezu (Illustrated Map of the Area Surrounding Kyōto) of 1653 (Shōō 2), the main stream of the Shirakawa no longer existed and one of its branches, the Ogawa, had taken its place. The present-day river which branches off southward from the main canal at Keiryū Bridge in front of Heian Shrine (Sakyō Ward), turns west in front of the old gate of Chion-in Temple (Higashiyama Ward) and merges with the Kamogawa Canal north of Shijō Street is also commonly called the Shirakawa. However, this river corresponds to the former Ogawa and is not actually the main stream of the original Shirakawa. From the mid Heian period onward, villas of the nobility and large temples, like the imperial palace of retired emperor Shirakawa and the Rokushō-ji temple complex, were constructed and imperial visits and sightseeing boomed. It was also known as a scenic spot for cherry blossoms, and hanami parties were often held there.

It was also known as a scenic spot for cherry blossoms, and hanami parties were often held there.

field_history_ja.value: 元々は三条通の北を西に流れて鴨川と合流していたが、承応二年（一六五三）の新改洛陽並洛外之図によると白川本流が廃絶しており、それに代わって白川の支流であった小川が、新たに白川とされた。そのため、現在平安神宮（現左京区）前の慶流橋から疏水と分れて南へ流れ、知恩院古門前（現東山区）を西に流れて四条通の北で鴨川運河に合流する川も白川とよぶが、これは昔の小川であり、かつての白川本流ではない。平安中期以降、白川院の御所や六勝寺などの貴族の別業や大寺院が造営され、行幸や遊覧が盛んであった。また、桜の名所としても知られており、花見の宴などもよく行われた。

field_topography_en.value: A river that originated between Mt. Hiei and Mt. Nyoigatake, flowed through Kitashirakawa to the southwest and merged with the Kamo River. The name also referred to the area of the Shirakawa river basin east of the Kamo River (today’s Sakyō Ward and Higashiyama Ward in Kyōto City). Today's Shirakawa originates in Yamanaka-chō (Ōtsu City), flows along the Yamanakagoe mountain pass, then continues southwestward from the northeastern edge of Kitashirakawa (Sakyō Ward, Kyōto City). From the northeast of Mt. Yoshida it flows south through the Shishigatani valley, arrives at the west of Nanzen-ji Temple and pours into the Lake Biwa Canal. The river basin consists of strata of white river sand and pebbles such as granite, leading to the origin of the name Shirakawa (white river). Biotite granite stones collected from the Shirakawa are a specialty of the region. The Shirakawa forms the Kitashirakawa alluvial fan as it pours out from between the mountains. Many archaeological discoveries from the Jōmon period have been made here.

field_topography_ja.value: 比叡山と如意が岳の間に発し、北白河を西南に流れ、鴨川と合流していた川。また、その川の流域の鴨川以東一帯（現在の京都市左京区・東山区）の地名でもあった。現在の白川は比叡山と如意が岳の間、山中や村（現大津市）に発し、山中越に沿って北白川（現左京区）の東北端から西南流、吉田山の北東から鹿ヶ谷を南流して南禅寺の西に至り、琵琶湖疏水に注いでいる。白川の名は流域一帯が花崗岩を含む礫質砂層で、川砂がために白砂であることによるという。また川から採れる白川石は特産とされる。山間を抜けでた白川は北白川扇状地を形成する。縄文時代の遺跡も多く発見されている。

attributes.title: 須磨

field_history_en.value: This place name has been used in waka poems since the times of the Man'yōshū. In the Kokinshū, there is a poem “If from time to time/ anyone should ask after/ me   answer them this/ on Suma Bay with tear-drenched/ sleeves I gather seaweed salt” by Ariwara no Yukihira entitled "Sent to someone at court during the time Yukihira was staying away at the place called Suma in Tsu Province after some incident in the reign of Tamura."(English translation respectively by Rodd, Laurel Rasplica; and Henkenius, Mary Catherine (1984): p.325-326), which suggests that he was living a secluded life in Suma. The image of Suma as a place of exile for an innocent nobleman was carried over into the Suma and Akashi volumes of the Genji monogatari. From the end of the Heian period to the Middle Ages, the area was often the scene of battles.

field_history_ja.value: 古く『万葉集』から和歌に詠まれた地名である。『古今集』にみえる「田村の御時に、事にあたりて津の国の須磨といふ所にこもり侍りけるに、宮の内に侍りける人につかはしける」と題した在原行平の「わくらばにとふ人あらば須磨の浦にもしほたれつつわぶとこたへよ」という歌から、彼が須磨に蟄居していたらしいことがうかがえる。この無実の貴公子が沈淪する流謫の地というイメージは、『源氏物語』須磨・明石巻へと継承されていくこととなる。平安末期から中世にかけてはしばしば合戦の舞台ともなった。

field_topography_en.value: An area at the southwestern end of the Rokkō mountain where the mountain massif approaches the coastline. It is located at the southeastern foot of Mount Hachibuse and Mount Tekkai and lies on the coast of Ōsaka Bay vis-à-vis Awaji Island. In former times it was also written with the characters ”須麻”, “陬麻”, “須馬” and “須間”. It was a key transport and military location in the south-west corner of Settsu Province at the westernmost point of the Kinai region. The area lies on the San’yō-dō (road), which leads to Harima Province and where Suma-eki (Suma station) and Suma-seki (Suma barrier) were located since the times of the Ritsuryō system.

field_topography_ja.value: 六甲山地の南西端、山塊が海岸線に迫る地域。鉢伏山・鉄拐山南東麓に位置し、大阪湾を隔てて淡路島に対する。古く須麻・陬麻・須馬・須間などとも表記される。摂津国の南西隅、畿内の最西端にあたる交通・軍事上の要衝で、山陽道が播磨国へと通じ、律令制下では須磨駅や須磨関が置かれた。

attributes.title: 住吉

field_history_en.value: Since ancient times, Sumiyoshi evoked the image of the sea coast. Furthermore, the deity of Suminoe was initially worshipped as the guardian of seafarers and a god of war. This goes back to the ninth book of Nihon Shoki, which states that the boats of Empress Jingū heading to attack Silla were protected by the gods Sokotsutsu no O no Mikoto, Nakatsutsu no O no Mikoto, and Uwatsutsu no O no Mikoto who were worshipped here. However, the deity of Sumiyoshi is characterized in chapter 117 of Ise Monogatari and in the first book of Fukurozōshi as composing poems. In the late Heian period, the deity came to be worshipped as the god of poetry, and some poems in the Shūishū, Shinkokinshū and other waka collections are ascribed divine authorship [shin’ei].

field_history_ja.value: 古くから、海辺のイメージで捉えられてきた。また、住吉の神は当初、航海安全の神・軍神として祀られた。これは『日本書紀』巻九に、新羅の戦いへ向かう神功皇后の船を守護した底筒男命・中筒男命・表筒男命を祀ったとあることによる。しかし、『伊勢物語』一一七段や『袋草紙』上巻に和歌を詠む住吉の神の姿が描かれ、さらに『拾遺集』『新古今集』などに神詠が採られるなど、平安後期には歌神として崇拝されるようになっていった。

field_topography_en.value: Corresponds to today’s Sumiyoshi Ward in Ōsaka City. It is said that Sumiyoshi Shrine once stood right by the sea. Several explanations and theories exist concerning the orthography and readings of suminoe and sumiyoshi. According to Kojikiden (Motoori Norinaga, late 18th century), the original place name was Suminoe: “Pronouncing Sumiyoshi [住吉] as ‘su-mi-yo-shi’ is a later development. Up to the Nara period, it was read only as ‘su-mi-no-e.’” Multiple characters were used to write the name, among them 墨江, 清江, and 住吉. It is thought that gradually, the most commonly used characters became 住吉, and these came to be read as “su-mi-yo-shi” in the Heian period. Though this theory is not without its inconsistencies, the characters 住吉 were normally read as su-mi-yo-shi in classical times and the Middle Ages.

field_topography_ja.value: 現在の大阪市住吉区の一帯。かつては住吉神社のすぐ近くまで海があったとされる。 「すみのえ」「すみよし」の表記・訓については様々な解釈や説が出されているが、「古事記伝」の「住吉を須美与志と唱るは、後世のことにて那良のころまでは、須美能延とのみ云り」という記述以来、地名の発生としては「すみのえ」が古く、墨江・清江・住吉など種々の字があてられたが、しだいに住吉の表記が一般化し、平安時代になると「すみよし」と読むことになった、とされる。しかし、この通説はすべてに適用することはできない。中古・中世の古訓では「住吉」は文字どおりに「すみよし」と訓読されることが多い。

attributes.title: 末の松山

field_history_en.value: In the Kana preface (kanajo) of the Kokinshū, the Jōgan tsunami in the year Jōgan 11 (869) was referred to as the Wave of Matsuyama. The tsunami did not reach Sue no matsuyama and it was passed on as a place of refuge from earthquakes and tsunami. This was then transmitted to the capital and included in waka poetry. It has been famous since ancient times as an utamakura signifying vows of love. It is also known as Sue no matsu and Matsuyama. In the Kokinshū, there are two poems: “The snow falling near the coast makes it seem as if waves were passing over Sue no Matsuyama” (Winter poems, 326, Fujiwara no Okikaze) and “Before I would ever leave you and have a fickle heart, the waves would have crossed over Sue no Matsuyama” (Azumauta, 1093). Afterwards the utamakura was developed into two directions: landscape poetry based on the style of Fujiwara no Okikaze and love poetry based on the Azumauta. Although there are cases where it is used in festive poems, most poems are about the promise and impermanence of love, such as the poem “If I think how we exchanged love vows I wring my sleeves (drenched with tears). How could have the waves passed over Sue no matsuyama” (Love poems, 770, Kiyohara no Motosuke) in the Goshūishū. As for its location, the Ōgishō describes Sue no Matsuyama as being far from the coast, which is consistent with its current location. This description was later adopted by poetic treatises. The Shūchūshō, based on the Ōgishō, relays the location of Sue no matsuyama as being in Mutsu. The inscription on the bell of the local Hachiman Shrine, dated the second month of Einin 7 (1299) (cited in the Hōnai fudoki), reads Ōshū Sue no matsuyama Hachimangū. This record provides evidence, that the lore of Sue no matsuyama was firmly established in this area at the end of the thirteenth century.

field_history_ja.value: 『古今集』仮名序では貞観11年（869年）の貞観津波は「松山の波」として取り上げられた。このとき「末の松山」のある小山には津波が届かなかったことから、地震と津波の避難地として「末の松山」が伝承され、それが都に伝わって和歌の中に詠み込まれたという。古くから恋の誓いをかける歌枕として有名である。「末の松」「松山」とも詠まれる。『古今集』では、「浦ちかくふりくる雪は白浪の末の松山こすかとぞ見る」（冬歌・326・藤原興風）と「君をおきてあだし心をわが持たば末の松山波も越えなむ」（東歌・1093）との二首がある。その後興風の歌風に基づく風景詠と、東歌にみられる愛をめぐる詠風との二つの方向に継承されていく。賀歌に詠まれる例もあるが、多くは『後拾遺集』における「契りきなかたみに袖をしぼりつつ末の松山波越さじとは」（恋四・770・元輔）のように、恋の契り、恋の無常を詠む歌の素材となった。その場所について、『奥義抄』に「末の松山」が海岸から離れているとの記述があり、現在の伝承地に符合している。この記述はのち歌論に引継がれていく。『袖中抄』は、『奥義抄』を踏まえながら、「顕昭云、すゑの松山とは陸奥にあり」と記す。当地の八幡社（沖八幡）の永仁七年（一二九九）二月日の紀年をもつ鐘銘（「封内風土記」所引）に「奥州末松山八幡宮」とあった。この記録は一三世紀末、「末の松山」の伝承が、当地に定着していたことの証拠となる。

field_topography_en.value: There is a theory that this place name refers to the Namiuchi Pass between Ichinohe and Fukuoka in Iwate Prefecture, but the more famous theory has been that it refers to the mountain Sue no matsuyama behind Hōkoku-ji in Tagajō City. It is the latter that Matsuo Bashō visited in Oku no hosomichi. Today, two huge pine trees tower behind the Hōkoku-ji and there is also a memorial stone with the poem of Kiyohara no Motosuke: “Have we not pledged, wringing our tear drained sleeves as remembrance, never shall a wave pass over Sue no matsuyama” [never shall our emotions change], which is also included in the Hyakunin isshu,

attributes.title: 長柄の橋

field_history_en.value: Since ancient times, there are many legends concerning the construction of the bridge. It is sometimes speculated that the bridge was built as a passage to the imperial court around the period from Taika 1 to Shuchō 1 (645-686), when Emperor Kōtoku's palace was established in Naniwa no Nagara no Toyosaki no Miya, but the truth is uncertain. The first reliable source is Nihon Kōki, which reports on the reconstruction of the bridge. There are theories that the initial construction took place from about the Jinki era to the Tenpyō era (742-749), while other theories date it even earlier to the period of Empress Suiko. After several destructions and reconstructions, the bridge built in the Kōnin era was destroyed after 40 years. Thereafter, although the bridge no longer actually existed, the utamakura “Nagara no hashi” became established and widely used. Furthermore, legends about human sacrifice (hitobashira) connected to the bridge spread. In 1873 (Meiji 6), a bridge called Toyosaki Bridge was constructed in approximately the same place as Nagara Bridge’s current location. It was overhauled in 1909 (Meiji 42) when the Shin'yodo River was dug. Later, in 1936 (Shōwa 11), the bridge was reconstructed, but at the end of the Second World War the pillars of the bridge were damaged in an air raid that caused many deaths. Finally, in 1983 (Shōwa 58), today’s Nagara Bridge was completed.

field_history_ja.value: 古代以来、架橋に関する伝が多く、孝徳天皇の宮殿が難波長柄豊埼宮に置かれていた大化元年～朱鳥元年（645～686）頃、皇居への道として架橋されたとされているが定かではない。確実性の高い文献の初出としては『日本後紀』があるが、これは再建についての記事であり、創架を神亀・天平（742～749）の頃に求める説や、さらに古く推古天皇期に求める説もある。幾度かの損壊と再架を繰り返し、弘仁の架橋40年で廃絶した。以降、橋は実在しないものの、歌枕としての「長柄の橋」が定着し広く詠まれるようになり、また橋にまつわる人柱伝説も人口に膾炙した。明治6年（1873）に現在地とほぼ同じ位置に「豊崎橋」という橋が架けられたのは明治42年（1909）の新淀川開削の際のことである。その後昭和11年（1936）に架け替えられるが、第二次世界大戦末期に爆撃のため橋桁が損傷し、多くの犠牲者を出した。そして昭和58年（1983）、現在の長柄橋が完成することとなる。

field_topography_en.value: From ancient times, this name has been widely known. However, the original location of the Nagara Bridge is unclear. One finds different accounts from ancient times. Nihon Kōki, scroll 22, Emperor Saga, Kōnin 3 (813), third day of the sixth month states, “He had a bridge built at Nagara, in Settsu province.” Montoku Jitsuroku, Ninju 3 (853), tenth month, reports that the bridges at Nagara and Mikuni broke down (in a flood) and that men and horses could not pass. It is assumed that the bridge was originally situated where the Shin'yodogawa and Yodogawa (Ōkawa) rivers branch off in the downstream section of the Yodo River. Moreover, it is thought that before the river regulations of 1896 (Meiji 29), the name Nagara referred to the fork in the river where the Nakatsugawa and Yodogawa rivers diverged. In the Nagara no Funase no Honki [Records of the Harbor in Nagara] in Sumiyoshi Taisha Jindaiki [Records of the Gods of Sumiyoshi Grand Shrine], the four sides of the harbor of Nagara are described as follows: “To the east, Takase and Ōba, to the south Ōe, to the west Tomobuchi, to the north Kawagishi.” It is also noted that “when the emperor wished to construct a mooring place on the right side of the harbor for boats loaded with tribute for missions to China, he told the grand deity, ‘I am going to build a harbor in Nagara.’” Goods bound for China were transported along the Yodo River system and loaded onto ships here. The bridge that is called Nagara Bridge today was completed in 1983 (Shōwa 58). It spans the Shin'yodo River in the former Ōyodo Ward (today’s Kita Ward) in Ōsaka city. From Kunijima station of the Hankyū railway line, it is possible to cross the bridge on foot in about seventeen minutes.

field_topography_ja.value: 古くから広くその名が知られているが、元々の橋の位置は明らかになっていない。古くは『日本後紀』巻22嵯峨天皇 弘仁３年（813）6月3日に「遣使造摂津国長柄橋」、『文徳実録』仁寿3年（853）10月に「長柄三国両河、頃年橋梁断絶、人馬不通」という記述がみられる。淀川下流域の新淀川と淀川（大川）の分岐点であり、明治29年（1896）の淀川改修以前の中津川と淀川の分岐点辺りを称したと考えられる。『住吉大社神代記』の「長柄の船瀬の本記」に長柄の船瀬（港津）の四至を記して「東限高瀬大庭 南限大江 西限鞆淵 北限川岸」とあり、「右船瀬泊は、遣唐貢調使の調物（みつぎ）を積む船舫（ふね）の泊（とまり）を造らんものと、天皇の念行（おもほへる）時に、大神の訓へ賜はく、「我長柄船瀬を造りて進（たてまつ）らむ」（原漢文）と記される。淀川水系で運ばれた荷物が、ここで遣唐船に積込まれた。現在長柄の橋と呼ばれている橋は、昭和58年に完成したものである。大阪市大淀区の新淀川に架かっており、阪急柴島駅から徒歩17分程度で渡ることが可能となっている。

attributes.title: 初瀬、長谷

field_history_en.value: In the Kojiki, Hatsuse (泊瀬) was mentioned in the section on Emperor Ingyō, while Hase (長谷) was mentioned in the section of Emperor Yūryaku and Emperor Buretsu. In the Man’yōshū there are several examples of poems on Hatsuse, like two poems in book 3: ”Is it not that the jade cord wrapped around the hand of Hatsuse Otome is broken and in disarray?“ and “In the midst of the cold wind, while lamenting I wander along the riverside, but I meet no one who even resembles the way you walk when we used to walk together.” (424, 425). In the Man’yōshū Hatsuse was described only in terms of its natural beauty, but in the Heian period (794-1185), it was also used in poetry as a famous place for cherry blossoms and other flowers. Ki no Tsurayuki’s poem “The state of human/ hearts I cannot know and yet/ the blossoms of this/ familiar village still greet/ me with the scent of years past” with its introduction “One day the poet came, after a long absence, to a house where he often lodged on his pilgrimages to Hatsuse. The host sarcastically sent a message saying there was always room at his inn. Tsurayuki plucked a branch from a flowering plum by the door and composed this poem” (English translation by Rodd, Laurel Rasplica; and Henkenius, Mary Catherine (1984): p. 61) mentions plum blossom, included in Kokinwakashū (Spring vol. 1, 42) and selected for Hyakunin isshu. In addition to waka poems the name Hase appears also in Kagerō nikki, Genji monogatari, Sarashina nikki, and other monogatari, zuihitsu, setsuwa, nikki, Nō (yōkyoku), travelogues (kikō) and records about pilgrimages (sankei-ki). As to the pronunciation of the name, the Wamyō ruijushō gives the transliteration with the characters 波都勢 and records the reading “hatsuse”. The Man’yō daishō-ki by Keichū and Kojiki-den by Motoori Norinaga also mention the problem, but nowadays it is pronounced “hase”.

field_history_ja.value:
古くは、『古事記』允恭天皇段に「泊瀬」、雄略天皇段、武烈天皇段では「長谷」の表記でその名が見える。
『万葉集』では巻三に、「こもりくの　はつせをとめが　てにまける　たまはみだれて　ありといはずやも」、「かはかぜの　さむきはつせを　なげきつつ　きみがあるくに　にるひともあへや」(424、425)の二首があるほか、いくつか用例を確認することができる。『万葉集』における初瀬は、ただその自然のみを歌に詠んでいたが、平安時代に入ると桜やそれ以外の花の名所 としても詠まれるようになった。紀貫之の「はつせにまうづるごとにやどりける人の家にひさしくやどらで、ほどへてのちにいたれりければ、かの家のあるじかくさだかになむやどりはあるといひいだして侍りければ、そこにたてりけるむめの花ををりてよめる」の「人はいさ心もしらずふるさとは花ぞ昔のかににほひける」（『古今和歌集』・春上・42）とある歌では梅を詠んでおり、『百人一首』にも選ばれている 。また、和歌以外にも『蜻蛉日記』や『更級日記』、『源氏物語』などの物語作品、随筆・説話・日記類、謡曲や紀行・参詣記などにも初瀬（長谷）の名が記されている。
初瀬（長谷）の名義について、『和名類聚抄』には「波都勢」の訓注を用いてハツセ、とある。契沖の『万葉代匠記』、本居宣長の『古事記伝』など様々な作品で名義についての記述を確認することができるが、現在はハセ、と発音されている。

field_topography_en.value: Present-day Hatsuse Town, Sakurai City, Nara Prefecture. The gorge was surrounded on three sides: apart from Hatsuseyama, it was surrounded by Makimuku-yama and Miwa-yama on the other side and thirdly by Tenjin-yama and Torimi-yama. It was also a major point on the traffic route leading to Iga and Ise Provinces. It is said to have been the location of the palaces of Emperor Buretsu and Emperor Yūryaku in ancient times. Hatsuse is also known as the location of Hase-dera, which was a famous place for pilgrimage (Hase mōde).

attributes.title: 松浦

field_history_en.value: Until about the 8th century, Matsura was used only for the area of the Tamashima River (also called the Matsura River) in today's Higashi-Matsuura District of Saga Prefecture. In Hizen no Kuni Fudoki (first half of the 8th century), Wamyō Ruijushō (c. 931-938) and other works, it is recorded that the Matsura District had been established and expanded to refer to present-day Matsura, which includes the Gotō Archipelago. In the Middle Ages, the names Kami-Matsura and Shimo-Matsura were used. After the reforms of the Meiji era, Kami-Matsura became today’s Higashi-Matsuura and Nishi-Matsuura Districts in Saga Prefecture, Shimo-Matsura became today’s Minami-Matsuura and Kita-Matsuura Districts in Nagasaki Prefecture, and “Matsura” came to be pronounced “Matsu-ura.”

field_history_ja.value: 八世紀ころまでは「まつら」は現在の佐賀県東松浦郡玉島川（別名松浦川）・松浦川流域に限定して用いられていた。『肥前国風土記』（8Ｃ前半頃）『和名類聚抄』（931～938頃）などには松浦郡が置かれていたことが記されており、その範囲は五島列島を含む現在の松浦と呼称される地域に拡大されていたことがわかる。中世には上松浦・下松浦の呼称が用いられ、上松浦は明治以後の佐賀県東松浦郡・西松浦郡、下松浦は長崎県南松浦郡・北松浦郡一帯を指し、「まつうら」と呼称されている。

field_topography_en.value: The collective name of areas of the shoreline of the northwestern part of Hizen Province (today’s Saga Prefecture and Nagasaki Prefecture). From ancient times, it was a strategic point for sea routes to China and Korea and also served as a base for envoys to China (kentōshi). “Matsura no Kuni” [末盧国] is first seen in Gishi Wajinden (around the 3rd century A.D.), while Kojiki (712) refers to “Matsura no Agata” [末羅県]. “Matsura” was also written with the characters 松浦, which eventually became the standard name used in works like Nihon Shoki (720) [松浦, 松浦県] and Man'yōshū (about 760) [松浦県, 松浦河].

attributes.title: 三笠

field_history_en.value: The mountain’s form, similar to a bamboo hat or umbrella (kasa), inspired the name Mt. Mikasa. It is first mentioned in Shoku Nihongi in the entry for the first year of the Yōrō era (717) on the first day of the second month. In Kokinshū, the poem “When I gaze far out across the plain of heaven, I see the same moon that came up over the hill of Mikasa at Kasuga” (Kokinshū Travel 406, transl. McCullough, p. 97), composed by Abe no Nakamaro, is famous. In the Heian period, an umbrella held over people of high rank, starting with the emperor, was called mi-kasa, while the government office of the imperial guards (konoe-fu) who guarded the emperor was called Mikasayama. In poems, these high officials of the imperial guard are also called Mikasayama. In the early modern period, the written representation was simplified from 御蓋山 to 三笠山. Gradually, it became conflated with Mt. Wakakusa because the two are adjacent and Mt. Wakakusa has a three-layered shape. In December 1935 (Shōwa 10), the distinction between Mikasayama and Wakakusayama was reestablished when Prince Takahito was conferred the title Mikasa no Miya.

field_history_ja.value: 三笠山は、蓋（笠）に似ていることからその名がついた。文献における初出は『続日本紀』養老元年（717）2月1日条である。和歌では『古今集』収載、阿倍仲麿の「あまの原ふりさけ見ればかすがなるみかさの山にいでし月かも」（羈旅歌・406）に詠まれているのが有名である。平安時代には、天皇をはじめ高貴な人にさしかける天蓋を御笠と称するのと掛けて、天子を警護する近衛府の高官を「三笠山」と呼ぶようになり、和歌でも近衞府の高官を「三笠山」と称して詠まれるようにもなる。表記は、近世に「御蓋山」をやさしくして「三笠山」とするのが一般化したが、次第に若草山と混同されるようになった。これはおそらく三笠山と若草山が隣接していることと、若草山の形状が三層になっていることに起因する。この混同は昭和10年（1935）12月、崇仁親王の宮号に三笠山が使われた際に若草山と三笠山の区別が確立した。

attributes.title: 武蔵

field_history_en.value: From ancient to medieval times, no relevant changes occurred with respect to the borders of Musashi Province. However, from the end of the Middle Ages to the beginning of the early modern period, there were territorial transfers with Kōzuke and Shimōsa Provinces. The area incorporated from Shimōsa Province became Katsushika District of Musashi Province (one section was incorporated into Saitama District). Today, the north half belongs more or less to Saitama Prefecture, while the south half belongs to the Tōkyō metropolitan area and Kanagawa Prefecture. “A gromwell’s / Single stem is reason enough: / Musashi Plain’s / Grasses, all are / Dear to me, indeed” (Kokinshū, miscellaneous 1, 867, anonymous) [translation by wakapoetry.net] is a famous poem, and references to it can be found in Ise Monogatari and Genji Monogatari. Furthermore, at the beginning of the Kamakura period (13.c.), there are several setsuwa with the subject of Musashi Province in the Kokon Chomonjū, Shasekishū, Hosshinshū and others. Apart from setsuwa, Gofukakusa-in Nijō (Dainagon Minamoto Masatada no Musume, Kamakura period), who had traveled to various places, wrote observations about Musashi Province in an elegant literary style in her autobiographical work Towazugatari.

field_history_ja.value: 古代・中世においては国境に大きな変化はなかったとみられるが、中世末から近世初期にかけて上野国・下総国との間で異動があり、下総国から編入された地域は新たに武蔵国葛飾郡となった（一部は埼玉郡に編入）。現在はおよそ北半分は埼玉県、南半分は東京都および神奈川県に属する。「紫のひともとゆゑに武蔵野の草はみながらあはれとぞ見る」（古今集・雑上・八六七・よみ人しらず）は有名で、『伊勢物語』や『源氏物語』にもこの和歌を踏まえた表現が見られる。さらに時代が下って鎌倉時代に入ると『古今著聞集』『沙石集』『発心集』などに武蔵国に題材を求めた説話がいくつか収録されるようになる。説話の他にも各地を遍歴した後深草院二条（大納言源雅忠女。鎌倉時代）の自伝的作品『とはずがたり』には武蔵国における見聞が流麗な筆致で描かれている。

attributes.title: 最上

field_history_en.value: An utamakura of Dewa Province in the Tohoku region. From ancient times, transportation by ship developed and many poems were composed on the basis of the poem Inabune: “Rice boats rowing up and down the Mogami River / it is not that I dislike you, just wait another month” (Kokinshū). Many poems were composed about the Mogami River, but most of them had no connection to the actual landscape. The inabune motif is often used for introducing the word ina (meaning both “rice plant” [稲] and “no” [否]). Examples include the following poem from Sukeyukishū: “All the rice boats are gone / all the rice from the boats is spent. If one is used to seeing them on the Mogami River, it looks as though they were there.” The image of boats going up and down the river was also used as a metaphor for rising and falling fortunes: “I am rising and falling in rank / as though I were ascending and descending Mt. Kurai / though I am not even a boat rowing on the Mogami River” (Hirota no Yashiro no Utaawase, Sanetsuna).

field_topography_en.value: The name refers mainly to the Mogami River. Designated by the Japanese government as a waterway of special importance, the river originates on the north side of Mt. Azuma in the southern tip of Yamagata Prefecture. It flows through the Yonezawa, Nagai, Yamagata and Shinjō Basins, uniting all the rivers in these basins before entering the Shōnai Plain. It continues in a northwestern direction across the plain and flows into the Sea of Japan at Sakata City. The main river has a length of 224.4 kilometers, while the total length including its tributaries is 2570 kilometers. The river basin area is 7042.6 square kilometers. Known for its rapid flow, it has been an important shipping transport route since ancient times. In Mogami Gorge, there are more than 40 waterfalls of various sizes. Among these, the Shiraito Falls have been renowned since ancient times.

attributes.title: 吉野

field_history_en.value:
In the 7th century, there was an imperial villa in the Yoshino River basin near Miyataki. During the Jinshin war (672), Ōama no Ōji (Emperor Tenmu) used Yoshino as his base. From the reign of Empress Jitō, the widow of Tenmu, it was revered as a sacred place and became the site of several imperial visits. Mt. Yoshino was not a common poetic motif in Man’yōshū, but became one from the Heian period onward. The motif of Mt. Yoshino conjures up the image of a secluded, isolated life, as in the poem, “I long for a house in the wilds beyond the hills of fair Yoshino – a hidden dwelling to use when the world is hard to bear” (Kokinshū, miscellaneous 2, No. 950, anonymous) (transl. McCullough, p. 208). From the Heian period, Mt. Yoshino also became a motif for a place covered in thick snow. “In dawn’s first dim light we might almost mistake them for morning moonbeams – the snowflakes newly fallen from Yoshino-no-sato.” (Kokinshū, winter, No. 332, Korenori) (transl. McCullough, p. 80) is the first famous example of this. From then on, combining Mt. Yoshino and snow became a poetic convention.

In the time of Man'yōshū, the Yoshino River was used in poems far more frequently than Mt. Yoshino. A well known example is, “Long though I gaze, Never shall I tire of Yoshino, Within whose stream The water-moss grows smooth forever, As I shall come to view these sights anew” (Man'yōshū, book one, 37) (translation by Edwin A. Cranston, 1993). (Alternately, “Like the eternal moss slick by the Yoshino River, on which I do not tire to gaze, may I never cease to return and gaze on it again”  transl. Levy, p. 57.) This poem was composed by Kakinomoto no Hitomaro on the occasion when he accompanied an imperial visit to Yoshino. In this poem, the image of Yoshino as a sacred site is expressed through the purity of the river flowing incessantly.

field_history_ja.value:
7世紀には吉野川流域の宮滝付近に離宮が営まれた。壬申の乱に際して大海人皇子（天武天皇）がここを拠点としたこともあって、天武天皇の妻・持統天皇の御代以降聖地として顧みられ、しばしば行幸が行われた。平安時代に入ると万葉時代とは異なり、吉野山も盛んに詠まれるようになる。「み吉野の山のあなたに宿もがな世の憂き時の隠れ家にせむ」（古今集・雑下・九五〇・よみ人しらず）のように、吉野山は人も通わぬ隠棲の地のイメージを持つことになる。くわえて吉野山が雪深い地として詠まれるようになるのも、平安時代以降であった。「朝ぼらけ有明の月と見るまでに吉野の里に降れる白雪」（古今集・冬・三三二・是則）の名歌をはじめ、『古今集』以後は吉野山と雪の組み合わせが常套となった。

万葉時代には吉野山よりも吉野川のほうが、圧倒的に多く和歌に詠まれた。吉野川の例としては、柿本人麻呂が行幸従駕の際に詠んだ「見れど飽かぬ吉野の川の常滑の絶ゆることなくまたかへり見む」（万葉集・巻一・三七）が有名だが、この歌は吉野の「聖地」としてのイメージが、流れの絶えない川の清浄さによって象徴されている。

field_topography_en.value: Utamakura of Yamato Province corresponding to today's Yoshino District in Nara Prefecture. Mt. Yoshino and the Yoshino River are particularly well known. In former times, the term Yoshinoyama referred not only to today’s Mt. Yoshino, but also included Kinpusen, Mikumariyama, Takagiyama, and Aonegamine. The Yoshino River originates at Ōdaigahara, runs through Miyataki, Kamiichi, Shimoichi, and Gojō, and changes its name to Kinokawa when it enters Kii Province (today’s Wakayama Prefecture).

attributes.title: 小倉

field_history_en.value: Ogura [小倉] was also written 小蔵, 雄蔵 and 小椋. It appears as an utamakura in treatises on poetry such as Nōin Utamakura, Godaishū Utamakura, Waka Shogakushō and Yakumo Mishō. On the occasion of the imperial visit of Emperor Uda to the Ōi River, Teishinkō (Fujiwara no Tadahira) composed the poem, “Oh autumn leaves on the peak of Mt. Ogura, if you have a feeling heart, stay on until the next imperial visit” (Shūishū, book of miscellaneous autumn poems, 1128). Ogura is a meisho for autumn leaves. Fujiwara no Kintō also composed poetry about the autumn leaves of Mt. Ogura, and it is recorded in Ōkagami how highly he praised them. In the Kamakura period, Fujiwara no Teika had a mountain villa built in Ogura.

field_topography_en.value: A mountain in the west of Saga, Ukyō Ward, Kyōto City. With the Ōi River (Katsura River) flowing at its southwestern foot, Mt. Ogura forms a picturesque landscape facing Arashiyama on the other side of the river. At its northeastern foot is Adashino, at its eastern foot the Sagano area and the famous temple Nison-in. The lower southeastern reaches of the mountain are referred to as Kameyama. Elevation is 283.7 meters above sea level.

attributes.title: 白河の関

field_history_en.value: Shirakawa no Seki was a barrier set up at the border with Shimotsuke Province and is known together with Nakoso no Seki (Iwaki City, Fukushima Prefecture) and Nezu ga Seki (Atsumi-machi, Yamagata Prefecture) as one of three great barriers of northeastern Japan. Its first appearance in waka is thought to be a Shūishū poem by Taira no Kanemori (Miscellaneous, 339) with the title “After crossing the barrier of Shirakawa in Michinoku”: “If only I could, I would send word to the capital, a message that I have crossed the Shirakawa Barrier” [Arokay]. In the Goshūishū (Travel, 518), there is a poem by Nōin with the preface, “When he went to Mutsu Province, he composed the following poem at the Shirakawa Barrier”: “I left the capital together with the spring haze, and now, autumn winds are blowing at Shirakawa Barrier” [Arokay]. Surprisingly, the Kokon Chomonjū reports that this poem was in fact composed in the capital, and that Nōin, who took delight in elegant pursuits, had just pretended to have traveled to the northern provinces.

Its first appearance in waka is thought to be a Shūishū poem by Taira no Kanemori (Miscellaneous, 339) with the title “After crossing the barrier of Shirakawa in Michinoku”: “If only I could, I would send word to the capital, a message that I have crossed the Shirakawa Barrier” [Arokay]. In the Goshūishū (Travel, 518), there is a poem by Nōin with the preface, “When he went to Mutsu Province, he composed the following poem at the Shirakawa Barrier”: “I left the capital together with the spring haze, and now, autumn winds are blowing at Shirakawa Barrier” [Arokay]. Surprisingly, the Kokon Chomonjū reports that this poem was in fact composed in the capital, and that Nōin, who took delight in elegant pursuits, had just pretended to have traveled to the northern provinces.

field_history_ja.value: 白川関は下野国との境界に設置された関で、勿来の関（福島県いわき市）、念珠の関（山形県温海町）とともに奥羽三関として知られる。和歌での初例は「みちのくにの白河の関越え侍りつるに」という詞書をもつ「たよりあらばいかで都へつげやらむ今日白河の関は越えぬと」（拾遺集・別・三三九・兼盛）と思われる。また『後拾遺集』には「陸奥国にまかり下りけるに、白河の関にてよみ侍りける」という詞書で能因法師の「都をば霞とともに立ちしかど秋風ぞ吹く白河の関」が載るが（後拾遺集・羇旅・五一八・能因法師）、『古今著聞集』ではこの歌は本当は都で詠まれたものであり、風流好みの能因が陸奥国にいった態を装い、この歌を披露したと伝える。

field_topography_en.value: The barrier of Shirakawa is supposed to have been located in either the Hatajuku or Shirasaka area of Shirakawa City in Fukushima Prefecture. Today, it is the former location that has been designated as the National Historical Site of the Shirakawa Barrier. It is situated at the uppermost reaches of the Yashiro River, a tributary of the Abukuma River. The border with Tochigi Prefecture lies three kilometers to the south. The archaeological site is located on the upper slope of a solitary hill along a long and narrow valley. This hill stretches about 140 m from east to west and 180 m from north to south, with a relative elevation of about 13 m. Shirakawa Shrine stands at the top. This site was called Seki no Mori (barrier woods) from ancient times, and in 1800 (Kansei 12), the lord of the Shirakawa Domain, Matsudaira Sadanobu, had a stone monument erected to commemorate the ancient barrier. Together with Nakoso no Seki and Nezu ga Seki, it is one of the three great barriers of the Ōu region (today’s Tohoku region) of Japan.

field_topography_ja.value: 現在の福島県白河市旗宿、もしくは白坂の地に比定されているが、前者が「白河関跡」として国指定史跡となっている。阿武隈川支流の社川最上流部にあり、南へ約三キロで栃木県境に達する。遺跡は山間の細長い谷地形にある独立丘陵の頂部から斜面部にかけて立地し、この丘は東西約一四〇メートル・南北約一八〇メートル、比高約一三メートル。丘の上には白河神社が祀られている。当地は古くから関ノ森とよばれ、白河藩主松平定信によって寛政一二年（一八〇〇）に古関蹟碑が建てられている。勿来の関・念珠の関とともに奥羽三関の一つに数えられる。

field_history_en.value: Known for its picturesque scenery since ancient times, many poems have been composed about Nagara. Among them, two are particularly well known. The first is, “Rippling waves! While the capital in Shiga has fallen into ruins, the cherry blossoms on Nagarayama are still as in olden times” (Senzaishū), composed by Taira no Tadanori when he fled from the capital. The second is, “Long standing as the rippling waves at Mount Nagara, should be the joy in this imperial reign” (Shūishū) by Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu.

field_topography_en.value: A mountain in Shiga District, Ōmi Province (today’s Ōtsu City, Shiga Prefecture) towering to the west of Mii-dera Temple, reaching Mt. Ausaka in the south and connecting the summits of Shiga with Mt. Hiei in the north. Its elevation is 354 meters above sea level. The mountain is the site of the Mausoleum of Emperor Kōbun. Nagara Park, situated at its eastern foot, is famous for cherry blossoms.

attributes.title: 阿武隈川

field_history_en.value: Early on, one of the Mutsu poems of the Kokinshū says, "In Abukuma the mist is rising and obscuring the morning, it is improbable to see you there, no sense in waiting”, which inspired the combination of Abukuma and mist in later poems. Often, “abu” is combined with the word “afu” (to meet) and it becomes popular in love poems to mean that a man and a woman meet each other like in the following from the Horikawa hyakushu: “Was it through false accusations that it leaked out? The name of Abukuma that brought me in disrepute”. In addition, the Abukuma "river" is sometimes used in conjunction with the words "to cross" and "to flow".

field_history_ja.value: 早く『古今集』東歌の陸奥歌に「阿武隈に霧立ちくもり明けぬとも君をばやらじ待てばすべなし」の歌が見えるが、これを踏まえて「阿武隈」に「霧」を取り合わせた和歌が後代に詠まれた。また「阿武隈」の「あぶ」に「逢ふ」を掛ける場合も多く、「濡れ衣といふにつけてや流れけん阿武隈川の名こそ惜しけれ」（『堀川百首』）のように男女が相逢うの意として恋の歌に用いる例が一般的である。なお、「川」の縁語として「渡る」「流る」などを合わせて使用されることもある。

field_topography_en.value: This river originates from the mountain Sanbon yari-dake on the border between Fukushima and Tochigi Prefectures, flows north through the Kōriyama and Fukushima basins, and empties into the Pacific Ocean at Arahama in Watari-chō, Miyagi Prefecture. The river is also called Ōkuma River because it originates from the Ōkuma River, or because it flows from the mountains where big bear lived. The total length of the river is 239 kilometers. From ancient times, the Abukuma River basin was an important route to the Mutsu area. It was also the main battlefield in the fight between Minamoto no Yoritomo and the Northern Fujiwara. In the early modern period, transportation by water developed and the river came to be used for the distribution of goods.

field_topography_ja.value: 福島県と栃木県境にある三本槍岳に発し、郡山・福島盆地を北流して宮城県亘理町の荒浜で太平洋に注ぐ川。その源流に大熊流があるので大熊川、または大熊の棲んだ山から流れるので大熊川ともいわれる。全長239キロメートル。阿武隈川流域は古代から陸奥方面への重要な道筋であり、源頼朝と奥州藤原氏との戦いでも主要な戦場となった。近世には舟運が発達し、物資の流通に活用された。

attributes.title: 有馬

field_history_en.value: The Arima hot springs were well known from ancient times as they were close to the capital(s) in the Yamato region. It is the first hot spring mentioned in Nihon Shoki, which records imperial visits there by Emperor Jomei and Emperor Kōtoku. It is theorized that the name comes from the legend that Emperor Kōtoku's child, Arima no Ōji, was born while his mother was taking a cure at the hot springs. In the classical period as well as the Middle Ages, it remained popular as a hot spring health resort for high-ranking people. Fujiwara no Michinaga, Fujiwara no Yorimichi, Fujiwara no Teika and others are reported to have gone there. Because it is situated between mountains and steep valleys, Arima was struck by disasters, but it recovered every time. During the Warring States period (16.c.), Arima came under the control of Toyotomi Hideyoshi. He organized tea ceremonies there, while his wife Kita no Mandokoro ordered the reconstruction of Buddhist temples destroyed by fire in the Kyōroku and Tenshō eras (1528-1592). As a result, Arima became a place connected with the memory of Hideyoshi.

field_history_ja.value: 有馬温泉は京畿に近いため古くから知られており、「日本書紀」に最も早く登場する温泉であり、舒明天皇と孝徳天皇が行幸したという記録が記されている。なお　孝徳天皇の子・有間皇子は有間湯治中に生れたことに由来するとの説がある。中古・中世にも貴顕の湯治場として人気があったようで、藤原道長や藤原頼通、藤原定家などが下向している。しかし山間渓谷に位置するため被災することもあり、温泉はその都度復興された。戦国時代には羽柴秀吉の蔵入地になり、秀吉による茶会を開かれたり、享禄・天正の火災に遭った寺院が北政所によって修復されるなど、秀吉のゆかりの地でもある。

field_topography_en.value: A hot-spring resort in Kōbe City’s North Ward. It is located on the north side of Mt. Rokkō, an area that has been known since ancient times for its scenic beauty. It was also referred to as “Yuyama” [hot spring mountain] because of the name Arima no yu. [Arima hot springs]. The hot springs, which contain salts of iron, are said to help against rheumatism and gynecological problems. There are differing opinions as to which hot springs are the three most famous in Japan, but the renowned Confucianist Hayashi Razan (1583-1657) lists Arima, Kusatsu and Gero hot springs (“Among the many hot springs in the various provinces of our country, the foremost are Arima in Settsu province, Kusatsu in Shimotsuke, and Yushima in Hida. These are the three places.”) (Hayashi Razan Shishû (1662) Book Three, Arima Yama Ontō). According to the ranking of the Shokoku Onsen Kōnō Kagami [Evaluation of the Benefits of Hot Springs in the Provinces] (1817), Arima is again ranked highly as “Ōzeki: Sesshū Arima no yu”.

field_topography_ja.value: 神戸市北区の温泉町。六甲山の北面、古くから知られた山紫水明の地。古来、「有馬の湯」と呼ばれていたので、「湯山」とも称する。温泉は含鉄類塩泉で、リウマチ、婦人病にきくといわれる。日本三大名泉には諸説があるが、林羅山は有馬温泉・草津温泉・下呂温泉（「我國諸州多有温泉、其最著者摂津之有間、下野之草津。飛騨之湯嶋、是三處也」『林羅山詩集』（1662）巻第三　有馬山温湯）としており、「諸国温泉功能鑑」（1817）の見立番付にも「大関　摂州有馬湯」と上位に位置されている。

field_history_en.value: There are three places called Mt. Otowa. Among them, Mt. Otowa at the border of Ōtsu and Yamashina is best known in poetry. Because it was situated at the provincial border, the Nōin Utamakura included it in two provinces, Yamashiro (Kyōto) and Ōmi (Shiga). According to Wakashogakushō, the place’s name originates from the fact that sounds are emitted from there (otosuru koto ni sofu). In poems, it is often connected with motifs like the cuckoo, autumn leaves and the autumn breeze. In the “Shii ga Moto” (Beneath the Oak) chapter of Genji Monogatari, it appears as a place name on the way to Uji.

field_history_ja.value: 音羽山と称されるところが三か所あるが、中でも山科・大津の音羽山は歌枕として知られている。国境に位置するため、「能因歌枕」には山城（京都）と近江（滋賀）にそれぞれ入れられている。地名の由来に関して「和歌初学抄」では「オトスルコトニソフ（音することにそふ）」と注している。郭公・紅葉・秋風などと詠合わせられることが多く、「源氏物語」椎本の巻には宇治への旅程中、地名として登場している。

field_topography_en.value: Mt. Otowa is located at the border between Yamashina Ward in Kyōto City and Ōtsu City in Shiga Prefecture, with Mt. Ōsaka (Ausaka) in the north and Mt. Daigo in the south. Its elevation is 583m above sea level. At the western foot of the mountain is Otowa village, with a side road of the Tōkaidō which leads to Fushimi crossing through the village. Hōgon-ji Temple is situated on the mountain, with many coming to worship its principal image, commonly called Ushio-Kannon. Confusingly, there are two other mountains named Mt. Otowa in addition to this one. Firstly, Mt. Otowa is the name of the mountain where Kiyomizu Temple stands in today’s Higashiyama Ward, Kyōto City. Secondly, there is a mountain called Mt. Otowa to the west of Mt. Hiei in today’s Sakyō Ward, Kyōto City.

field_topography_ja.value: 音羽山は京都市山科区と滋賀県大津市との境に位置しており、北は逢坂山、南は醍醐山に連なる山である。標高５８３メートル。西麓に音羽の里があり、東海道の追分から伏見に至る道がここを通る。山中に法厳寺があり、本尊は牛尾観音と俗称され、諸人の信仰を集めた。この音羽山の他に、清水寺（現東山区）の山号である音羽山と比叡山西方（現左京区）にある音羽山がある。

field_history_en.value: There is a legend that Minamoto no Yorimitsu killed the demon Shuten-dōji on Mt. Ōe. Because of this demon legend, there are place names like Oni-ga-chaya and Oni-no-iwaya found here. In fact, however, this legend is not about Mt. Ōe in Fukuchiyama but rather the identically-named Mt. Ōe near Kyōto City (Oi-no-saka), and arose from the fact that bandits gathered there to harass travelers. This was misinterpreted as the deeds of demons. The utamakura Ōeyama can also be taken to refer to Oi-no-saka. The Nō play Ōeyama dramatizes how Yorimitsu defeated Shuten-dōji.

field_topography_en.value: Ōe is a mountain in the northwestern part of Kyōto Prefecture forming the border between the Tanba and Tango regions, corresponding to the border of Fukuchiyama City and Yosano Town. It is also called Senjōgatake. Its elevation is 832 meters above sea level. The Yura River flows through the area with Mt. Ōe rising in the north. There are few paddy fields, but the cultivation of traditional Kyōto vegetables like ebiimo (taro root) and Horikawa gobō (burdock) prospers. There are also poultry and dairy farming. Along the Miyagawa river, there are settlements called Naikū (inner shrine) and Gekū (outer shrine), and it is said that this area was once the site of the imperial shrine before it was relocated to Ise Shrine. Therefore, the area is commonly referred to as Motoise (the original Ise).

attributes.title: 大原（大原野）

field_history_en.value: Ōharano was a hunting location for successive generations of emperors, a place for imperial visits by emperors and empresses of the Fujiwara clan, and a site of pilgrimages and outings by imperial regents. In poems, it was a famous place (meisho) for flowers, and there are many examples of the abbreviated name “Ōhara” being used in poems. To differentiate it from the identically named Ōhara in Kyōto City’s Sakyō Ward, one has to refer to the preface or imagery of the poem in which it appears. In poems by Ariwara no Narihira (Kokinshū, Ise Monogatari) and Ki no Tsurayuki (Gosenshū), Ōharano is likewise referred to as “Ōhara.”

field_history_ja.value: 歴代天皇の御狩場であり、藤原氏出身の后妃や天皇の行幸啓、摂政関白らの参詣遊行も多かった。歌では花の名所として詠まれており、歌では単に「大原」と称す例が多い。左京区の大原との区別は、詞書や共に詠まれる景物によって判断することになる。在原業平（「古今集」「伊勢物語」）や紀貫之（「後撰集」）による大原野の和歌にも「おほはら」と詠まれている。

field_topography_en.value: Name referring to the Ōharano area in Kyōto City, Nishikyō Ward. Small hills extend to the east with Mt. Ōhara (Mt. Oshio) in the background to the west. The old Ōharano village includes sections like Ishizukuri, Oshio, Ueba, Iwami and Haigata. Ishizukuri village (Otokuni District, Yamashiro) mentioned in Wamyō Ruijushō corresponds to this area, and in Man'yōshū it is referred to as Irino (written 入野 or 納野). The place name of Ōharano first appears in the early Heian period, and the area became famous for hunting. Subsequently, Ōharano Shrine was ceremonially transferred here. Furthermore, temples like Konzō-ji Temple, Shōji-ji Temple (Hana-no-tera), Yoshimine-dera Temple, Sanko-ji Temple and Jūrin-ji Temple were active at the foot of the mountain. Numerous famous monks practiced in these temples, like Jien, Shōkū, Utsunomiya Yoritsuna (Renshō) and others.

field_topography_ja.value: 京都市西京区大原野一帯の地名。西に大原山（小塩山）を背負い、東に低く小丘陵が起伏する。旧大原野村は、石作・小塩・上羽・石見・灰方などの大字を含む。『和名類聚抄』山城国乙訓郡石作郷はこの地であり、『万葉集』では納野・入野とみえる。平安時代初期から大原野の地名は現われ、遊猟の地としても有名である。ついで大原野神社が勧請され、また金蔵寺・勝持寺（花の寺）・善峰寺・三鈷寺・十輪寺などが山麓に営まれ、慈円・証空・宇都宮頼綱（蓮生）などこれらの寺で修行した著名僧も多い。

attributes.title: 桂

field_history_en.value: Since the Heian period, Katsura was a resort destination for nobles. Katsura prospered as an area of villas, beginning with Fujiwara no Michinaga's Katsura Sansō Estate and the mansion of Minamoto no Tsunenobu, who was known as Katsura Dainagon. Poems composed with this motif draw on the Chinese legend that katsura [laurel] trees grow on the moon, often incorporating moon imagery and making word plays on the place name Katsura and the identically-pronounced laurel tree. Katsuragawa [Katsura River] and Katsura no sato [Katsura village] are also used as utamakura. In the early modern period, Katsura remained a frequent poetic motif, the poems often following traditional concepts and rhetoric.

field_history_ja.value: 平安時代から貴族の遊覧の地となり、藤原道長の桂山荘をはじめ、桂大納言と呼ばれた源経信の邸宅もあり、別荘地として栄えた。歌に詠まれた例を見ると、月には桂の木（月桂樹）が生えているという中国の伝説に基づく発想により、地名の桂に植物の桂を掛けて、月と合わせて詠む例が多い。さらに「桂川」「桂の里」も歌枕として用いられている。桂は近世以降もよく詠まれたが、発想・修辞面において古歌を踏襲するものが多い。

field_topography_en.value: This denotes the area on the west bank of the Katsura River in Nishikyō Ward of southwestern Kyōto City. The name Katsura is said to originate from the old place name Kazurano [葛野]. Since the Heian period, villas of nobles were built there. On the banks of the Katsura River, a holiday villa of the Katsura no Miya (Hachijō no Miya) family was built in the Edo period, as well as the Katsura Imperial Villa with its outstanding architecture and garden. The Katsura River flows southward through Kyōto City's western district and is one of the biggest rivers in Kyōto. It flows through the Kadono District and Otokuni District in former Yamashiro province and the Funai District, Kita-Kuwada District and Minami-Kuwada District (today’s Kameoka City) in former Tanba province. In Shimotoba (in today’s Fushimi Ward), it merges with the Kamo River and flows into the Yodo River. The total length of the Katsura River is 107.8 kilometers.

attributes.title: 賀茂

field_history_en.value: The Kamo Festival is one of the three main festivals of Kyōto. Because the participants’ headgear and carts are decorated with hollyhock [aoi], it is also called the Aoi Festival. The Kamo Festival (North Festival, Aoi Festival), centered around the Day of the Rooster in the fourth month of Japan's old calendar, and the Kamo Rinji Festival, held on the Day of the Rooster in the latter half of the tenth month of Japan's old calendar, often appear in classical literature. In the Heian period, the Kamo Festival was such an important annual event for residents of the capital that it was known simply as “The Festival” [matsuri]. Today, it is held on May 15.

field_history_ja.value: 賀茂祭は京都三大祭りの一つで、祭人の冠や牛車などをアオイで飾るところから葵祭ともいう。旧暦四月中の酉の日を中心とする賀茂祭（北祭・葵祭）と、旧暦十一月下の酉の日に行われる賀茂臨時祭とが、古典文学にしばしば登場しており、平安時代には単に「祭」といえば賀茂祭を意味するほど、都人にとっては大きな年中行事であった。現在は五月十五日に行われる。

field_topography_en.value: Name of an old town in the south of Kyōto Prefecture's Sōraku District, today a sector in the eastern part of Kizugawa City. It borders on Nara Prefecture to the south. In the year 740 (Tenpyō 12), Emperor Shōmu planned the relocation of the imperial court from Heijō-kyō and established a new capital at Kuni-kyō. However, just four years later, the site was abandoned and a provincial temple (kokubunji) was erected on the ruins of the council hall of the former imperial palace (daigokuden). The foundations of the main temple structure and the pagoda were preserved, and the area was officially designated a historical site. Zezu, in the east of the ruins of Kuni-kyō, is a place where Wadō kaichin, Japan's first coins, were minted in the early 8th century. In recent years, a melting pot and Wadō coins have been excavated there. Close to the border with Nara Prefecture is Gansen-ji Temple, which is said to have been established by Gyōki. In addition, Jōruri-ji Temple is known for its main hall constructed in the late Heian period and its three-storied pagoda (both National Treasures), as well as a famous garden of exceptional scenic beauty. Many tourists visit these sites as well as the nearby stone Buddhas.

field_topography_ja.value: 京都府南端、相楽郡にあった旧町名で、現在は木津川市の東部を占める一地区。南は奈良県に接する。740年（天平12）に聖武天皇が平城京からの遷都を図って恭仁京を開いたが、4年ほどで廃都となり、大極殿跡に国分寺が置かれた。金堂と塔の礎石が残り、国史跡に指定されている。恭仁京跡東方の銭司は、古代の銭貨である和同開珎が鋳造された所で、近年るつぼや和同銭が発掘された。奈良県境近くには行基創建と伝える岩船寺や、平安後期の建築の本堂、三重塔（ともに国宝）や、特別名勝・史跡の庭園を残す浄瑠璃寺があり、付近の石仏巡りを兼ね、観光客が多い。

attributes.title: 嵯峨

field_history_en.value: Since the beginning of the Heian period, Saga developed as an area where nobles hunted and amused themselves. Beginning with the Saga-in Palace of Emperor Saga, many villas of the imperial family and court aristocracy were established. Furthermore, Saga was a place for imperial visits. On the occasion of Emporer Uda's sightseeing trip to Ōigawa in 909 (Engi 7), Ki no Tsurayuki praised the beauty of the autumn leaves of Ōigawa and Mt. Ogura in the Ōigawa Gyokō Wakajo. In chapter 164 of Makura no Sōshi, it says, “Fields: the fields of Saga, what else,” while Nōin Utamakura states, “If you compose about fields, [you have to choose] the fields of Saga.” Poems about Sagano (Saga Plain) primarily evoke the feeling of autumn.

field_history_ja.value: 平安時代前期より貴族の遊猟地として発達し、嵯峨天皇の嵯峨院をはじめ、皇族、貴族の別荘が多く設けられた。また、嵯峨は行幸の地であり、延喜七年（909）の宇多天皇の大井河遊覧御幸の際には紀貫之が『大井河行幸和歌序』で大井川、小倉山の紅葉の美しさを讃えている。『枕草子』一六四段に「野は嵯峨野、さらなり」、『能因歌枕』に「野をよまば、さがの」とあり、嵯峨野は秋の風情を詠むのが本義である。

field_topography_en.value: The area name of today's Saga in Ukyō Ward of Kyōto City. It refers to the plateau and plain enclosed by the slope of Mt. Atago to the north, Mt. Ogura to the west, the Ōi River (Katsura River) and Arashiyama to the south, and Utano and Uzumasa to the east. There are several theories about the origin of the name. It could be derived from a word referring to the topography of the place, such as saka, meaning slope, or sagashi, meaning steep or rugged. Alternately, the name could have been taken from Mt. Cuó'é on the outskirts of Chang’an, China, which was commonly called Mt. Saga in Japanese. North of Saga, there is an area at the base of the Nishiyama mountain range which comprises a section of the Tanba Plateau. It was a flood plain of the Katsura River until the Hata clan opened up the area in the 7th century for cultivation.

field_topography_ja.value: 現在の京都市右京区嵯峨を中心とする地域名。北は愛宕山麓、西は小倉山、南は大堰川（桂川）・嵐山、東は宇多野・太秦を境とする台地および平野部。地名の由来については、坂あるいは険（さが）しの意に解して地形に起源を求める説、中国長安郊外のさつがつ山（俗称、嵯峨山）の名を移したものとする説などがある。東は太秦に続き、西は小倉山の山麓、北は丹波高地の一部をなす西山山地の山麓の地域で、かつて桂川の氾濫原であったが、7世紀に秦氏一族が改修して田野が開けたという。

attributes.title: 信夫

field_history_en.value: “To secretly foster feelings of love” [思ひしのぶ] is the central concept of Shinobu as a poetic motif. Its first appearance is in the following poem of Ise Monogatari, chapter fifteen: “Ah, Mount Shinobu, I would gladly find a way in secret to frequent her, that I might further explore the recesses of her heart.” (transl. Mostow and Tyler, p. 49). From then on, poems of “secret love” (shinobu koi) were composed in connection with “the depths of the heart” (kokoro no oku). After its first appearance in the imperial anthology Gosenshū, its use was discontinued for some time. However, it reappeared and became a popular motif in the Senzaishū and Shinkokinshū (late Heian and early Kamakura, 1180s to 1210s). Many later poems were influenced by the poem from Ise Monogatari cited above.

field_topography_en.value: Old district name in Fukushima Prefecture corresponding to today’s Fukushima City. Together with the Date District, it formed Shinobu Province in ancient times. At the time of the Taika reforms, it became a district of Mutsu Province. In the first year of Meiji (1868), because of the segmentation of Mutsu Province, it was integrated into Iwashiro Province. As a result of the territorial reform in the Meiji period, the area was adjacent to the Date District in the east and north, Fukushima Prefecture’s Yama District and Yamagata Prefecture’s Higashi-okitama District (separated by Mt. Azuma) to the west, and the Adachi District to the south. Today, the entire area is incorporated into Fukushima City.

field_topography_ja.value: 福島県の旧郡名で、現在の福島市にあたる。上代、伊達郡と共に信夫国を形成。大化改新のときに陸奥国の郡となり、明治元年（一八六八）陸奥国の分割により岩代国に属した。明治の郡区編制では、東・北は伊達郡、西は吾妻山によって耶麻郡と山形県東置賜郡、南は安達郡に接していたが、現在は全域が福島市の中に編入されている。

attributes.title: 竜田

field_history_en.value: Tatsuta is well known for its red autumn leaves, but in Man'yōshū no strong association is found between the two. It was at the beginning of the Heian period that the Tatsuta River came to be connected with autumn leaves in poetry. The Kokinshū poem “Were one to cross it, the brocade might break in two – colored autumn leaves floating in random patterns on the Tatsuta River” (Kokinshū 283, transl. McCullough, p. 70) is one of seven poems depicting the sight of autumn leaves floating on this river. Apart from the autumn leaves, poems referring to “frost,” “cherry blossoms” and “yūtsuke-dori” (rooster) can also be found.

field_topography_en.value: Place name referring to the vicinity of Sangō-chō and Ikaruga-chō in the Ikoma District of northwestern Nara Prefecture. It corresponds to the area on the northern bank of the river outlet where the Yamato River flows from the Nara Basin into the Ōsaka Plain. The Tatsuta River flows southward through the Tatsuta Mountain and Ikoma Valley regions of the southern Ikoma Mountain Range before flowing into the Yamato River. Tatsuta Shrine (Tatsuta Taisha) is located in the Tatsuno area of Sangō-chō. Tatsuta-dō road, which crossed the Tatsuta Mountains and connected the provinces of Yamato and Kawachi, was a prominent traffic route in ancient times. At the time of the Jinshin War, warriors were deployed to Tatsuta. In the eighth year of Emperor Tenmu’s reign (679), a barrier crossing was established in the Tatsuta Mountains as it was an important traffic route. Tatsuta Taisha enshrines the deities Ame no Mihashira no Mikoto and Kuni no Mihashira no Mikoto and is well known for the Wind God Festival (Tatsuta Festival) that, according to Nihon Shoki, was first celebrated in the fourth year of Emperor Tenmu’s reign (675) in the Tatsuno area of Tatsuta.

field_topography_ja.value: 奈良県北西部の生駒郡三郷町・斑鳩町付近の地名。大和川が奈良盆地から大阪平野に流れ込む出口北岸部にあたり、生駒山地南部の竜田山や生駒谷を南流して大和川に注ぐ竜田川が存在し、三郷町立野には竜田神社（竜田大社）が鎮座している。竜田山を越えて大和と河内を結ぶ竜田道は古代の有力な交通路であり、壬申の乱の際に竜田に兵が派遣されたり、天武天皇八年（679）に竜田山に関が設けられたりするなど、交通の要地であった。竜田神社は天御柱命・国御柱命を祭神とし、天武天皇四年に風神を竜田の立野にまつらしめた（『日本書紀』）ことに始まる風神祭（竜田祭）で著名である。

attributes.title: 名取川

field_history_en.value: Starting with the Kokinshū poem “How painful to have this groundless reputation, as though I were kin to the River of Scandal flowing in Michinoku.” (transl. McCullough, p. 141), the place name Natorigawa became a metaphor for the expression “nakina (a groundless rumor, with neither roots nor leaves) o toru” [無き名を取る]. Additionally, it is used in love poems as a metaphor for emerging rumors, like submerged trunks emerging from the riverbed as they are washed away by rapid currents.

field_topography_en.value: A river flowing eastward through Miyagi Prefecture. It has a length of about 55 kilometers. The river basin size is about 939 square kilometers. It originates near the Futakuchi-tōge mountain pass in the Ōu Mountains at the border with Yamagata Prefecture. Merging with the Goishi River, Hirose River and other tributaries, it flows into Sendai Bay at the border of Sendai City and Natori City. At various points on the main river and its branches, there are small basins like Ayashi or Kawasaki where terraces of several levels developed. In these areas, together with the Sendai Heiya plain at the lower reaches of the river, water-filled paddy fields were set up. In the time of the Sendai Domain (during the Edo period), the Sasaya Kaidō road was an important route for transporting goods from Sendai to Yamagata along the banks of the Natori and Goishi Rivers.

field_topography_ja.value: 宮城県中部を東流する川。延長約55キロメートル、流域面積939平方キロメートル。山形県境の奥羽山脈二口峠付近に発し、碁石川、広瀬川などを合して仙台市と名取市の境界で仙台湾に注ぐ。本流と支流には愛子、川崎など小盆地があり、数段の段丘が発達して、下流の仙台平野とともに水田が開ける。仙台藩時代には仙台から名取川、碁石川に沿って笹谷街道が通じ、山形への重要な物資輸送路であった。

attributes.title: 難波

field_history_en.value: A harbor called Naniwa developed at the mouth of the Yodo River. From ancient times, it was an important transportation hub. According to Nihon Shoki, Emperor Nintoku opened up the Naniwa canal to facilitate water transportation. In ancient times, several residences for emperors were built here. The prosperity of Naniwa during this period is evident from the poem, “In the old days they called it Rustic Naniwa. But now That we have moved our palace here, How like a capital it’s become” (Man'yōshū) (transl. Levy). On the other hand, Naniwa harbor was also the place where sakimori, soldiers that had been dispatched to Dazaifu in Kyūshū, set sail from. After the capital was moved, royal residences were no longer established there, and the area of Naniwa declined. Instead, traffic intensified as people passed through the area on the way from the capital to Tennōji, Sumiyoshi Shrine or Kumano pilgrimages. Naniwa developed further with the construction of Toyotomi Hideyoshi's Ōsaka Castle. In the world of poetry, the motif of Naniwa had been widely established by the Middle Ages and continued with little change after that.

field_history_ja.value: 淀川河口には難波津と呼ばれる良港が発達し、古代より交通の要衝であった。仁徳天皇が難波堀江を開堀して水利を整えたという（『日本書紀』）。当地には古代に歴代の天皇の宮が築かれた。その難波の賑いは、「昔こぞ難波田舎と言はれけめ今は都引き都びにけり」（『万葉集』）の歌に窺うことができる。一方、難波津は大宰府へ赴く防人が出港するところでもあった。都が移り、宮が置かれなくなってから難波の地は衰退するが、都からの天王寺・住吉参詣、あるいは熊野詣でなどの通路にあたり、往来はなお頻繁であった。難波は豊臣秀吉の大坂城築城によって発展を遂げるが、和歌世界では中世までに広がりを見た詠歌の範囲をほぼ継承しているといってよい。

field_topography_en.value: An old name for the vicinity of Ōsaka City, especially for the northern part of the Uemachi Plateau. Except for the Uemachi Plateau, the land is neither sea nor land, but a marsh. It is said that common reed grew thickly there, as in the poem, “Naniwa, where the common reed spreads” (Man'yōshū, 4398). Since ancient times, Naniwa Harbor was an important port as it was the entry point from western Japan to the Yamato area, Nara and Kyōto. In ancient times, a succession of imperial palaces was established there, including Emperor Nintoku's Kōzugū, Emperor Kōtoku's Nagara no Toyosaki no Miya and others. In the early modern period, Naniwa (written 難波 or 浪速) came to be used as an alternative name for Ōsaka. Today it refers to the area between the Dōtonbori River’s south bank and the Kizu River's east bank.

field_topography_ja.value: 大阪市付近の古称で、特に上町台地の北部一帯をさす。上町台地を除けば海ともつかず陸ともつかずといった低湿地で、葦が生い茂り「葦が散る難波（万葉・四三九八）」といわれた。難波津は古くからの重要な港で、大和地方、奈良、京都に対する西方からの出入り口に当り、仁徳天皇の高津宮、孝徳天皇の長柄豊碕宮など、古代にはしばしば都が置かれた。難波（浪速）は近世には大坂の異称として用いられ、現代には道頓堀川の南側、木津川の東側の地域をさす。

attributes.title: 富士

field_history_en.value: The origin of the name “Fuji” allegedly goes back to Taketori Monogatari, where the emperor sends warriors up the mountain to burn a magic potion of eternal life left behind by Kaguyahime as a present. As a result, the mountain was named Fuji no Yama, meaning “abounding in warriors.” In ancient and classical times, Mt. Fuji was known as an active volcano with burning fire. From the end of the Heian period to the early Middle Ages, the number of people travelling from the capital to the east increased, and in the Middle Ages, many poems were composed about the sight of Mt. Fuji. In early modern times, because Mt. Fuji could be seen in the distance from the city of Edo, it was not only included in poems but also became a motif of pictorial art like Katsushika Hokusai’s Fugaku Sanjūrokkei (36 Views of Mt. Fuji).

field_history_ja.value: 「富士」の名前の由来として、『竹取物語』ではかぐや姫の置き土産の不死の薬を焼くために、御門の命で「土（つはもの）」が多く登ったので「士」に「富む」山、即ち「富士の山」と名付けられたと語る。古代・中古には火の燃える活火山として知られていたが、平安末期から中世初期にかけて都から東国へ旅する人も多くなり、中世には富士山の風景を詠じた和歌が数多く創作された。また、江戸は富士を遠くから望むことができる都市であり、近世期においても和歌を含め、葛飾北斎「富嶽三十六景」などの画題にも使用された。

field_topography_en.value: A cone-shaped stratovolcano towering above the border of Shizuoka and Yamanashi Prefectures. An active volcano, Mt. Fuji is also well known abroad as a symbol of Japan. Its elevation is 3776 meters above sea level. At the summit, there is a volcanic crater 800 meters in diameter. The highest point of the crater wall is called Kengamine. The inclination at this part of the mountain is 32 to 35 degrees, while that at the foot of the mountain is 2 to 3 degrees. This results in a beautiful curve. The diameter of the base is 35 kilometers from east to west and 38 kilometers from north to south.

attributes.title: 伏見（大和）

field_history_en.value: In Nihon Shoki, it is recorded that Emporer Suinin was buried in the “Sugahara Fushimi Imperial Tomb.” It is also one of the regions where the Haji clan was based. Inspired by the place name, Sugawara no Michizane's great-grandfather and forefathers changed the family name from Haji to Sugawara. In waka poetry, it is associated with a neglected, lonely image. It was sometimes conflated with Fushimi in Yamashiro Province.

The area on the right bank of the Akishino River is known for temples like Saidai-ji, Kikō-ji (Sugawara-dera), and Sugawara Tenmangū Shrine. Many place names containing sugahara or sugawara exist in this region, seemingly indicating that sedge [suge or suga] once grew in abundance here.

attributes.title: 三輪

field_history_en.value: Miwa has a mysterious atmosphere rooted in ancient beliefs like worship of the white snake (shirohebi shinkō) and the legend of Mt. Miwa (Miwayama setsuwa). In the Nara period, it was viewed with awe as well as reverence and affection. From the Heian period, Mt. Miwa became an important motif in poems, such as: “I live in a cell at the foot of Mount Miwa. If you should miss me please come and pay a visit – the gate where the cedar stands” (Kokinshū 982, transl. McCullough, p. 214-215). In the early modern period, the tradition to combine Miwa with the worship of Shintō divinities, like Miwa no kamisugi or Miwa no hibara, continued.

field_history_ja.value: 三輪は白蛇信仰や三輪山説話など古代信仰に支えられた神秘的な雰囲気が漂う地であり、奈良時代には異怖と敬愛の信仰の中心でもあった。平安時代以降、「わが庵は三輪の山もと恋しくはとぶらひ来ませ杉立てる門」（『古今集』）の歌により三輪山が詠歌対象として注目された。近世期以降も「三輪の神杉」「三輪の檜原」など、三輪と神の信仰とを結びつける伝統は絶えることなく詠み継がれた。

field_topography_en.value: A mountain in Sakurai City in the northern part of Nara Prefecture. At the southwestern tip of the Yamato Plateau, it forms a mountain ridge with Makimukuyama and Haseyama on the eastern side. Its elevation is 467 meters above sea level. The mountain is of granite, the peak of coarse-grained gabbro. Yamato Ichinomiya Ōmiwa Shrine, which belongs to the cult of Mt. Miwa, is situated at the western foot of the mountain. There are huge stone clusters called iwakura [dwelling place of a god] on three levels surrounding the mountain.

attributes.title: 八橋

field_history_en.value: Yatsuhashi’s renown stems from a poem by Ariwara no Narihira in Ise Monogatari, chapter nine: “They came to a place called Yatsuhashi, Eight Bridges, in the Province of Mikawa. The name derived from the sight as the river fanned out there into eight streams, like a spider’s legs, with a bridge over each one. … The marsh was full of irises in magnificent bloom. The sight moved a companion to say, ‘Make a poem about our journey, with one of the five syllables of ka-ki-tsu-ba-ta [iris] at the head of each line,’ and so he did.” This is followed by the famous poem, “Robe from far Cathay / Long and comfortably worn / Bound by love to stay / I cover these distances / Shrouded in melancholy” [translation by Joshua S. Mostow and Royall Tyler 2010]. This poem went on to be included in Kokinshū, as well as in Gosenshū, Shūishū and others. In this way, Yatsuhashi became an utamakura which was utilized in many poems.

field_history_ja.value: 八橋が名高いのは『伊勢物語』九段にある在原業平の歌による。「三河の国八つ橋といふ所に至りぬ。そこを八橋といひけるは水ゆく河の蜘蛛手なれば、橋を八つ渡せるによりてなむ八橋といひける。…その沢に杜若いとおもしろく咲きたり。それを見てある人のいはく、杜若といふ五文字を句の頭にすゑて旅の心をよめといひければ、よめる」のあと、「唐衣着つつ馴れにしつましあればはるばる来ぬる旅をしぞ思ふ」という有名な歌が続く。この歌は以降、『古今集』をはじめ『後撰集』『拾遺集』などに所収され、八橋は歌枕として多くの歌に詠まれるようになった。

field_topography_en.value: An area in Chiryū City in Aichi Prefecture. The place name originates from the fact that the Aizumao River branched off into eight streams, and eight bridges were suspended over them. Yatsuhashi is well known as a famous spot for kakitsubata (Iris laevigata). Today, the grounds of nearby Muryōju-ji Temple are famous as a place for kakitsubata viewing.

attributes.title: 淀

field_history_en.value: In the section “famous places” of Yakumo Mishō, four places are listed under the place name Yodo: Mutta no Yodo (Yoshino River), Nanase no Yodo (Matsura River), Ōkawa Yodo (Yoshino River), and simply Yodo, which implies that the name on its own was associated with the Yodo River in Yamashiro. The poetic image of the Yodo River was shaped by the actual landscape as well as by a poem in Kokinshū: “They may seem stagnant like the waters of the Yodo River, but on the contrary, my emotions are surging and deep.” There are also numerous poems that play on the word koi, meaning “carp,” and its homophone koi, meaning “love.” One such example can be found in Kokin Rokujō: “Although he has not been living at the bottom of the Yodo River, if the carp appears the fish cannot sleep anymore.”

field_history_ja.value: 『八雲御抄』の名所部「淀」の項には、六田の淀・七瀬の淀・大川淀・淀の四か所が挙げられており、淀というと山城の淀川と認識されていたとみえる。淀川のイメージは『古今集』の「淀川のよどむと人は見るらめど流れて深き心あるものを」と淀川の実景によって形作られている。また、『古今六帖』「淀川の底にすまねどこひといへばすべていをこそ寝られざりけれ」のように「恋」の意を掛けて「鯉」が歌われることが多々ある。

field_topography_en.value: Yodo is the area name for the southwestern part of Fushimi Ward in Kyōto, close to the confluence of the Uji River, Katsura River and Kizu River. The location prospered as a river port for ship traffic on the Yodo River. Since it was situated by the western edge of Ogura-ike pond and its water was normally stagnant [Japanese: yodomu], the place name became Yodo and the river's name Yodogawa. The Yodo River emerges from the southern tip of Lake Biwa, flows through the Kyōto Basin and the northern half of the Ōsaka Plain, and pours into Ōsaka Bay. The total length is 75 kilometers. The river basin encompasses 8240 square kilometers, which is about a quarter of the Kinki region.

attributes.title: 和歌浦

field_history_en.value: Emperor Shōmu, who visited Waka-no-ura Bay in the tenth month of Jinki 1 (724), greatly admired the scenery and changed the name from Waka no Hama [弱浜] to Aka no Ura [明光浦]. He also contributed to the preservation of the landscape and ordered that the regional deity Tamatsushima be enshrined and venerated there. Yamabe no Akahito, who was traveling together with Emperor Shōmu on his imperial visit, composed the poem, “At Waka-no-ura, when the tide rises and the tideland vanishes, cranes fly toward the reedy shores, calling” (Man'yōshū). From around the middle of the Heian period, numerous aristocrats like Fujiwara no Yorimichi visited Waka-no-ura and the seashore of Fukiage on pilgrimages to Mt. Kōya, Kokawa-dera Temple and the Kumano Sanzan shrine complex.
