field_history_ja.value: 神亀元年（七二四）十月和歌浦に行幸した聖武天皇はその風景を絶賛し、「弱浜（わかのはま）」を「明光浦（あかのうら）」と改め景観保護を行い、さらに当地の地神である玉津島の神を祀ることを命じている。なお、聖武天皇の御幸に同行した山部赤人は「若の浦に潮満ち来れば潟を無み葦辺をさして鶴鳴き渡る」（『万葉集』）の歌を残している。平安時代中期ごろからは、藤原頼通など多くの貴族たちが、高野・粉河、熊野参詣の途上に、吹上の浜とともに和歌浦遊覧を行なっている。

field_topography_en.value: The name refers to the southern edge of Wakayama City at the mouth of the Waka River. Waka-no-ura is the area around the inlet encircled by the Kataonami sandbank. A small island called Tamatsu Island used to be in the northwestern corner of this bay, but is now connected to the mainland. At the foot of Mt. Tengu is Tamatsushima Shrine, where Princess Soto'ori, one of the three gods of waka [waka sanjin], is worshipped.

attributes.title: 猪名

field_history_en.value: Inagawa [Ina River] is used as a poetic motif (utamakura), such as in the Man'yōshū poem “I have been thinking of her as deeply as the depths of the Inagawa, and have no idea what has become of her.” Inano［猪名野 / 為奈野, Ina Plain］also appears in poems of the Man'yōshū like Takechi no Kurohito’s. In the Heian period, this place became a destination for hunting and amusement for imperial princes and prominent nobles. In early modern times, rice for sake, agar-agar, freeze-dried tofu (kōri dōfu), chestnuts, charcoal and black cattle were produced in the villages of the mountainous area on the upper stream of the Ina River. The first three of these were referred to as the “three white products,” while the latter three were known as the “three black products.” The groundwater of the Ina River was used to make the sake of Ikeda, which was not only shipped to Ōsaka but also to Edo.

field_history_ja.value: 「万葉集」に「かくのみにありけるものを猪名川の沖を深めてわが思へりける」と「猪名川」が歌枕としてみられ、「猪名野」または「為奈野」も同じく『万葉集』の高市連黒人の歌などに見える。この地は、平安時代には親王や有力貴族の遊猟地となっていた。近世期には猪名川上流の山地農村で酒米・寒天・凍豆腐と栗・薪炭・黒牛を生産し、三白三黒の物産とよばれており、大坂のみならず江戸にも出荷された池田の酒は猪名川の伏流水を利用したものであった。

field_topography_en.value: The name denotes the area along the Ina River from Itami City to Amagasaki City in Hyōgo Prefecture. The Ina River originates near Nishi-tōge at the border with Ōsaka Prefecture. As it flows south through the Ina Plain, it merges with the Kanzaki River at Amagasaki City and pours into Ōsaka Bay. Emerging from among the Hokusetsu Mountains in the northern part of Ōsaka Prefecture; it flows down the Ōsaka Plain and merges with the Kanzaki River. Downstream, it forms a river delta together with the Muko River. Upstream, it is known for the picturesque scenery of Inagawa Keikoku Prefectural Natural Park and the Kagobō hot springs. Midstream, there are many historic landmarks connected to the Tada Genji family. In the early modern period, the downstream portion was also called the Ikeda River. The total length is 43.2 kilometers.

field_topography_ja.value: 兵庫県伊丹市から尼崎市にかけての猪名川沿いの地域である。猪名川は大阪府境の西峠付近に源を発し、猪名野を南流しながら尼崎市で神崎川と合流して大阪湾に注ぐ。大阪府北部とその周辺に広がる北摂山地に発して、大阪平野に流下して神崎川に合流する。下流部では武庫川とともに三角州を形成する。上流部は猪名川渓谷県立自然公園の景勝地で、籠坊温泉もある。中流は多田源氏ゆかりの史跡が多い。近世では下流は池田いけだ川ともよばれた。延長43.2キロメートル。

attributes.title: 大江（老坂）

field_history_en.value: In Nihon Kōki, the mountain appears written as 大井山 (Ōi Mountain), while in Man'yōshū it is written as 大江乃山 (Ōe no Yama). It is the place where Minamoto no Yorimitsu is reported to have repelled bandits. It is often mixed up with the identically named Ōe in Fukuchiyama. As the San’indō road crossed through there, it became a passage for military forces. Minamoto no Yoshitsune used this route at the time of the Battle of Ichi-no-Tani, Ashikaga Takauji during the attack on Rokuhara Tandai, and Akechi Mitsuhide at the time of the Honnōji Incident.

field_topography_en.value: A mountain pass in the Ōe Massif, situated in the southwest of Kyōto Prefecture between the Kyōto Basin and the Kameoka Basin, also written 大枝. Its elevation is 193 meters above sea level. The San’indō road, which was the sole transportation route connecting Kyōto and the Tanba area until the Edo period, passed through Ōe. It is said that the Ōe Barrier [Ōe no Seki] had already been established under the reign of Emperor Tenmu as a strategic traffic and military checkpoint.

attributes.title: 伏見（山城）

field_history_en.value: The picturesque scenery of Fushimi has been beloved since the Heian period, and Fujiwara no Yorimichi's son, Tachibana no Toshitsuna, notably occupied a villa here renowned for its elegance. The poem, “The townsfolk go home when it gets dark, from now on I will not place my hopes on the name of the village of Fushimi” (Goshūishū) remains from this era. In this manner, Fushimi is often associated with fushi, meaning to “lie down.” Fushimi manors were constructed around the mountain villa of Toshitsuna, and in the Middle Ages they became the financial base of imperial households for the lineage from Emperor Gofukakusa to Emperor Gokomatsu. These were passed down among the Fushimi-no-miya branch of the Imperial Family, and from the Middle Ages Fushimi in Yamashiro province eclipsed Nara’s Fushimi in terms of fame.

field_history_ja.value: 伏見の景勝は平安時代から愛されたが、とくに藤原頼道の息・橘俊綱はここに風流を尽くした別荘を営み、「都人暮るれば帰る今よりは伏見の里の名をも頼まじ」（『後拾遺集』）の作を残した。このように、伏見にはしばしば「伏し」が掛けられる。この俊綱の山荘を中心に伏見庄が形成され、中世には皇室御領として持明院統の経済基盤となり、また伏見宮家に相伝されていった。それゆえ、中世以降は圧倒的に山城のほうが有名になった。

field_topography_en.value: Located in the southern part of Kyōto City in the vicinity of today’s central Fushimi Ward, Fushimi encompasses the lowland flood plain of the Kamo River and Momoyama Hill to the east. In the Heian period, it was a site of villas of the court aristocracy. After Toyotomi Hideyoshi built Fushimi Castle (Momoyama Castle), it developed as a castle town. In the Edo period, it prospered as a river port on the Yodo River, a waterway connecting Kyōto and Ōsaka.

attributes.title: 大原（愛宕郡）

field_history_en.value: As Ōhara lies at the northwestern foot of Mt. Hiei, it was under the strong influence of Enryaku-ji Temple. At the same time, it was a place of retreat for believers who were dissatisfied with the secularization of Mt. Hiei. From the late Heian period onwards, it was known as a place of seclusion of many prominent figures, including Kamo no Chōmei. Jakkō-in Temple, the place where Emperor Antoku's mother Kenreimon’in (Taira no Tokuko) secluded herself and the scene of the “Imperial Visit to Ōhara” chapter of Heike Monogatari, is also in Ōhara.

field_topography_en.value: A mountain in the Ōhara area of Kyōto City's Sakyō Ward. From classical times, many Buddhist temples practicing bonbai shōmyō [songs in praise of Buddha] were concentrated at the foot of this mountain. It is also said that there were many hermits’ retreats in Ōhara. Surrounded by mountains, the narrow Ōhara basin forms a small expanse stretching from north to south. Along the river, the Wakasa Kaidō road leads to the northern country. In the Middle Ages and the early modern period, this area was called Ōhara Village [大原郷] or Eight Ōhara Villages [大原八郷] because there were eight villages there.

field_topography_ja.value: 京都市左京区大原にある山で、その山下には中古より梵唄声明を伝える寺院が多く並び、また隠遁者の庵を結ぶものも多かったという。周辺の山々に囲まれて南北に狭小な大原盆地が一小天地をなし、川沿いに若狭街道が北国へ向かう。中近世にはその地域にある八ヵ村をもって、大原郷あるいは大原八郷ともいわれた。

attributes.title: 朝倉

field_history_en.value: In waka poetry, it mainly appears as "Mount Asakura". In the tenth chapter of the Makura no sōshi (The Pillow Book) it says: "Mountains: … Mount Asakura. In combination with the phrase ‘seen somewhere else’ it is charming.” Alluding to the poem from the Kokin rokuchō “I saw a man that I knew a long time ago, in the great distance of the clouds of Mount Asakura”, Asakura is often combined with the words “somewhere else”, “between the clouds”, “far up in the clouds” (meaning court aristocracy), and cuckoo. Based on its pronunciation it is associated with “the morning is dark” (asa kurashi). When it is used simply as "Asakura", it normally refers to the Kagura song “Asakura” and the lines: “Asakura! When I am at the palace of wood [created for Saimei tennō in Eso], who can it be who enters calling out his name”.

field_history_ja.value: 和歌では主として「朝倉山」で詠まれ、『枕草紙』十段に「山は…朝倉山。よそに見るぞおかしき」がみられる。また「昔見し人をぞ我はよそに見し朝倉山の雲ゐはるかに」（『古今六帖』）の歌を本歌とし、「よそ」「雲ゐ（はるか）」「不如帰」と一緒に詠まれる場合が多く、発音に因み「朝暗（し）」を掛けることもある。単に「朝倉」と読む場合は、地名とは区別して神楽歌「朝倉」（本歌「朝倉や木の丸殿に我が居れば」、末歌「我が居れば名告りをしつつ行くは誰」）を指すのが通例である。

field_topography_en.value: The city is located in the south-central part of Fukuoka Prefecture. The northern and eastern parts of the city are lined with the mountains of the Kosho Mountains, including Mount Kosho and Mount Umami. The western part of the city is a fan-shaped area of the Koishiwara and Sada Rivers and the alluvial plain on the right bank of the Chikugo River. There are many places with legends related to Emperor Saimei, such as the Eso Hachimangū Shrine, where Emperor Saimei, who made an expedition to help Baekje (Kudara) in the 7th century, is said to have prayed for victory by invoking Hachiman Daijin, and Asakura no Tachibana no hironiwa Shrine, where the emperor is said to have died during his visit. The area is also known as the location of the imperial residence of Emperor Yūryaku.

field_topography_ja.value: 福岡県中南部にある市。市域の北部から東部一帯には、古処山、馬見山など、古処山地の山々が連なる。西部は小石原川、佐田川の扇状地と、それに続く筑後川右岸の沖積平野が広がる。7世紀に百済救援のため西征した斉明天皇が、戦勝祈願のため八幡大神を勧請したと伝える恵蘓八幡宮、天皇が客死した地とされる朝倉橘広庭宮など、斉明天皇にまつわる伝承地が多い。また、雄略天皇の皇居があった地としても知られる。

attributes.title: 天の香具山

field_history_en.value: In volume 3 of the Man’yōshū the poem "Song of Mount Kagu by Kamonokimi no Tarihito” mentions “The heavenly Kaguyama that has descended from heaven” referring to the legend reported in the Iyo no kuni Fudoki (Topography of Iyo Province; around 720) according to which after descending from heaven, the mountain split into two, one part becoming the Amayama of Iyo. After the Man'yōshū, the motif has not been used much, but from the mid-Heian period onward it appears in poems like: “Even around the peaks of Kagoyama covered by white clouds, it is the same height that the moon can be seen” (Shikashū). Even after the Middle Ages, the perception of Mt. Kaguyama as a sacred mountain remained unchanged, and this poetic image was continued in early modern waka poetry.

field_history_ja.value: 『万葉集』巻三に「鴨君足人が香具山の歌」では「天降りつく天の香具山…」という歌があるが、これは『伊予国風土記』に天の香具山が天から降り、二つに分かれて、一方は伊予の天山になったという伝承を踏まえたものである。『万葉集』以来はあまり用いられなかったが、平安中期以降になると「かご山の白雲かかる峰にても同じ高さぞ月は見えける」（『詩歌集』）などの作例がみられるようになる。中世以降も天の香具山を神聖な高山と同一視する認識は変わらず、近世和歌の作例にもそのような読まれ方が踏襲された。

field_topography_en.value: A small hill-like mountain in the east of Kashihara City, Nara Prefecture. In ancient times, it was also called "Ame-no-kaguyama" or "Ama-no-kagoyama," and is also known simply as Kaguyama. Together with Mount Miminashi and Mount Unebi, they are known as the "Three Mountains of Yamato". As Amano kaguyama is the only one of non-volcanic origin it was venerated by the ancients as the divine mountain protecting the eastern part of the capital Fujiwara-kyō. A legend has it that it is a mountain originally located in the heavenly realm of Takamagahara which descended to earth. It is 152 meters high.

field_topography_ja.value: 奈良県橿原市の東にある丘のような小山。古くは「あめのかぐやま」「あまのかごやま」ともいわれ、単に香久山、賀久山とも称される。耳成山・畝傍山と合わせて大和三山として人々から親しまれるが、天の香具山だけは火山性ではないため、藤原京の東方を鎮護する神山として古代人の崇敬を集めたという。天界である高天原にあった山が地上に降りてきたものという伝説がある。標高152メートル。

attributes.title: 天橋立

field_history_en.value: In the Tango no kuni Fudoki (Topography of Tango Province), it is written, "Izanagi no Mikoto built a bridge as a passage to heaven. Therefore, it is called Amano hashidate. When the divinity slept it lay down.” In the age of the gods it is said to have been a ladder connecting heaven and the earth. The earliest example of this as a pillow word for poetry is found in Ise shū (Poem anthology of the poetess Ise) “Even if there was the famous bridge Amano hashidate built, should I love somebody who is unattainable for me”. The son of Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu, Sukechika, constructed a garden with a model of Amano hashidate. These examples show that at least from the middle of the Heian period, the scenic spot with white sand and green pines was well known among the poets of the capital. The famous poem by the daughter of Izumi Shikibu, Koshikibu no naishi, “Ōeyama, as the road to Ikuno is so far, I have not seen even a letter from Amano hashidate” (Kin’yōshū), was later integrated into the poetic treatises Toshiyori zuinō and Fukurozōshi together with a narrative about her separation from her mother, as well as into the Hyakunin isshu (One hundred poets, one poem each), and rendered this place name an immortal utamakura. It is also the site of Sesshu's late work, "Picture of Amano hashidate” (ca. 1501-06) depicting white sand and pine trees.

field_history_ja.value: 『丹後国風土記』には「伊射奈芸命（いざなぎのみこと）、天に通ひ行でまさむとして、橋を作り立てたまひき。故、天の橋立と云ひき。神の御寝ませる間に仆れ伏しき」との記述があり、神代は天と地とを結ぶ梯であったという。歌枕として最も古い例は「音にきく天の橋立たてたてておよばぬ恋も我はするかな」（『伊勢集』）があり、能宣の息輔親は自邸に天の橋立を模した庭園を築いたと伝えられ、少なくとも平安中期あたりにはすでに白砂青松の景観が都の歌人の耳目を集めていたことが窺える。和泉式部の娘・小式部内侍の歌「大江山いくのの道の遠ければふみもまだみず天の橋立」（『金葉集』）は、のちに『俊頼髄脳』『袋草紙』に説話とともに収載されるほか、『百人一首』にも採られるなど天橋立を不滅の歌枕にした。なお、雪舟の晩年の作『天橋立図』に描かれた白砂青松の地でもある。

field_topography_en.value: It is a huge spit of sand stretching from the northwest coast of Miyazu Bay in Miyazu City, Kyōto Prefecture, dividing the Yosa Sea into east and west. It is one of the three most famous scenic spots in Japan, along with Matsushima in Mutsu and Miyajima (Itsukushima) in Aki. It is also called Hashidate. It is an unusual formation with about 7,000 pine trees growing on a sandbar about 20 to 170 meters wide and about 3.6 kilometers long, formed by the accumulation of sand carried by the wind and currents flowing through the bay. The area between the tip of the sandbar and Monju is called "Monju no kireto", which is a narrow channel with a swivel bridge for the convenient passage of ships. In the northwest on Mount Nariai, there is Nariai Temple, the 28th temple of the 33 sacred Kannon temples of Western Japan.

The area between the tip of the sandbar and Monju is called "Monju no kireto", which is a narrow channel with a swivel bridge for the convenient passage of ships. In the northwest on Mount Nariai, there is Nariai Temple, the 28th temple of the 33 sacred Kannon temples of Western Japan.

field_topography_ja.value: 京都府宮津市、宮津湾北西岸から、与謝の海を東西に分けて延びる巨大な砂嘴で、陸奥の松島、安芸の宮島（厳島）とともに日本三景の一つに数えられる景勝の地である。「橋立」ともいう。幅は約20～170m・全長約3.6kmの砂州に約7000本もの松が生い茂る珍しい地形で、湾内を流れる潮流と風によって運ばれた砂の堆積により造形された。砂州の先端と文珠との間は「文殊の切戸」とよばれ、狭い水路をなし、通船に便利なように回旋橋が架けられている。また、北西の成相山には西国三十三所28番札所の成相寺がある。

attributes.title: 嵐山

field_history_en.value: In the beginning, it appears as Arashi no yama, but later it became Arashiyama. It was known as a famous place for autumn leaves, as shown in the poems by Fujiwara no Kintō, "As it is still cold in the morning at Arashi no yama, there is no one who would not wear a brocade, like that of the autumn leaves" (Shūishū), or "As I came to visit Ōigawa River's flowing stream of old, I see the autumn leaves at Arashi no yama" (Goshūishū). In addition, there are many examples of the place name used as pivot word with "storm" (arashi) and "is probably not" (araji). After cherry blossoms from Yoshino had been transplanted to Kameyama-dono, the detached palace of Emperor Go-Saga located in Arashiyama, the area became a famous site for cherry blossoms in poems since the Middle Ages, and also appears as such in the noh theater "Yoshino" and "Saigyō-zakura”. It continues to be used as a famous place for cherry blossoms and autumn leaves in travelogues and haibun (haiku) of the early modern period.

field_history_ja.value: 最初は「嵐の山」と詠まれたが、後に「嵐山」に定着した。藤原公任の歌「朝まだき嵐の山の寒ければ紅葉の錦着ぬ人ぞなき」（『拾遺集』）、「大井川ふるき流れを尋ねきて嵐の山の紅葉をぞ見る」（『後拾遺集』）のように紅葉の名所として知られていた。また「嵐」や「あらじ」と掛詞にして読む例も多い。嵐山に位置する後嵯峨上皇の離宮・亀山殿に吉野の桜が移植されたことから、中世以降は歌に桜の名所として詠じられるようになり、謡曲「吉野」や「西行桜」の詞章にも花の名所として引かれている。近世以降にも紀行、俳文などに花・紅葉の名所として描かれている。

field_topography_en.value: A mountain in Saikyō-ku, Kyōto City. It is 381.5 meters high. The Katsura River (Ōigawa River and Hozu River) flows from north to east at the foot of the mountain. It is a famous place for cherry blossoms and autumn leaves. The Togetsukyō Bridge over the Ōigawa River is well known and designated as a national historic site of scenic beauty. At the top of the mountain are the ruins of the medieval Arashiyama Castle, Senkōji Temple on the northern flanks of the mountain, which appears in one of Bashō's haiku "On the mountain of blossoms ascending two hundred meters, there stands the Daihi hall", Hōrinji Temple at the eastern foot of the mountain, which was according to temple legend built by Gyōki (8th century), and the Ichitani Shrine near the Togetsu Bridge.

attributes.title: 生駒

field_history_en.value: Since it is located on the border between Nara and Ōsaka Prefectures, it has been an important transportation point since ancient times. As shown in the verses "I saddled up my horse to go to see my beloved, as I cross Ikoma Mountain, yellow leaves are falling" and "It is so painful I cannot see my beloved, so I will step on the rocky roots of Ikoma Mountain, and then I will come" (Man'yōshū), there is an early association between Ikoma Mountain and "crossing a mountain". As an utamakura, it was established from around the anthology Goshūishū, with poems of Nōin “When the small branches at my hut sprout in summer, the mountain of Ikoma has already vanished from sight”, or of Ryōzen “At the seashore, when I took shelter at the coast of Ōe, high up in the clouds I saw Ikoma Mountain”. It can be written with different characters.

field_topography_en.value: A place name from the northwestern part of Nara Prefecture, an area at the eastern foot of Mount Ikoma, in the upper reaches of the Tomio and Ikoma Rivers (Tatsuta River). It prospered as the town built at the foot of Hōzanji Temple (Ikoma shōten), and after World War II, it developed into a residential city of Ōsaka. Ikoma is the main peak of the Ikoma Mountains, located on the border between Nara and Ōsaka Prefectures. The summit is gently flat, while the Kawachi side shows a steeply sloping fault topography, and the east slope is gently sloping toward Ikoma Valley. It is 642.3 meters high.

attributes.title: 和泉

field_history_en.value: One of the five Kinai provinces, it was formerly called Chinu and became Kawachi-Izumi-gun in the Taika Reform. In the first year of the Tenpyō Hōji era (757), the area was established as Izumi Province after being separated from and reincorporated into Kawachi Province. It is also called Senshu, and is known for its many manors belonging to the imperial family, regent families, and temples and shrines since the Heian period. During the Nanbokuchō period (14th century), the area was under the control of the Kusunoki clan of Kawachi, but later, the governorship changed to the Yamana, Ōuchi, Hosokawa, and Miyoshi clans respectively. Around the time of the Ōnin War (1467-77), Sakai replaced Hyōgo in Settsu Province as the prospering trading city, and the city administration was run by an association of influential merchants. Oda Nobunaga suppressed this with military force and appointed magistrates to rule, and Toyotomi Hideyoshi and Tokugawa Ieyasu followed suit. As an utamakura it appears often in combination with “the woods of Izumi” (Izumi no soma), based on the Man’yōshū poem, "The people who stand in the forest of Izumi where the wood for the palace is drawn from, without a pause they continue their yearning”, and is introduced in the poetic treatise Yakumo mishō as a pillow word of Izumi Province. Variants of the above poem are found in anthologies like Kokin rokuchō, Shinchokusenshū, and it is also cited in the preface of Shinkokin wakashū proving that it was well known: “wood for the palaces growing abundantly in the forest of Izumi, it will never be used up how much of it you might use”.

field_history_ja.value: 五畿内の一つで、古くは茅渟（ちぬ）といい、大化改新で河内和泉郡となった。河内国からの分立、再編入ののち、天平宝字元年（七五七）に和泉国として確定した。泉州ともいい、平安時代以後、皇室・摂関家・寺社の荘園が多かったことで知られる。南北朝時代には河内の楠木氏の勢力範囲となったが、その後、守護は山名、大内、細川、三好氏と転変。応仁の乱ごろから摂津国の兵庫に代って堺が貿易都市として繁栄し、市政は会合衆と呼ばれる有力商人によって運営されたものの、織田信長はこれを武力で抑え、奉行を置いて支配、豊臣秀吉・徳川家康もこれを踏襲した。歌枕としては「（和）泉の杣」のかたちで登場することが多く、「宮材引く泉の杣に立つ民の休む時なく恋ひ渡るかも」（『万葉集』）が基になり、『八雲御抄』に和泉国の歌枕として紹介されている。『万葉集』の歌は『古今六帖』『新勅撰集』などに類歌が収録されており、また『新古今集』序にも「泉の杣しげき宮木は、ひくとも絶ゆべからず」と引用されているように著名であった。

field_topography_en.value: This ancient province is located in the southern part of Ōsaka Prefecture, slightly north of the center of the Izumi region. It is bordered by Takaishi City to the north, Sakai City from north to east, Kawachi-Nagano City to the southeast, Katsuragi Town in Ito-gun, Wakayama Prefecture across the Izumi Mountains to the south, Kishiwada City to the west, and Tadaoka Town and Izumi-Ōtsu City in Senboku-gun to the northwest. The Ikegamisone site (now Izumi City and Izumi-Ōtsu City) is a large site that dates from the Yayoi period, especially the middle period, and together with the Yotsuke site (now Sakai City) in the former Ōtori County to the north, it occupies the position of the mother village of the Izumi region during this period. Large-scale upland settlements of the late Yayoi period include the Sonoike and Kannonji-yama sites (now in Izumi City). This area was a cotton-growing area during the Edo period, and even today the tradition of Izumi cotton is continued, small and middle scale factories can be found in the agricultural parts along Matsuogawa and Makiogawa. Modern factories of wool production, bleaching and domestic industry such as of cultured pearl can also be seen here.

field_topography_ja.value: 大阪府の南部、和泉地方の中央やや北寄りに位置する。北は高石市、北から東にかけては堺市、南東は河内長野市、南は和泉山脈を挟んで和歌山県伊都郡かつらぎ町、西は岸和田市、北西は泉北郡忠岡町・泉大津市で、市域は南北に長い。郡内には原始以来の諸遺跡が多く、池上曾根遺跡（現和泉市・泉大津市）は弥生時代の全期間とくに中期を中心とした大遺跡で、北方の旧大鳥郡の四ッ池遺跡（現堺市）とともにこの時期の和泉地方の母村的位置を占め、各種の遺構や遺物が出土している。弥生時代後期の大規模な高地性集落としては惣の池・観音寺山の両遺跡（現和泉市）がある。なお、この付近一帯は江戸時代綿作地であったことで、現在も和泉木綿の伝統を受け継ぎ、綿織布の生産が盛んで松尾川・槇尾川沿いの農村部にも中小工場が散在する。毛織物・晒の近代工場、模造真珠などの家内工業もみられる。

field_history_en.value: It is famous as the setting for the myth of Susanoo-no-Mikoto who saved Princess Kushi-inadahime by killing a giant snake that drank heavily and ate one young girl every year, and obtained the Kusanagi sword by splitting its tail. It is also the scene of the poem "The eightfold fence of Izumo where the eightfold clouds rise, to hide away my beloved I put up an eightfold fence, an eightfold fence”, which belongs to the songs recorded in the first Japanese histories (Kojiki, Nhonshoki) and is allegedly the origin of waka poetry. Since then, it has been occasionally included in waka poems, such as "The clouds rising from the edge of the mountains, the maiden of Izumo, like the mist that hangs around the peaks of Yoshino” (Man’yōshū) or “I live in simplicity in my native place the blooming capital, but now I will go to Izumo where the eightfold clouds are said to rise” (Goshūishū). It is also a metaphor for the art of poetry like in “The eightfold fence of Izumo where the eightfold clouds rise, even until today its ancient traces have not faded away” (Akishino gessei shū, 1204).

field_history_ja.value: 素戔嗚尊が大酒を飲み、毎年一人ずつ娘を食う大蛇を退治して奇稲田姫を救い、その尾を割いて天叢雲剣を得たという八岐大蛇神話の舞台として有名である。なお、和歌の始原とされる記紀歌謡「八雲立つ出雲八重垣妻籠みに八重垣作るその八重垣を」でも読まれる。それ以降、和歌には「山の際ゆ出雲の児らは霧なれや吉野の山の嶺にたなびく」（『万葉集』）や「ふるさとの花の都に住みわびて八雲立つてふ出雲へぞ行く」（『後拾遺集』）のように時に詠まれている。また、「八雲立つ出雲八重垣けふまでも昔の跡はへだてざりけり」（『秋篠月清集』）のように歌道を喩す例もある。

field_topography_en.value: It is located in the western part of San'indō Road, the eastern part of present-day Shimane Prefecture. It is bordered by Hōki Province (Tottori Prefecture) to the east, Bingo Province (Hiroshima Prefecture) to the south, Iwami Province (western Shimane Prefecture) to the west, and faces the Sea of Japan to the north. The Chūgoku Mountains run east to west in the south, there is a mountain over 1,000 meters high on the border to Bingo Province, and the terrain leans to the north. Parallel to this mountainous area, there is another of about 400 meters on the Shimane Peninsula in the north, and the area in between is the Shinji Rift System. The western part of this rift valley is the sedimentation area Hikawa Plain, the central part is Lake Shinji, and the eastern part is the lake Nakaumi. Although there is nothing large in terms of rivers, Hii River and Kando River create sedimentation plains, and Iu River, Iinashi River, and Hakuta River flow into Nakaumi. In ancient times, it formed a cultural sphere separate from Kinki and Kitakyūshū, but after it came under the control of the Yamato Imperial Court, its chief became the Izumo kuni no miyatsuko (administrator of the province). The story how the land was pulled together to create Izumo, one of the local myths, or the traces of the deity Ōkuninushi, reflect the history and culture of the region at that time, while the stories of Ōkuninushi handing over the country, the story of Yamato Takeru being sent to Izumo tell the story of the Yamato Court's rule over Izumo. It is also known as the site of Izumo Taisha Shrine.

field_topography_ja.value: 山陰道の西部に位置し、現在の島根県の東部にあたる。東は伯耆国（鳥取県）、南は備後国（広島県）、西は石見国（島根県西部）に接し、北は日本海に面している。南部に中国山地が東西に走り、備後との境には1000メートル以上の山岳があり、地勢は北に傾いている。この山地に平行して北部の島根半島には400メートル程度の山地があり、その間は宍道地溝帯で、この地溝帯の西部は簸川平野、中部は宍道湖、東部は中海となっている。河川には長大なものはないが、斐伊川と神戸川が簸川平野をつくり、意宇川・飯梨川・伯太川が中海に注いでいる。古く近畿・北九州とは別の文化圏を形成していたが、大和朝廷の支配下に属した後、その首長は出雲国造となった。出雲神話の国引きの話、大国主神の事跡などは、当時のこの地域の歴史・文化を反映し、大国主神の国譲り、日本武尊の出雲建征伐の話などは、大和朝廷による出雲支配の経緯を物語っている。出雲大社が鎮座する地としても知られる。

attributes.title: 江口

field_history_en.value: From the Heian to the Kamakura period, Eguchi prospered as a place of amusement and entertainment for aristocrats. It was also a hub for traffic and distribution between Kinai (central provinces) and the San’yō, Saikai, and Nankai roads, and thus, along with Kanzaki, it flourished as a place for prostitution. In consequence, it is also known as the birthplace of song and music. In particular, the poems exchanged between Saigyō and Tae, a prostitute from Eguchi, which were included in Saigyō’s Sankashū are famous (“How hard it is to renounce the world! And you are reluctant to provide me with a temporary abode?”, “As I heard you have renounced the world, so why should you set your heart on this impermanent world / temporary abode”. Later, this was extended to a tale in the setsuwashū Senshūshō, and inspired the creation of the noh play Eguchi and the nagauta Shigure Saigyō.

field_history_ja.value: 平安から鎌倉にかけて貴族の遊興歓楽地として殷賑をきわめた地で、機内と山陽・西海・南海道との往還、物流の拠点であったことから神崎と並び遊女の里としても繁栄した。よって詩歌や管絃の発生の場としても知られる。とくに西行と江口の遊女である妙との贈答歌（「世の中を厭ふまでこそかたからめかりの宿りを惜しむ君かな」、「世を厭ふ人とし聞けばかりの宿に心とむなと思ふばかりぞ」『羈旅』）が有名で、『山家集』にも採られている。のちに『撰集抄』に説話化され、謡曲「江口」、長唄「時雨西行」などを創作を促している。

field_topography_en.value: A district located at the junction of the Yodo River and the Kanzaki River in Higashi-Yodogawa Ward in the northern central part of Ōsaka City. Since the Heian period (794-1185), the area has prospered as a river port for boat transportation to Kyōto. Jakkōji Temple (the hall of Eguchi no Kimi), famous in literature, is said to have been built in 1205, and is known for a poem exchange between the monk Saigyō and Eguchi no Kimi, Taejo. At present, dyeing, papermaking, and machinery factories are located along the riverbank, and the hinterland is covered with municipal residential areas.

field_topography_ja.value: 大阪市中北部、東淀川区の淀川と神崎川との分岐点にある地区。平安朝以来、京都への舟運の中継河港として栄えた。文学上名高い寂光寺（江口の君堂）は1205年（元久2）の創建と伝えられ、僧西行と江口の君・妙女との問答歌で知られる。現在、河岸には染色、製紙、機械工場などが立地し、後背地には市営住宅地が広がる。

attributes.title: 大津

field_history_en.value: It is known as the site of Emperor Tenchi's Ōmi-Ōtsu Palace. After this capital was abandoned in 672, it was called "Furutsu" (Old-Tsu) for a while, but was restored to its old name when the capital was moved to Heian in 794. It has a long history as a scenic spot in poetry. In the Man’yōshū, among the poems about ancient capitals there is a poem by Hitomaro "…Tenchi tennō reigning over the land from his palace in Ōtsu in Ōmi Province with the curling waves”. After the relocation of the capital, many poems were sung about the dilapidation of the city, such as "Curling waves, the bay of Ōtsu exists just in name, mist lies over the land and there is no guardian for the palace trees” (Shūishū). In the Middle Ages, however, it became common to read the poem in contrast to the eternal natural scenery of the four seasons. Combining it with the word “many” is another typical rhetorical device: “When I hear from him who is known for having many lovers, my sleeves get wet with tears of love” (Izumi Shikibu shokushū).

field_history_ja.value: 天智天皇の近江大津宮があった地で知られる。廃都後は「古津（ふるつ）」と称された時期もあるが、平安遷都とともに旧称に復した。歌枕としての歴史が長く、『万葉集』に「…石走る近江の国の楽浪の大津の宮に天の下知らしめしけむ…」（巻一）という人麻呂の歌など旧都詠歌群が収録されている。遷都以降は「さざなみやおほつのうらは名のみして霞たなびき宮木守なし」（『拾遺集』）のようにその荒廃ぶりを歌うものが多くなったが、中世には悠久の四季自然の景と対照させる読み方も定着した。なお、修辞的には「思ふ人おほつよりとぞきくからにあやしかりつる袖の濡れぬる」（『和泉式部続集』）のように、「多（し）」を掛けるのも特徴である。

field_topography_en.value: The city, the capital of the prefecture, is located in the southwestern part of Shiga at the southern end of Lake Biwa and consists of the alluvial lowlands along the lake shore and the hills and mountains behind it, where houses developed densely on the slopes along the curved lake shore. The area is rich in archaeological sites dating back to the Jōmon period. In ancient times, the Ōmi Ōtsu Palace, where the capital was moved in the 6th year of Emperor Tenchi's reign (667), and the Hora Palace, which was temporarily built during the renovation of the Heijō Palace, are among the important political historical sites. In the Heian period (794-1185), it was a point of military importance for the capital for transportation. At the same time, there were monasteries established like Enryakuji on Hieizan, Enjōji (Miidera) on Nagarayama, and Sakamoto and Ōtsu flourished as temple towns supplying commodities. In the Middle Ages, the Rokkaku clan, the military governors of Ōmi Province, appointed a magistrate for Ōtsu, Oda Nobunaga also kept Ōtsu under his control, along with Sakai and Kusatsu, while Toyotomi Hideyoshi established the system of Ōtsu hyakusōbune and granted the privilege of transportation on the lake to the city of Ōtsu.
field_topography_en.processed: The city, the capital of the prefecture, is located in the southwestern part of Shiga at the southern end of Lake Biwa and consists of the alluvial lowlands along the lake shore and the hills and mountains behind it, where houses developed densely on the slopes along the curved lake shore. The area is rich in archaeological sites dating back to the Jōmon period. In ancient times, the Ōmi Ōtsu Palace, where the capital was moved in the 6th year of Emperor Tenchi's reign (667), and the Hora Palace, which was temporarily built during the renovation of the Heijō Palace, are among the important political historical sites. In the Heian period (794-1185), it was a point of military importance for the capital for transportation. At the same time, there were monasteries established like Enryakuji on Hieizan, Enjōji (Miidera) on Nagarayama, and Sakamoto and Ōtsu flourished as temple towns supplying commodities. In the Middle Ages, the Rokkaku clan, the military governors of Ōmi Province, appointed a magistrate for Ōtsu, Oda Nobunaga also kept Ōtsu under his control, along with Sakai and Kusatsu, while Toyotomi Hideyoshi established the system of Ōtsu hyakusōbune and granted the privilege of transportation on the lake to the city of Ōtsu.

field_topography_ja.value: 滋賀県の南西部に位置する市で、県庁所在地。琵琶湖の南端に位置しており、湖岸の沖積低地および背後の丘陵地・山地からなり、湾曲した湖岸に沿った斜面に人家が密集して発達した。縄文期からの遺跡に富む。古代には天智天皇6年（667）に遷都した近江大津宮、平城宮改作の際一時造営が進められた保良宮等重要な政治史上の名がみえる。平安時代には京都への軍事上、陸水運の要地となる一方、比叡山に延暦寺、長等山に園城寺が造営され、坂本・大津は僧寺への物資供給地、門前町として発達した。中世、要地として注目した近江国守護六角氏は大津奉行を置き、ついで織田信長も堺・草津とならび大津を管掌、豊臣秀吉もこの地に大津百艘船を設置し、湖上運送の特権を認めた。

attributes.title: 春日

field_history_en.value: There are more than fifty poems about Kasuga in the Man’yōshū, and it is used with the motifs plum blossom, mist, autumn leaves, etc. There are poems about the moon rising from behind the mountain, because it is located to the east of the capital Heijō-kyō, and also poems about hunting and field games. In the Heian period (794-1185), under the influence of the first lines of the Ise Monogatari, which begins, "Once upon a time, a man, newly come of age, went hunting in the village of Kasuga, near the Nara capital”, the image of a peaceful early spring day in idleness was established, and motifs like young greens, spring snow appeared: “I thought in Kasugano it is only the snow that piles up but now I see that it is the young herbs covering the ground” (Goshūishū), “Over the grass that is covering the ground in Kasugano, how cold hearted, light snow of spring has fallen” (Shinkokinshū). In the case of Mount Kasuga, on the other hand, there are many poems that include wisteria (fuji) and pine (matsu) because Kasuga-yama was a sacred place associated with the Fujiwara clan. “Mount Kasuga, I will address my prayers to the pine trees, even if the number of leaves of the wisteria outnumber them”. “Fuji no matsuba/sueba” means the descendants of the Fujiwara, and the evergreen pines on Mount Kasuga are used as symbols for the prospering of the Fujiwara clan, which gives the poem an interpretation as a prayer for advancement in official rank.

field_history_ja.value: 『万葉集』には春日を詠じた歌が五十数首あり、「梅花」「霞」「紅葉」などと共に読まれるほか、平城京の東方に位置する山であることからそこからのぼる月や、狩りと野遊びをモチーフにして読まれたものもある。平安時代には「むかし、男、初冠して、奈良の春日の里に、しるよしして、狩りにいにけり」で始まる『伊勢物語』初段の影響で、開放的で、のびのびとした早春のイメージが形成され、「春日野は雪のみつむとみしかどもおひいづるものは若菜なりけり」（『後拾遺集』）、「春日野のしたもえわたる草の上につれなくみゆる春のあは雪」（『新古今集』）など若菜・春雪と結合して詠まれる例が増加した。一方、春日山の場合になると「藤」「松」を読み込む作が多数みられるが、それは春日山が藤原氏の氏神をまつる一族ゆかりの聖地であったことによる。例えば、「春日山松にたのみをかくるかな藤の末葉の数ならねども」（『千載集』）の歌のなか「藤の末葉」は藤原氏の末裔を意味し、「春日山松」は藤原氏繁栄の象徴として詠じられており、この歌に官位昇進の期待をかけていると解釈できる。

field_topography_en.value: The name of Nara City and its vicinity. It refers especially to the area around Kasuga Taisha Shrine. The whole of Mount Hanayama, Mount Wakakusa, and Mount Mikasa behind Kasuga-taisha Shrine is called Kasuga-yama, and a wide area around the foot of Mount Kasuga is called Kasugano, which was widely used as a poetic place name. It is also known as the location of Kasuga Taisha Shrine, housing the deity of the Fujiwara clan. After the relocation of the capital to Heijōkyō, the shrine had a close relationship with the Japanese envoys to the Tang Dynasty, as in 717 when they before departing worshipped a deity to the south of Futayama, or in 751 when the ambassador to Tang China worshipped the gods on the festive day of the Kasuga Shrine, or in 777 when the envoys prayed to the gods of heaven and earth for a safe passage to China. After their tutelary deity was transferred to the shrine, the Fujiwara clan monopolized Mt. Kasuga, and in 841, hunting and felling trees was forbidden on the mountain of the Kasuga Deity. Currently, the area is designated as a Historic Preservation Area and a Special Historic Preservation District.

field_topography_ja.value: 奈良市およびその付近の称。特に、春日大社のあたりをさす。春日大社の背後に連なる花山、若草山、三笠山の全体を春日山と称し、また春日山をとりまくかなり広い範囲の山裾の野を春日野と称するが、これらは歌枕として広く使用された。藤原氏の氏神である春日大社がある地としても知られる。平城遷都後は、養老元年（717）に遣唐使が出発に先だち蓋山の南に神祇をまつり、天平勝宝３年（751）の春日祭神の日に入唐大使が神をまつり、宝亀８年（777）にも遣唐使が春日山下に天神地祇を拝して渡海の無事を願うなど遣唐使との関係が深い。春日社勧請後は、藤原氏による春日山の独占が進められ、承和８年（841）には春日大神の山内での狩猟と伐木が禁じられた。なお現在は歴史的風土保存区域、および歴史的風土保存特別地区に指定されている。

attributes.title: 象潟

field_history_en.value: The first person in history to visit and compose a poem in Kisagata was Nōin hōshi: “How life goes by as I dwell here, in this rush-thatched fishermen’s hut in Kisagata” (Goshūishū), “I will ask Toyooka hime who dwells in heaven, how many generations old are the gods of Kisagata” (Nōin hōshi shū). Due to the influence of the first poem which was inspired by the scenery of fishermen’s thatched huts, tomoya was used as a motif of taking an abode on a journey and to evoke the spirit of travel. On the other hand, urami (view of the bay / resentment) was used as a pivot word (kakekotoba) due to the geographical features, and this aesthetic sense of "gloominess" reverberates in Bashō's Oku no Hosomichi (The Narrow Road to the Interior), where he wrote, "Kisagata has an air of resentment. To the feeling of loneliness comes grief, as if evoking the gloomy soul of the place.” And the famous haiku “Kisagata! In the rain Seishi is asleep like the wet mimosa flowers”.

field_history_ja.value: 歴史上初めて象潟の地に訪れ、歌を詠じた人は能因法師であり、「よの中はかくてもへけりきさかたのあまの苫屋をわが宿にして」（『後拾遺集』）と「あめにますとよをか姫にこととはむいくよになりぬきさかたの神」（『能因法師集』）を残している。なお、海人の苫屋の風景をモチーフにした前者の歌の影響で、旅寝や旅の心を歌う際に読まれることがあった。一方、地理的な特徴に因み、「裏見」が掛詞に用いられたが、こうした「うらみ（恨）」の美意識は芭蕉の『奥の細道』に書かれた「象潟はうらむがごとし。寂しさに悲しみをくはへて、地勢魂をはやますに似たり」の一文や「象潟や雨に西旅がねぶの花」の名句にもよくあらわれている。

field_topography_en.value: Facing the Sea of Japan, it is currently located on a sand dune at the northwestern foot of Mount Chōkai. In the past, there was a lagoon 1.5 km long from east to west and 5 km long from north to south, dotted with many islands, and there existed the scenic view of Tsukumo Island and 88 lagoons. Different characters like “blood clam” are used for rendering Kisagata. It used to be under the level of the sea, but the seabed was uplifted by the great earthquake of 1804 and became land. On the shore of the lake, overlooking Mt. Chōkai to the southeast and the Sea of Japan to the west, there is Kanmanji Temple founded by Jikaku Daishi, which is also famous for recording visits by Nōin hōshi and Matsuo Bashō. It is said that there stood a famous tree called Saigyō-zakura.

field_topography_ja.value: 日本海に臨み、現在は鳥海山北西麓の砂丘上にあたる。かつて東西1.5キロ、南北約5キロの潟があり、その中に多くの島が点在し、九十九(つくも)島や八十八潟の勝景があった。蚶方（延喜式）、蚶潟・象滷とも記す。かつては海であったが、文化元年（1804）の大地震で海底が隆起して陸地となった。南東に鳥海山、西に日本海を望む湖畔には、慈覚大師草創の蚶満寺があり、能因や芭蕉の足跡をとどめたことでも著名である。西行桜と称する名木もあったという。

attributes.title: 貴船

field_history_en.value: The Kibune Shrine, located in this area, was first dedicated to the local deity, the god of water, but from around the middle of the Heian period until the beginning of the Meiji period, it became a subsidiary shrine of the Kamigamo Shrine and was regarded as enshrining the god of rain. The following is a representative poem: “Hold on the water that the divine fields may thrive and let it stream down the weir! Divinity of the upstream” (Shinkokinshū). He is also worshipped as a god who grants many-fold wishes. For example, when Izumi Shikibu had a broken heart, she wrote, "When I am lost in thoughts, the fireflies over the mountain stream seem as if they were my own longing soul” (Goshūishū). To this poem the god of Kibune is said to have responded, as the legend about the merits of the magical power of poetry has it. This anecdote was later included in Jikkinshō and Kokon chomonjū.

field_history_ja.value: この地に位置する貴船神社は、最初水の神を祭る地主神であったが、平安中期頃から明治の初めまで上賀茂社の摂社となり祈雨の神とされた。「大御田のうるほふばかり堰きかけて井堰に落とせ河上の神」（『新古今集』）はその代表的な歌である。また、諸願を叶える神としても祭られる。例えば、和泉式部が失恋したことを哀しみ、「物思へば沢の蛍もわが身よりあくがれ出づる魂かとぞ見る」（『後拾遺集』）と詠んだのに対し、「奥山にたぎりて落つる滝つ瀬のたま散るばかり物な思ひそ」（『後拾遺集』）の貴船明神の返しを与えられたという逸話は、霊験ある歌徳説話として広く伝播され、のちに『十訓抄』『古今著聞集』などにも収録された。

field_topography_en.value: It is located in the northern part of Sakyō Ward, Kyōto City, at the foot of Mount Kibune, which is opposite Mount Kurama. There are several character variants for Kibune. It is famous as the location of Kibune Shrine. The Kibune River originates from Seryō Pass in the north of Kibune and flows through the village of Kibune to Kibune-guchi, where it joins the Kurama River. It is over 6 kilometers long. The Kibune River is together with Kurama River the upstream of the Kamo River, and has had a close relationship with the inhabitants of Kyōto since the Heian period. As can be seen from the fact that the Kibune Shrine, which stands directly at the river and enshrines the god of water is also called the "God of the upstream (Kawakami)", has been revered since ancient times, as the flood water often caused damage to the city of Kyōto downstream. However, during normal times, the river was known as the Mitarashi River and was revered as a sacred river, and was also well known as a place to view fireflies (hotaru).

field_topography_ja.value: 京都市左京区北部、鞍馬山と対する貴船山のふもとの地名であり、貴布禰、木布禰、木船とも称した。貴船神社が鎮座する所でも有名である。また、この地に流れる貴船川は貴船北方の芹生峠より発し、貴船の集落を貫流して貴船口に至り、鞍馬川と合流する。延長６キロ余。木舟川とも記される。貴船川は鞍馬川とともに賀茂川の上流にあたり、平安時代以来京の人々と深い関わりをもってきた。川のほとりにあって水の神を祀る貴船神社が、「河上の神」ともいわれて古くから崇敬されてきたことでもわかるように、その水量の増加はしばしば下流の京の町に被害をもたらしていたという。しかし平常時には御手洗川ともよばれたように、神聖な川として親しまれており、蛍の名所としても知られていた。

field_history_en.value: Kiyomizu Temple is known as a holy place of worship for Kannon, and the poems "You have to put your faith in me! As long as there will be mugwort (moxa) on the plain of Shimejigahara” and “This world full of memories, full of lament, it is no more than the dew on the blossoms of the morning glory” " (both Shinkokinshū) are dedicated to the Kiyomizu Kannon. The temple is also mentioned as a place of scenic beauty in Ryōjin hishō (setsuwa) and Nōin utamakura (poetic treatise). In history, it often came under fire in disputes between Kōfukuji and Enryakuji over the conversion of the temple to a branch temple and in arguments with Gion (Yasaka Shrine) as it is reported in Heike monogatari. It is mentioned in Makura no sōshi (The Pillow Book) among the things that are noisy (Sawagashiki mono) and the Yūgao (Evening Glories) chapter of the Tale of Genji depicts this turbulence. It appears as an important stage of several tales of the Middle Ages (otogizōshi) like Monogusa Tarō or Issunbōshi.

field_history_ja.value: 清水寺は観音信仰の聖地と知られており、『新古今集』に入集された「なほ頼めしめぢか原のさせもぐさわが世の中にあらむ限りは」と「何か思ふ何とか歎く世の中はただ朝顔の花の上の露」の歌は清水観音の託宣歌である。なお『梁塵秘抄』『能因歌枕』などにも名勝として歌われており、興福寺と延暦寺との末寺化をめぐる争いや祇園（八坂神社）との相論でしばしば炎上、その有様は『平家物語』に語られる。また『枕草子』「さわがしきもの」段や『源氏物語』夕顔の巻にその賑わいぶりが描かれ、お伽草紙の『ものくさ太郎』や『一寸法師』ははじめ、物語の重要な舞台にもなった。

field_topography_en.value: Kiyomizu-dera Temple in Higashiyama-ku, Kyōto City, also known as Seisui-dera. An ancient temple of the Hōssō school of Buddhism located at the end of Kiyomizu-zaka, with its back against Mt. Otowa, belonging to the 33 sacred Kannon temples of Western Japan. As it was located near the capital, it has prospered as a sacred place for the Kannon faith since ancient times. Near Kiyomizu Temple, there are many famous places such as "Kiyomizu-no-butai" (platform), "Otowa-no-taki" (waterfall), "Tamurado" (Tamura hall) and others. Kiyomizu-zaka served as a refuge for the outcasts of society. Gojō Bridge, famous for the anecdote of Ushiwakamaru and Benkei in the Yoshitsune legend, was also under the control of Kiyomizu Temple.

field_history_en.value: Kurama is an utamakura in Yamashiro Province according to Nōin utamakura, Waka iroha, Yakumo misho and other poetic treatises and as a note in the Waka shogakusho says, "It is often attached to dark but also to horse”, it is often used associated with darkness. “In the forest of Kurama that is dark as ink, those who enter how far they may follow the road, will they ever find out?” (Gosenshū) “In the bright moonlight of the capital that has become so familiar, oh how I long for the mountain of Kurama” (Goshūishū). Kurama is also known as the place where Saigyō lived after being ordained as a Buddhist priest, and where Ushiwakamaru practiced asceticism, which is why it is the setting for the noh piece Kurama tengu.

field_history_ja.value: 『能因歌枕』をはじめ『和歌色葉』『八雲御抄』などの歌枕書に山城の歌枕として見られ、『和歌初学抄』の注記に「くらきにもそへ、又馬にも」とあるように、「暗し」の意を掛けて詠まれることが多い。例えば「墨染めのくらまの山に入る人はたどるたどるも帰り来ななん」（『後撰集』）や「すみなるる都の月のさやけきに何かくらまの山は恋しき」（『後拾遺集』）の歌がそれにあたる。鞍馬の地は西行が出家後に住んだところでも知られており、また、牛若丸（源義経の児名）が修行したところでもあるゆえ、謡曲「鞍馬天狗」の舞台になっている。

field_topography_en.value: A district in Sakyō Ward, to the northeast of Kyōto City. Formerly Kurama Village. The village is located in the Kitayama Mountains, where there is little flat land and where wood, charcoal, and lumber are produced. On the southern flank of the mountain stand Kurama Temple. The Kurama River, which is the source of the Kamo River, flows along the west side of the mountain, and the Kurama Highway runs along the river, connecting Kyōto and Tanba. Small villages are scattered in the mountains along the highway, but the center is the village at the entrance to Kuramadera Temple. This area belonged to the Kuramadera domain throughout the middle ages and the early modern period. Mt. Kurama, covered with huge old cedars, is also known for the legends of Kurama Tengu and Ushiwakamaru's (Minamoto no Yoshitsune) training. There is a theory that the name Kurama was derived from the word saddle, saddled horse as the Miyako meishozue reports “In the eleventh year of Hakuhō (ca. 660), Tenmu tennō hunted by the prince Ōtomo fled to this place where he tied his saddled horse to a pole. From this the name Kurama derives.” Another origin could be the word kurabu, to compare or to darken (kuramu) but there is no proof for either of them.

field_topography_ja.value: 京都市北東部、左京区の一地区。旧鞍馬村。北山山地に位置し、平地に乏しく、薪炭、木材を産す。鞍馬山の南面中腹には鞍馬寺があり、山の西麓に鴨川の源流をなす鞍馬川が流れ、川沿いに鞍馬街道が通じて京と丹波とを連絡している。集落は街道に沿う山間に散在するが、中心をなすのは鞍馬寺登拝口に形成された門前村である。当地は中・近世を通じて鞍馬寺領に属した。老杉に覆われる鞍馬山は鞍馬天狗や牛若丸(源義経の児名）修業の地の伝説でも知られる。鞍馬の名については「白鳳十一年天武帝大友王子に襲（をそはれ）此所まで逃のび玉ひて鞍をける馬をつなぎしより鞍馬と名つけ初しなり」（『都名所図会』）という説や「くらぶ」の転とする説もあるが、明らかでない。

attributes.title: 更科

field_history_en.value: Sarashina is the area around the mountain Obasute (Ubasute) where according to a legend, old women (mothers, grandmothers, aunts) were abandoned in the mountains, and the two are often mentioned together in poems such as "My heart cannot be soothed if I look at the moon shining on Sarashina and the mountain where old women are abandoned " (Kokinshū). There are also examples for the mountain to be called "Sarashina no yama" (Sarashina Mountain), as in "The moonlight will not appear how long one may wait and watch, so do not stay for long at the foot of Mount Sarashina" (Shuishū). It is the origin of the legend according to which a man living in Sarashina abandoned his aunt - who had raised him - on the mountain and ashamed of the brightness of the shining moon he went to bring her back the next morning. Matsuo Bashō wrote in his Sarashina kikō (Sarashina Travels), "In the village of Sarashina, there is still another, looking at the moon over Obasute Mountain and appreciating the emotions of wind and clouds that are driven by fierce autumn winds arousing intense feelings in your heart. His name is Etsujin.” Bashō left several famous poems about Sarashina.

field_history_ja.value: 更科は姨捨山の一帯で、「我が心なぐさめかねつ更科や姨捨山に照る月をみて」（『古今集』）をはじめ両者がともに詠まれる場合が多く、ことに山の斜面の田に映る月は田毎の月として賞せられる。「月影はあかず見るとも更科の山の麓に長居すな君」（『拾遺集』）のように姨捨山を「更科の山」と称する作例もある。更級に住む男が、山に捨てた親代わりの伯母を、明月の輝きに恥じて翌朝には連れ戻しに行ったという姨捨山伝説でも知られる。なお、松尾芭蕉は『更科紀行』の中に、「さらしなの里、おばすて山の月見ん事、しきりにすゝむる秋風の、心に吹さはぎて、ともに風雲の情をくるはするもの又ひとり、越人と云」などと書きおこし、多くの名句を残している。

field_topography_en.value: A county located in the northern part of Nagano Prefecture. It is also the name of the area including Sarashina District and Kōshoku City. The slopes are lined with rice paddies in the shape of a staircase, and the area is known for the image of the "moon in every rice paddy" (the moon reflected in each small rice paddy) at the foot of Mt. Obasute. It is also famous for its buckwheat. Located in the southwestern part of the Nagano Basin, Mt. Obasute (also called Mt. Sarashina) rises on the border between Chikuma City and Chikuhoku Village and is famous of the legend of Obasute (abandoning the old aunt). It is 1,252 meters high. The mountain has the shape of a summit hill, it is not very high, but it is steep and covered with forest.

field_history_en.value: As the Kokinshū says, "The Sumida River lies between the provinces of Musashi and Shimōsa", it used to be a river that formed the border between the two provinces. Therefore, the Kenpo meisho hyakushu (1215) describes it as a famous place in Shimōsa Province, while the Utamakura nayose, vol. 21, lists it as a famous place in Musashi Province. Until the regulation of the Tonegawa River in the early modern period, the Arakawa River and many other rivers flowed into the area and formed a huge stream. It is famous as the place where Ariwara no Narihira wrote a waka poem about the miyakodori (bird of the capital) in the ninth chapter of Ise monogatari (The Tales of Ise), and it is also the setting for Sumidagawa, a masterpiece of the noh drama in the category of “mad women” written by Kanze no Motomasa. One of the earliest examples of a poem written about this area is "The white waves against the weir of Sumidagawa, will they ever return to where they came from” by Minamoto no Moroyori in the Horikawa hyakushu (1179). From the end of the Heian to the Kamakura period, the Sumida River had a strong image in poetry as "the great river of the eastern provinces," but with the establishment of the Edo shogunate, it came to be regarded as the river of the eastern capital, comparable to the Kamo River in Kyōto. In particular, poets living in Edo wrote about the Sumida River as a river closely related to their daily lives, rather than as a conventional utamakura, such as Katō Chikage "Sumida River, rowing across in the evening, looking at the snow that continues to the edge of Tsukuba Ridge" or Murata Harumi "Sumida River, the Chinese brocade on the bank of flowers, spring has come and who would not go and see it?”

field_history_ja.value: 『古今集』に「武蔵の国と下つ総の国との中にあるすみだがは」とあるように、昔は両国の境をなす川であった。それゆえ『建保名所百首』では下総国の名所とし、『歌枕名寄』巻二一では武蔵国の歌枕としているが、いずれも誤りとはいえない。近世初期のいわゆる利根川締め切りの大工事までは、荒川のみならず、多くの河川が流れ込む大河であったかと考えられる。『伊勢物語』九段に見え、在原業平が都鳥の和歌を詠んだ所として有名で、観世元雅の作とされる謡曲の狂女物の傑作『隅田川』の舞台ともなった。歌の作例としては『堀川百首』における源師頼の「すみだ川ゐせきにかかる白浪の立ち帰るべき心地こそせぬ」が早い例にあたる。平安末から鎌倉時代にかけて歌における隅田川は「東国の大河」というイメージが強かったが、江戸幕府が開かれると、京都の賀茂川に匹敵する東都の川と意識されるようになる。とくに加藤千蔭の「すみだ河夕漕ぎ渡り筑波嶺の端山に続く雪を見るかな」や村田春海「すみだ河堤の花の唐錦春はきて見ぬ人やなからん」など、江戸在住の歌人にとって隅田川はもはや歌枕というより生活に密着した身近な河川として詠まれた。

field_topography_en.value: The Sumida River is a branch of the Arakawa River that flows through eastern Tōkyō and branches off from the Arakawa River at Iwabuchi, Kita Ward. It extends about 25 kilometers from Iwabuchi. There are 16 bridges from the Senju Bridge to the Kachidoki Bridge, extending downstream from Kanegafuchi in Sumida Ward. Different writing conventions exist. During the Edo period, the downstream was called the Ōkawa River, and popular culture such as kabuki, ukiyoe, haiku, senryū, and music was born on the Ōkawa River. The history of the river's affinity for water was carried on into the Meiji era, and the river functioned as a major industrial base. Modern industries such as shipbuilding, cement, chemicals, paper manufacturing, and machinery, as well as urban consumer goods industries, traditional crafts, and the production and distribution base for many manufacturers and wholesalers, gave birth to the downtown small and medium business district. The prosperity of the economy based on shipping and production activities led to the development of entertainment areas on both banks of the river.

field_topography_ja.value: 東京都東部を貫流する荒川の分流であり、北区岩淵で荒川から分岐する。岩淵から延長約25キロ。墨田区鐘ヶ淵から下流をいうこともあり、千住大橋から勝鬨橋まで16の橋が架かる。墨田川、角田川ともいう。江戸期、下流は大川とよばれ、歌舞伎・浮世絵・俳句・川柳・音曲などの大衆文化は大川筋から誕生した。その親水の歴史は明治になっても継承され、工業の基地として大きく機能した。造船・セメント・化学薬品・製紙・機械工業などの近代工業、さらに都市型日用消費財産業・伝統工芸、多くの製造卸の生産・流通基地として下町中小企業地帯を生んだ。舟運と生産活動による経済の繁栄は川の両岸に盛り場を発達させた。

attributes.title: 高砂

field_history_en.value: The name of this place does not seem to have existed until the time of the Man’yōshū, but it appears in saibara songs of the Heian period, and in the kana preface to the Kokinshū, there is the phrase, "The pine trees of Takasago and Suminoe (Sumiyoshi) are as if they had been born together.” There are three poems about Takasago in the Kokinshū, and they were used together with the motifs "bellowing deer" and "pine trees": "Autumn bush clovers are in full bloom, the deer on the peak of Takasago must certainly be bellowing now" and "Who is it I should make my friend now [that I have become so old]? As the pine of Takasago has not been my friend in the past". In particular, since the Saishō Shitennō-in shōji waka (Screen Poems for the Residence of the Four Deva Kings, 1207), the expression "the pine trees on the peak of Takasago" has been firmly established, and many waka poems about Takasago used the phrase, such as "The color of the roaring wind is invisible in the pine trees on the peak of Takasago " (Shinkokinshū), but also “Onoe no matsu”, Onoe being a place name in the vicinity of Takasago.

field_history_ja.value: 『万葉集』時代までこの地名は存在しなかったようであるが、催馬楽にも謡われ、『古今集』仮名序には「高砂住江の松も相生ひのやうに覚え」という文言がある。なお『古今集』には高砂を詠んだ歌が三首あり、「鳴く鹿」や「松」とともに詠じられた様子が窺え（「秋萩の花咲きにけり高砂の尾の上の鹿は今や鳴くらん」「誰をかも知る人にせむ高砂の松も昔の友ならなくに」など）、後代の和歌にも踏襲された。とくに「最勝四天王院障子和歌」以来、「高砂の尾の上の松」という表現が定着し、「吹く風の色こそ見えぬ高砂の尾の上の松に秋は来にけり」（『新古今集』）をはじめ、「尾の上の松」の句を用いた多数の高砂の和歌が創作された。

field_topography_en.value: Takasago is a port town located at the mouth of the Kako River, which flows through the center of Hyōgo Prefecture into the Seto Inland Sea, and is famous as the setting for the first act of the noh drama Takasago. In the early Kamakura period, Emperor Takakura, on his way to Itsukushima, and priest Hōnenbō Genkū, who was exiled to Tosa, stopped at Takasago, which was located on the east bank of the Kakogawa. The foundation of today's town development on the west bank of the Kakogawa was laid by Ikeda Terumasa in 1601. At the same time, salt fields were cultivated, and in the Genroku period (1688-1704), annual tax rice from the Himeji area in the Kakogawa basin was transported by Takase boats, and the town prospered as a transit port on the Seto Inland Sea.

field_topography_ja.value: 兵庫県の中央部を流れる加古川が瀬戸内海に流入する河口部に位置する港町で、謡曲「高砂」の前場の舞台でも有名である。鎌倉時代初期に厳島参詣途中の高倉上皇や、土佐に配流された法然房源空が立ち寄った高砂の泊は加古川東岸にあった。今日の加古川西岸に展開する町づくりの基礎は、慶長六年（1601）池田輝政によってなされた。同じころ塩田が開拓され、元禄には高瀬船で加古川流域の姫路領年貢米が運ばれ、瀬戸内海の中継港として繁栄した。

attributes.title: 那智

field_history_en.value: It is known as a sacred place of the Kumano faith. It appears already in the "Waterfalls" section of the Makura no sōshi (The Pillow Book): "It is moving to hear that there is the Nachi Falls in Kumano.” And in Ryōjin hishō it says: “Where are sacred places? The stone sledge of Ōmine Katsuragi, and in the south it is the shrine of Nachi.” In waka poetry, Kazan-in’s poem is an old example: "They could be mistaken for the waterfall that runs over the rocks, the white clouds of blossoms when I look at the high peaks of Mount Nachi” (Fubokushō, 1310). The motifs were the high peaks of Nachi, the beach of Nachi, the waterfall, later the moon and the wind were used in the poems. Many poems were composed after the Insei period, when the Kumano faith began to flourish, and they were generally poems about people practicing asceticism in the Nachi mountains or under the waterfalls. Saigyō composed: “At the peaks of Nachi the clouds are fading away, the moon is rising, and the white threads of the waterfall traverses its shining light”.

field_history_ja.value: 熊野信仰の霊地として知られ、早くは『枕草紙』「滝は」の段に「那智の滝は熊野にありと聞くがあはれなるなり」とあり、『梁塵秘抄』には「聖の住所はどこどこぞ　大嶺葛城石の槌…南は熊野の那智新宮」と見える。和歌では花山院の「石ばしる滝にまがひて那智山の高峯を見れば花の白雲」（『夫木抄』）が古い例であり、「那智の高峯」「那智の浜」「那智の滝」などがよく詠まれ、のちに月・風が詠み込まれた。熊野信仰が盛んになる院政期以降の詠作例が多く、概して那智山中や滝の下で修行する人物の叙景歌の場合が多い。例えば、藤原定家は「那智、深山風」の題で「風の音もただ世の常にふかばこそ深山出でての形見にもせめ」（『拾遺愚草』）と詠み、西行も「雲きゆる那智の高嶺に月たけて光をぬける滝の白糸」（『山家集』）と詠んでいる。

field_topography_en.value: A place name in Nachi-Katsuura Town, Higashimuro-gun, Wakayama Prefecture. The town is located in the basin of the Nachi River, which originates from Mount Nachi, forms Nachi Falls, and flows into the Kumano Sea. It prospered as it was situated at the foot of one of the three Kumano sanctuaries, the Nachi Kumano Gongen (divided into Kumano Nachi Taisha Shrine and Nachi-san Seigantoji Temple after the separation of Shintoism and Buddhism in the Meiji era). Since the end of the Heian period, pilgrims came from all over the country to visit the Kumano Gongen sanctuary, it even was called “Kumano pilgrimage of ants”, and many temple lodgings were established along the old pilgrims’ route.

field_topography_ja.value: 和歌山県東牟婁郡那智勝浦町の地名。那智山に源を発し、那智滝をつくり、熊野灘に注ぐ那智川の流域にある。熊野三山の一つ那智熊野権現（明治以降神仏分離により熊野那智大社・那智山青岸渡寺に分かれる）の門前町として発達。平安末期以降「蟻の熊野詣」といわれたように、参詣者が全国から集まり、旧参道付近は宿坊が軒を並べていたという。

attributes.title: 鳴海

field_history_en.value: The name "Narumi ga ura" (bay of Narumi) is to be found in the title of a love poem of the Kenpō meisho hyakushu (1215), but "Narumi Lagoon," "Narumi Sea," and "Plain of Narumi” also appear. In the past, the coastline formed a deep inlet (Narumi Lagoon) and was called Narumi no ura, but the inlet receded in the early modern era. The place appeared often in combination with water birds such as plovers, as in "Is it because in Narumi lagoon the morning tide is so high that the cranes fly up crying, even without looking for food" (Horikawa hyakushu, 1105) and "The sound of plovers in the night is near, and while the moon is setting will the tide in Narumi Lagoon reach its height?” (Shinkokinshū). There are also poems combining "Narumi" with naru (to become) and "ura" with urami (resentment).

field_history_ja.value: 『建保名所百首』の恋題に「鳴海浦」が見え、「鳴海潟」「鳴海の海」「鳴海の野辺」とも詠まれた。かつては海岸線が深い入江（鳴海潟）を形成して鳴海の浦と呼ばれたが、近世初期に入江が後退したという。「鳴海潟朝満つ潮や高からんあさりもせでぞたづ鳴きわたる」（『堀川百首』）、「小夜千鳥声こそ近く鳴海潟かたぶく月に潮や満つらん」（『新古今集』）のごとく、景物としては千鳥などの水鳥と組み合わせて多く詠まれ、「鳴海」と「成る」、「浦」と「恨み」を掛けて詠むこともみられる。

field_topography_en.value: Narumi is a district in Midori-ku, Nagoya City, Aichi Prefecture, and was a post town on the fifty-three stations of the Tōkaidō highway in the Edo period. Narumi Lagoon stretched from the western end of the post town to Kasadera, continuing up to the Ayuchi Lagoon mentioned in the Man’yōshū. Futamura-yama on the hill is slightly north of the Tōkaidō on the Kamakura kaidō route. Narumi Shrine, a shrine enlisted in the Engishiki, is dedicated to the gods Yamato Takeru and Miyazuhime, and has been producing the famous Arimatsu and Narumi shibori (tie-dying) since the Keichō era (1596-1615).

field_topography_ja.value: 愛知県名古屋市緑区の一地区で、江戸時代には東海道五十三次の宿場町でもあった。鳴海潟は、宿場西端から笠寺への道程に広がり、『万葉集』にみえる年魚市潟（あゆちがた）に続いていた。丘陵上の二村山は鎌倉街道のルートで東海道筋よりやや北側にある。式内社成海神社は日本武尊、宮簀媛が祭神で、慶長（1596～1615）以来の特産には「有松・鳴海絞り」がある。

attributes.title: 比良

field_history_en.value: It is famous for the fierce winds that blow from the north of Mount Hiei over the mountains to Lake Biwa, as can be seen in the poem of Volume 9 of the Man’yōshū “Oh those small waves, when from Mount Hira the wind blows over the lake one can see the sleeves of the fishermen being tossed in the wind”. There are many waka poems in which the words "(Hira) yamakaze (Mountain wind)" are used. The Hira oroshi, which blows in spring, is also called "Hira hakkō”. There are also many poems which use the words "Hira no takane (lofty peak of Hira)" or "Hira no yama (Mount Hira)" and for the description of the cold winter landscape with its cold mountain wind the words “yama okoshi (to rouse the mountain)”, “to cool down” and “to freeze” are used. Some of the poems are accompanied by the names of surrounding places, such as "Shiga no umi", "Shiga no karasaki", "Niho no umi" and "Mano no ura". On the other hand, the snow-covered peaks of the Hira Mountains on the western shore of Lake Biwa are regarded as one of the Eight Views of Ōmi and were used as the subject of the painting 'Evening snow at Hira'.

field_history_ja.value: 『万葉集』巻九の「ささなみの比良山風の海吹けば釣する海人の袖かへるみゆ」でみられるように、比叡山の北から山を越して琵琶湖に吹きつける風の激しさで有名で、「（比良）山風」と詠み込んだ和歌が多い。春に吹く比良おろしを「比良八荒」ともいった。その他、「比良の高嶺」「比良の山」という形で詠まれることも多く、山風が冷たい冬の風景を主題にして「山おこし」「冴ゆ」「凍る」などの語を詠み込んだものもある。なお、「志賀の海」「志賀の唐崎」「にほの海」「まのの浦」など周辺の地名を伴う歌も散見する。一方、琵琶湖の西岸の比良山地の峰に雪が積もった情景は近江八景の一つとされ、「比良暮雪」という画題として用いられた。

field_topography_en.value: Hira Village, Shiga District, Ōmi Province. It was later divided into North-Hira (Komatsu Village) and South-Hira (Kido Village). It is now part of Ōtsu City in mid-western Shiga Prefecture. The village is located along the western shore of Lake Biwa, with the Hira River running through the center. It is located on the route from Kyōto to the regions along the Hokurikudō (Hokuriku road) and is famous for its beautiful mountain and river landscape, with the magnificent Hira mountain range behind it. In texts of the ancient times words like “Hira no ura miyadokoro (imperial residence in Hira bay)”, “Hira no miya (imperial palace in Hira)” and “Hira no minato (Hira port)” appear and refer to this place. In ancient times Hira-maki (pasture), and in the Middle Ages Hira-shō (village), were located here and the lakeshore was used as a port.

field_topography_ja.value: 近江国志賀郡比良村の地で、のち北比良（小松村）と南比良（木戸村）に分れた。現在の滋賀県中西部、大津市の一地区にあたる。琵琶湖西岸に沿う地域で、中心を比良川が流れている。京都から北陸道への通路に当り、背後に山勢雄大な比良山系が連なる山水景勝の地で有名である。古い文献にみられる「平浦（ひらのうら）宮処」「比良宮」「枚乃湖（ひらのみなと）」などは、いずれもこの地をさしており、古代には比良牧、中世には比良荘 が置かれ、湖岸は港として利用されてきた。

attributes.title: 深草

field_history_en.value: As Fukakusa was used as a mausoleum for the imperial family and the high ranking class, some poems mention it as the place of funerals and cremations, such as "Oh cherry trees of/ Fukakusa Field if you/ truly have a heart/ this year at least you’ll be dressed/ in blossoms dyed inky black" (Kokinshū, Grief, Kamitsuke no Mineo; English translation by Rodd, Laurel Rasplica; and Henkenius, Mary Catherine (1984): p.288) and “Even the lifeless form/ empty as the cicada’s/ shell comforted me/ oh Mount Fukakusa keep/ the smoke spiraling skyward” (Kokinshū, Grief, Shōen, English translation by Rodd, Laurel Rasplica and Henkenius, Mary Catherine (1984): p.287-288.). On the other hand, Fukakusa is often associated in connection with its image of a field of deep grass with the Japanese quail, which appears in the 123rd chapter of the Ise monogatari in the poem exchanged between Ariwara no Narihira and a woman. When Narihira, who had been living together with the woman in the village of Fukakusa, was about to leave her and return to Kyōto, he wrote a poem, "Many years have passed/ since I made our village home,/ and once I am gone,/ Fukakusa grass, I fear,/ May deepen to wilderness.” the woman replied “If to wilderness,/ then I shall become a quail,/ crying through the brakes./ Surely, love, you will not fail/ To come at least for the hunt.” (English translation by Mostow, Tyler (2010): p.244). Narihira was so impressed by the woman's reply that he refused to return to Kyōto. Based on this, Fujiwara no Toshinari composed the famous poem, “Daylight fades away/ and the autumn wind on the fields/ pierces to the soul:/ a quail cries from the deep crass/ of Fukakusa Village.” (Senzaishū, Autumn I, English translation by Carter, Steven (1991): p.150) and thereafter, in connection with Fujiwara no Toshinaris poem, poems like, "Except for Autumn, you won’t hear the voice of the quail in the fields, whom do I ask then, in the village of Fukakusa?" (Akishino gessei shū) and “The evening breeze from the village of Fukakusa is blowing and the quails are singing in the fields of Fushimi” (Shūigusō) increased.

On the other hand, Fukakusa is often associated in connection with its image of a field of deep grass with the Japanese quail, which appears in the 123rd chapter of the Ise monogatari in the poem exchanged between Ariwara no Narihira and a woman. When Narihira, who had been living together with the woman in the village of Fukakusa, was about to leave her and return to Kyōto, he wrote a poem, "Many years have passed/ since I made our village home,/ and once I am gone,/ Fukakusa grass, I fear,/ May deepen to wilderness.” the woman replied “If to wilderness,/ then I shall become a quail,/ crying through the brakes./ Surely, love, you will not fail/ To come at least for the hunt.” (English translation by Mostow, Tyler (2010): p.244). Narihira was so impressed by the woman's reply that he refused to return to Kyōto. Based on this, Fujiwara no Toshinari composed the famous poem, “Daylight fades away/ and the autumn wind on the fields/ pierces to the soul:/ a quail cries from the deep crass/ of Fukakusa Village.” (Senzaishū, Autumn I, English translation by Carter, Steven (1991): p.150) and thereafter, in connection with Fujiwara no Toshinaris poem, poems like, "Except for Autumn, you won’t hear the voice of the quail in the fields, whom do I ask then, in the village of Fukakusa?" (Akishino gessei shū) and “The evening breeze from the village of Fukakusa is blowing and the quails are singing in the fields of Fushimi” (Shūigusō) increased.

field_history_ja.value: 深草は皇室や権門の陵墓となったので「深草の野辺の桜し心あらば今年ばかりは墨染に吹け」（古今集・哀傷・岑雄）、「うつせみは骸を見つつもなぐさめつ深草の山煙だに立て」（古今集・哀傷・勝延）のように葬送・火葬の場面で詠まれた歌がある。一方、草が深い野というイメージとともに、『伊勢物語』百二十三段にみえる業平と女の贈答から「鶉」と結びつけて詠まれることも多い。深草の里に共に暮らしていた業平が女を捨てて京へ戻ろうとし「年をへて住みこし里をいでていなばいとど深草野とやなりなむ」と詠むと、女は「野とならば鶉と鳴きて年はへむかりにだにやは君が来ざらむ」と答えた。業平は女の答歌に感心し、京へ赴く思いを断ったという。このような流れを踏まえ、藤原俊成が詠んだ「夕されば野辺の秋風身にしみて鶉鳴くなり深草の里」（千載・秋上）が有名で、そのあと俊成の歌を意識した「秋ならで野辺の鶉の声もなし誰に問はまし深草の里」（秋篠月清集）、「深草の里の夕風かよひ来て伏見の小野に鶉鳴くなり」（拾遺愚草）などの歌が激増した。

field_topography_en.value: An area in the northern part of Fushimi District, Kyōto City, expanding from the western foot of Mount Inari to the left bank of the Kamo River. In this region there are the so called “Twelve Emperor Tombs of Fukakusa”, which are the tombs of the Emperors from Emperor Ninmyō and Emperor Go-Fukakusa to the Emperor Go-Yōzei. In former times it was the residence of the Hata-clan, and it is said that the Fushimi Inari-Taisha located on Inari Mountain was first worshiped by them. In the Heian period, the area was used as a place for the leisure residences of aristocrats because of its scenic beauty. After the construction of Fushimi Castle by Toyotomi Hideyoshi, the town developed as a “Shrine town” (monzen-machi, a town originally built around a temple or shrine) for the Fushimi Inari Taisha along the highway between Kyōto and Fushimi. Apart from the “Shrine town”, there were many farming villages, and in the Edo period, the ceramic industry producing roof tiles and Fushimi dolls also flourished.

field_topography_ja.value: 京都市伏見区の北部、稲荷山西麓から鴨川左岸にかけての地区で、仁明天皇深草陵と後深草天皇から後陽成天皇までの深草十二帝陵（深草北陵）がある。古くは秦氏一族の居住地であり、稲荷山に位置する伏見稲荷大社は秦氏によって祀られたのが始まりといわれる。風光のよいところから平安時代には貴族の別荘地として使われており、豊臣秀吉の伏見城築城後、京都と伏見を結ぶ街道沿いに伏見稲荷大社の門前町として発達した。門前町以外には農村が多かったが、江戸時代は瓦や伏見人形を産する窯業も盛んに行われるようになった。

attributes.title: 待兼山

field_history_en.value: In association with the word "machikane (cannot await)" the word "yobuko-dori (presumably a cuckoo; a little bird calling)" is often mentioned in poems on Machikaneyama: "Even though the Cuckoo of Mt. Machikane in Tsu Province is calling, there is no one who would respond he is coming" (Kokin rokuchō) and "Just like the cuckoo at the mountain waiting impatiently for someone who is not coming (machikaneyama), I am feeling the same while listening” (Shikashū, Spring, Higo). Later on, the word „hototogisu (lesser cuckoo; Cuculus poliocephalus)” increased in the poems: “Night upon night so/ difficult to wait high on/ Mount Machikane/ I hear one song resound from/ beyond the clouds nightingale” (Shinkokinshū, summer, Suō no Naishi; English translation by Rodd, Laurel Rasplica (2015): p.92). In the early modern period, the phrase “Machikaneyama no hototogisu” was used as an aesthetic expression for “machikaneru (to wait impatiently)” and can be seen in many Haiku and in the performing arts: “At the side of the theater in Shijōkawara (the riverside near the Shijō-Ōhashi-Bridge in Kyōto), the cuckoo of Machikaneyama is calling tōkara, tōkara, the joke of the whole town since the early morning.” (Jōruri, Honchō nijūshi-kō), “‘Cuckoo, cuckoo’ is the message of the cuckoo of Machikaneyama I want to hear it right now. Cry out, cry out!” (Kabuki, Ōtō no miya asai no yoroi), „Selling snacks, cannot await it, cuckoo on the mountain” (Haifū Yanagidaru, 17).

field_history_ja.value: 「待ち兼ね」という語による連想から「津の国の待兼山の呼子鳥鳴けどいま来といふ人もなし」（古今六帖）、「来ぬ人を待兼山の呼子鳥同じ心にあはれとぞ聞く」（詞花集・春・肥後）のように「呼子鳥」とともに詠まれることが多かったが、のちには「夜をかさねまちかね山のほととぎす雲ゐのよそに一声ぞきく」（新古今・夏・周防内侍）のように「ほととぎず」と詠まれることが増えた。近世期には「待ち兼ねる」の洒落た表現として「待兼山の時鳥」を用いられ、「四条川原の芝居側、朝はとうからとうからと、待兼山の時鳥、それは町中のじゃれ詞」（浄瑠璃「本朝二十四孝」）、「ヲヽ、其便リ待兼山の時鳥、早ふ聞たい。早ふ呼べ〳〵」 （歌舞伎「大塔宮曦鎧」）、「肴売りまちかね山のほととぎす」（誹風柳多留・十七）など芸能・俳諧からの用例が確認できる。

field_topography_en.value: A mountain on the western edge of the Senri ridge in Toyonaka City, Ōsaka Prefecture. It is about 77 meters high and the remains of the Machikane-yama burial mound (kofun) are located there. The site is now a residential area, but the topography suggests that the tomb was originally a south-facing keyhole-shaped mound (zenpō kōen-fun). It is a scenic spot along the Nishikuni Highway and is mentioned in the Makura no sōshi (13, Mountains): "Mount Miwa is beautiful. Also Tamuke, Mount Machikane and Mount Tamasaka.” In 1964, the first crocodile fossil in Japan was discovered on the campus of the Faculty of Science of Ōsaka University and was named machikane-wani (Machikane crocodile; Toyotamaphimeia machikanensis). It is also the location of the Toyonaka Campus of Ōsaka university.

field_topography_ja.value: 大阪府豊中市、千里丘陵西端にある山。標高77メートルで、待兼山古墳の跡が残っている。現在その場所は宅地となっているが、地形からみて、もとは南向きの前方後円墳であったことが想定されている。西国街道沿いの景勝地で、『枕草子』（十三・山）に「三輪の山をかし。たむけ山。まちかね山。たまさか山。みみなし山」と記されている。1964年、大阪大学理学部構内から日本で初めてワニの化石が発見され、マチカネワニと命名された。大阪大学豊中キャンパスが位置する地でもある。

attributes.title: 松島

field_history_en.value: Since the Heian period (794-1185), Matsushima has been known as a utamakura, appearing in anthologies, monogatari, diaries and travelogues, and many people have visited the island since the time of Saigyō Hōshi (a Japanese poet, 1118-1190). In poems, the place “Ojima” and “fisher” are often mentioned together as in the poem “In Matsushina, are the sleeves of the fishermen who are collecting clam on the shore of Ojima as drenched as mine?” (Goshūishū, Love 4, Minamoto no Shigeyuki) and in the poem “In Matsushima , the waves that reach the shore of Ojima reflect like ice in the moonshine while plovers sing” (Shunzei no musume shū). In addition, the kakekotoba “matsu” (to wait) is often used. In the early modern period, Matsuo Bashō praised Matsushima in Oku no hosomichi as "the most beautiful scenery in Japan", and the Haiku poet Ōyodo Michikaze left behind the Matsushima chōbō-shū (Collection of the Views of Matsushima). There are many memorial stones with haiku poems in Ojima and other islands, as well as a large number of waka poems, haiku poems, travelogues, and reports of the famous place, that are preserved until today, and which illustrate the prominence of Matsushima.

field_history_ja.value: 松島は平安時代から歌枕として知られ、歌集・物語・日記・紀行などに登場、西行以来訪れる人も多い。「松島や雄島の磯にあさりせし海人の袖こそかくは濡れしか」（後拾遺集・恋四・重之）、「松島や雄島が磯による浪の月の氷に千鳥なくなり」（俊成女集）のように、「雄島」という地名や「海人」と一緒に詠まれることが多い。なお「待つ」を掛詞にした表現も多数みられる。近世期に入ってからは、芭蕉が『奥の細道』で「扶桑第一の好風」と讃えて松島に一節をさき、俳人の大淀三千風は『松島眺望集』を残した。雄島などに残る多くの句碑や、現在に遺る多数の和歌・俳句・紀行文・名跡誌などが、松島の著名ぶりをものがたっている。

field_topography_en.value: A scenic spot in Matsushima Bay, in the center of Miyagi Prefecture, it has a beautiful scenery with more than 260 islands of various sizes which have been formed by sea erosion and are densely covered with pine trees. The view from Ōtakamori, Toyama, Mount Ōgidani and Mount Tamon is especially beautiful and is known as the four great views of Matsushima. The Zuigan-ji Temple, Godai-dō Hall, Shiogama Shrine, and the Kanrantei Building are famous tourist attractions. Since the beginning of the Edo period Matsushima has been regarded as one of the "Three Views of Japan" (Nihonkoku  jiseki-kō) along with Amanohashidate and Aki no Miyajima (Itsukushima). At the mouth of the bay lies Katsura-jima and other large islands, making the bay an inland sea. Sabusawa island developed as a port for the shipment of rice (tribute) and in the early Meiji period the port of Ishihama on Katsura island also played an important role.

field_topography_ja.value: 宮城県中部、松島湾一帯の景勝地で、海食により奇観を呈する大小260余の島があり、松が茂る。大高森・富山・扇谷山・多聞山からの眺望がすぐれ、これらは松島四大観と称される。瑞巌寺・五大堂・塩竈神社・観瀾亭などが観光名所として有名である。江戸時代初期より天橋立・安芸の宮島（厳島）とともに「三処の奇観」（『日本国事跡考』）の一とされた。湾口には、桂島などの大島が横たわり湾内を内海と化し、寒風沢は城米の積出港として発達、明治初期、桂島の石浜港も加わって重要な役割を果たした。

attributes.title: 御熊野

field_history_en.value:
As an utamakura it is often used in the form of “Mikumano ura”, “Makumano” as mentioned in the Man’yōshū is another form of “Mikumano” (“Could these be fishermen of Shima in the Land of Miketsu? You can see them row a small boats of Kumano along the shore.”, Book 6, Ōtomo no Yakamochi). In connection with “Mikumano no ura” a lily (Crinum asiaticum), a perennial plant of the family of Amaryllidaceae is often mentioned. The Man’yōshū poem “Just like the leaves of the spider lily on the shore of Mikumano are layered a hundred times, I keep thinking of you, but I cannot  meet you in person.” (Man’yōshū, Book 4, Kakinomoto no Hitomaro) served as reference for many later poems: „As I look into my beloved’s heart, that is like the lily of Kumano, how many layers might it have?” (Shūishū, Love 4, Taira no Kanemori), and “Just like the lily at the coast of Mikumano I shall think of you wholeheartedly when evening comes.”  (Kanesuke shū) All of these waka were composed as love poems using expressions such “a hundredfold” and “single layered” in reference to the layered leaves of the lily. On the other hand, there is a small number of poems in which the word “resentment” (urami) is used in connection with “Mikuma no ura”: “I have seen him as a cold person, even though I resent him, why do I still miss him?” (Shikashū, Love 2, Izumi Shikibu).

Fudarakusan-ji Tempel is situated here, famous for dispatching high ranking priests to discover Fudaraku (Potalaka) in the south sea. In the Tale of the Heike (Vol. 10) and Genpei seisuiki (Vol. 41), there is the story of Taira no Koremori, who set sail from the Hamanomiya Shrine and threw himself into the sea to attain rebirth. The Fūgashū contains a poem by Kenreimon’in Ukyō no daibu, "How sad to see a this ill fate, to sink into the waves of the sea at Kumano bay," which she composed when she heard that Koremori had died in the sea.

field_history_ja.value: 歌枕としては「御熊野浦（みくまのうら）」のかたちでよく使われており、『万葉集』にみられる「ま熊野」も「み熊野」と同じである（「御食つ国志摩の海人ならしま熊野の小舟に乗りて沖辺漕ぐ見ゆ」巻六・家持）。なお「御熊野の浦」はヒガンバナ科の多年草「浜木綿（はまゆふ）」とともに詠まれる場合が多く、「み熊野の浦の浜木綿百重なす心は思へど直に逢はぬかも」（万葉・巻四・人麻呂）を本歌にして、「さしながら人の心をみ熊野の浦の浜木綿幾重なるらむ」（拾遺集・恋四・兼盛）、「み熊野の浦の浜木綿夕されば我もひとへに思ひやはする」（兼輔集）といった多くの和歌がつくられた。一方、少数ではあるが、「いくかへりつらしと人をみ熊野のうらめしながら恋しかるらむ」（詞花集・恋下・和泉式部）など、「み熊野の浦」に「恨み」を掛けて詠んだ歌もある。補陀落渡海の住僧を出した寺院として名高い補陀洛山寺が位置し、「平家物語」巻一〇・「源平盛衰記」巻四一には浜宮王子の前から船出して入水往生をとげる平維盛の話がある。これに関連して、「風雅集」には「左近中将維盛熊野の浦にて失せにける由聞きてよみ侍りける」との詞書がある、建礼門院右京大夫の「悲しくも斯る憂き目を三熊野の浦わの波に身を沈めける」が載る。

field_topography_en.value: Kumano is an area on the coast in the southern part of the Kii Peninsula, centred in Kumano village, Muro District, Kii Province (present-day Shingū City, Wakayama Prefecture). It is also known by the name "Mikumano" with the honorific prefix "御" (mi). Today it refers to the coast facing Kumano-nada in Wakayama Prefecture, but originally it encompassed a large area extending as far as Mugisaki in Shima District, Mie Prefecture (Ise Province). The word "Mikumano", a homophone (written with the character of “three” and “Kumano”), refers to the three Shrines of Kumano: the Kumano Nimasu Shrine (the former name of Kumano Hongu-Taisha), the Kumano Hayatama-Taisha and the Kumano-Nachi-Taisha. They were sacred places for mountain asceticism.

field_topography_ja.value: 熊野は紀伊国牟婁郡熊野郷（現和歌山県新宮市）を中心とした紀伊半島南部の海岸の一帯で、「御（み）」の接頭語をつけた「御熊野」の美称でよく知られている。現在は和歌山県の熊野灘に面した海岸をさすが、本来は三重県（伊勢国）の志摩郡麦崎あたりまで及ぶ広い地域を意味した。同じ発音の「三熊野」といえば、熊野坐（クマノニマス）神社（熊野本宮大社の旧称）・熊野速玉大社・熊野那智大社の三社からなる熊野三山のことで、山伏修行の霊地であった。

attributes.title: 絵島

field_history_en.value: As one can see from the Yakumo mishō in which Ejima is mentioned as “(W)ejima”, “rocky seashore of Ejima”, and “cape Ejima”, Ejima is often mentioned in waka poems as “rocky seashore of Ejima”, “cape Ejima” and the “seashore of Ejima”. In connection with “picturesque (絵)”, „colour/love“ and „to change colour” is used: "Oh, how do the white waves seem to beat against the shore when the wind blows, is this the colour of Ejima" (Fujiwara no Norinaga-shū). And in connection with Suma and Akashi on the opposite shore, “plover” and “moon” are mentioned, as in: “At the seashore of Ejima, where the plovers sing, I see the reflection of the shining moon in the waves, this evening” (Sankashū). In the section 204 of the Makura no sōshi “Ejima” is mentioned among the islands appropriate for waka and chapter 5 “moon viewing” of the Heike monogatari refers to the year 1180 in which in order to see the moon at a famous spot the people living in the new capital in Fukuhara went “from Suma along the seashore of Akashi, crossing the Awaji Strait to the rocky shore of Ejima to view the moon”. This suggests that it was considered as a scenic spot.

field_history_ja.value: 『八雲御抄』に「ゑじま」「ゑじまが磯」「ゑじまが崎」があげられたように、和歌の中では「絵島が磯」「絵島が崎」「絵島の浦」のかたちで使われる場合が多く、「絵」の縁で「風吹けばあらふと見ゆる白浪のいかに色どる絵島なるらむ」（教長集）のごとく「色」「色どる」とともに詠まれるか、対岸の「須磨」「明石」との縁で「千鳥なく絵島の浦にすむ月を浪にうつして見る今宵かな」（山家集）のごとく「千鳥」「月」とともに詠まれることもある。また、『枕草子』第二〇四段には「島は…」として「絵島」が言及されており、「平家物語」巻五「月見」には、治承四年（一一八〇）福原の新都に住む人々が名所の月を見るために「須磨より明石の浦づたひ、淡路のせとをおしわたり、絵嶋が磯の月をみる」という件があり、景勝地として考えられていたことが窺える。

field_topography_en.value: It is a small rocky island facing the sea on the east side of the northern end of Awaji Island, in present-day Iwaya, Awaji-chō, Tsuna-gun, Hyōgo Prefecture. The island has a circumference of about 400 meters. Since ancient times it has been known as a famous place for the moon. If viewed from the south-east, Ejima looks like a deserted island. The name derives from the picturesque (絵) appearance of the vermilion to dark brown striped sedimentary rocks. It is one of the islands reputed to be the “Onogoro Island” appearing in the myth of the creation of Japan.

attributes.title: 姨捨山

field_history_en.value: According to the 156th story in the Yamato monogatari a man living in Sarashina, urged by his wife, was about to abandon his aunt on the top of the mountain, when he composed the following poem "Above the mountain– / Old Forsaken Woman of / Sarashina the/ melancholy moon shines  how/ inconsolable my heart" (Kokinshū, Miscellaneous I, Poet unknown; English translation by Rodd, Laurel Rasplica; and Henkenius, Mary Catherine (1984): p.302). And he went to bring her back. It is said that because of this the mountain is called Obasuteyama (or oyasute “abandoning a parent”). Even though there are slight differences the same story can be found in the Konjaku monogatarishū and Toshiyori zuinō. It is also a famous place for viewing the moon as shown by poems from well-known poets: "I should be lamenting my unenlightened heart, as I regard the moon at Obasuteyama [whose essence] I am so ignorant of " (Shinchokusen-shū, Saigyō); “Haven’t I seen tonight’s moon in the past, when I spent the night at Obasuteyama in Sarashina” (Shinchokusen-shū, Nōin); "When I hear that you are going to Obasuteyama, I will keep on looking at the moon with longing” (Shokugoshūi-shū, Ki no Tsurayuki) and “At Sarashina, is it the light of the moon of old days? It is the autumn wind! At Obasuteyama” (Shūigusō, Fujiwara no Sadaie).  In the Nō play “Obasute” a person from the capital who went to Obasute to view the moon meets an old woman who was abandoned on the mountain. In the Sarashina kikō Matsuo Bashō wrote, "The autumn wind inspired me to go to see Sarashina village and the moon over Mount Obasute. It stirred my heart, and there was another man seduced by wind and clouds, named Etsujin.” and he left several famous haiku.

field_history_ja.value: 『大和物語』百五十六段によれば、更級に住む男が、妻のすすめで山の頂に捨てた伯母を「我心なぐさめかねつ更科やをばすて山にてる月を見て」（古今・雑上・読人しらず）と歌い、迎えに行ったというところから姨（親）捨山と名づけられたと伝わり、異同はあるが、『今昔物語集』『俊成髄脳』からも同様な内容が確認できる。なお、月の名所として有名で、「あらはさぬ我が心をぞうらむべき月やはうとき姨捨の山」（新勅撰集・西行）、「更科や姨捨山に旅寝してこよひの月を昔見しかな」（新勅撰集・能因）、「君がゆく所と聞けば月見つゝ姨捨山ぞ恋しかるべき」（続後拾遺集・紀貫之）、「さらしなは昔の月のひかりかはたゞ秋風ぞ姨捨の山」（拾遺愚草・定家）など、著名な歌人による歌が残されている。謡曲「姨捨」には、都の人が姨捨の月を観に来たところ、捨てられた老女が現れたという物語が収録されており、『更科紀行』のなか、松尾芭蕉は「さらしなの里、おばすて山の月見ん事、しきりにすゝむる秋風の、心に吹さはぎて、ともに風雲の情をくるはするもの又ひとり、越人と云」と書きおこし、多くの名句を残している。
