field_topography_en.value: This is another name for Mount Kamuriki, also known as Mount Sarashina, in present-day Kōshoku City, Nagano Prefecture. The Mountain is approximately 1252 meters high and rises on the border of Chikuma City and Chikuhoku Village. Even though it has a round hilltop (dome-shaped) and is not very high, it is steep and covered with forest. Not only has the mountain been known since ancient times as the mountain of the Obasuteyama legend (“abandoning an old woman”), but it has also been a famous site for viewing the moon since the Heian-period. Especially the picturesque scenery at the slope overlooking the Nagano Basin, which is lined with small rice paddies in which the moon is reflected (tagoto no tsuki) and the moon rising behind the Mountain Kyōdai on the other side are well known. In 1999 it was designated as a national place of scenic beauty “Obasute (Tagoto no tsuki)”.

field_topography_ja.value: 現在の長野県更埴市にある冠着山の別称で、更級山ともいう。標高1252メートル。千曲市 、筑北村の境にそびえて山容は円頂丘をなし、標高は高くないが、全体に険しく全山森林に覆われている。古来、姥捨山伝説 のある山として知られるほか、平安時代以来、観月の名所としても有名である。とくに長野盆地に臨む斜面一帯は小さな水田が階段状に並んでいるが、その水田に映る月（「田毎の月」）や、対岸の鏡台山に昇る月は絶景であり、国の名勝として1999年に「姨捨（田毎の月）」が指定された。

attributes.title: 淡路潟

field_history_en.value: Awajigata was already mentioned in the Man’yōshū, but it is particularly famous for the poem quoted in the “Akashi” volume of the Genji monogatari "on Awaji Isle/ seen but dimly in distant/ skies     did tonight’s bright/ moon seem nearer to me just because of where I am now" (Shinkokinshū, Miscellaneous I, Ōshikōchi no Mitsune; English translation by Rodd, Laurel Rasplica (2015): p.622) and for the poem by Minamoto no Kanemasa appearing in the Hyakunin isshu and Kin’yōshū "Those plovers crying/ between Awaji Isle and land – /how many long nights/ do they keep the guards from sleep/ at their posts on Suma’s shore.” (English translation by Carter, Steven D. (1991): p.230-231.). Those had a great influence on later waka poems about Awaji. For example, ”From the bay at Sumiyoshi, I am regarding the moon setting in the West behind the Mountain of Awaji Island.” (Juntokuin-shū) was influenced by the former poem and “At dusk when the tide is low in the strait of Awaji Island, the plovers coming from Suma, are calling." (Sankashū) is hinting at the latter poem. In all these waka, "the mountain of Awaji Island ", "Awaji strait" and “Awajigata (Awaji Lagoon)” are versions of Awaji Island. The image of many waka poems about Awaji are – as the character 淡 “faint, thin” indicates – based on the image of a hazy, misty sea and the shining of the full moon.

field_history_ja.value: 淡路潟は早く『万葉集』にも見えるが、『源氏物語』明石の巻に引かれた「淡路にてあはとはるかに見し月の近き今宵は所がらかも」（新古今集・雑上・躬恒）と『百人一首』『金葉集』に収録された源兼昌の「淡路島かよふ千鳥の鳴く声に幾夜寝ざめぬ須磨の関守」が特に有名で、後世の淡路を詠んだ和歌に多大な影響を与えた。例えば、「住吉の浦よりをちになりにけり月見る西の淡路島山」（順徳院集）は前者の例で、「淡路島瀬戸の潮干の夕暮に須磨よりかよふ千鳥鳴くなり」（山家集）は後者の例にあたる本歌取りだが、これらの和歌に詠まれた「淡路島山」「淡路の瀬戸」は「淡路潟」と同じく淡路島のことを意味する。なお、「淡」の字から淡路を詠んだ和歌の中には、あわく霞んだ海上の雰囲気や、くまなき月影のイメージを踏まえたものが多い。

field_topography_en.value: Awajigata refers to the coast of Awaji Island, especially the area around Akashi. Awaji Island is located in the eastern part of the Seto-Inland Sea and is its largest island. It is divided from Honshū by the Akashi Strait in the north and the Kitan Strait in the east, and from Shikoku by the Naruto Strait in the west. It has an area of approximately 591 square kilometres. It is the fifth largest island in Japan, after Okinawa, Sado, Amami-Ōshima, and Tsushima, excluding Honshū, Hokkaidō, Kyūshū, Shikoku, and the islands Iturup and Kunashir. It is known as the first island created by Izanagi no Mikoto and Izanami no Mikoto, which is mentioned in the Nihon shoki and Kojiki.

field_topography_ja.value: 淡路潟は淡路島の海岸のことで、とりわけ明石に面したあたりをさす。淡路島は瀬戸内海の東部に浮ぶ瀬戸内海最大の島で、北は明石海峡、東は紀淡海峡によって本州と分たれ、西は鳴門海峡によって四国と分たれている。面積は約五九一平方キロ。本州・北海道・九州・四国および択捉島・国後島を除けば、沖縄島・佐渡島・奄美大島・対馬に次ぐ第五位の面積を持つ。『日本書紀』『古事記』に見えるイザナギの命・イザナミの命が最初に作った島として知られている。

field_history_en.value: In the Heian period (794-1185), Ishiyama was a sacred place for the worship of Kannon, and was visited by many women from the capital. It is mentioned in literary works such as Kagerō nikki, Izumi shikibu nikki, Genji monogatari and Sarashina nikki. In the medieval annotations to Genji monogatari, the legend emerged, that Murasaki Shikibu visited Ishiyama Temple, worked on the Genji monogatari and drafted the Suma scroll while looking at the reflection of the moon on Lake Biwa. Like in the "Autumn Moon of Ishiyama", one of The Eight Views of Ōmi, Ishiyama is often mentioned together with the “moon” in waka poetry. An important example is: In the capital/ surely, they must be waiting – / on Ishiyama’s/ peak it lingers a bright moon/ in the chilly autumn night (Shinkokinshū, book 16: Miscellaneous I, Fujiwara no Nagatō; English translation by Rodd, Laurel Rasplica (2015): p.621). There are also poems in which the word “rock, cliff” (iwao) is used such as: “On this day that hardly seems to dawn, I got to know Ishiyama with its mountain rock to pray at” (Kintōshū).

field_history_ja.value: 平安時代に観音信仰の聖地として都の女性たちが多く出かけた地で、『蜻蛉日記』『和泉式部日記』『源氏物語』『更級日記』などの文学作品でも言及されている。中世の『源氏物語』注釈書には紫式部が石山に参詣して作品を執筆し、琵琶湖の湖上に映る月を見ながら須磨の巻を構想したなどという伝説が記されている。「石山の秋月」が近江八景の一つに数えられているように、和歌において石山は「月」とともに詠まれることが多く、「都にも人や待つらむ石山の峰に残れる秋の夜の月」（新古今集・雑上・長能）はその代表的な例である。なお、「暮れがたき今日にて知りぬ石山の山のいはほを祈るしるしは」（公任集）のように「いはほ（巌）」を詠んだ歌もある。

field_topography_en.value: It is a district in the southern part of Ōtsu City, Shiga Prefecture, which encompasses the Seta River in the east and the Mount Otowa and Mount Kasatori in the west and extends to Kyōto. It is famous for the "Autumn Moon at Ishiyama", in The Eight Views of Ōmi, and the "Clear Stream at Seta Ishiyama", in the The Eight Views of Lake Biwa. The name "Ishiyama" is said to have originated from the exposed Wollastonite (keikai-seki, designated a national natural monument) in the area of the Ishiyama Temple. There are remains of shell mounds in archaeological sites in Ishiyama and Hotarudani, and the construction of Emperor Kōken's palace, called Horanomiya, is also said to have taken place in this area. In the Nara period (710-794), the Ishiyama-in was established, which managed the transport of lumber to Heijō-kyō (etc.). It was the predecessor of the Ishiyama Temple. In the Heian period (794-1185), Ishiyama Temple became a center of Shingon Buddhism and was a site of worship of the imperial family, aristocrats, and common people. This led to a flourishing of the “pilgrimage to Ishiyama”. Because of its strategic location, the area was often the scene of battles and small forts were built (although the decade-long battle of Ishiyama between Oda Nobunaga and the Jōdo-Shinshū Honganji forces (1570-1580) took place in a different location, in Ishiyama in Settsu Province).

field_topography_ja.value: 滋賀県大津市南部の一地区で、東は瀬田川、西は音羽山、笠取山を越えて京都に連なる一帯である。近江八景の「石山の秋月」、琵琶湖八景の「瀬田石山の清流」で著名な景勝地である。石山寺山内には硅灰石の露出（国の天然記念物）がみられるが、これが石山の名の由来であるといわれる。石山貝塚、蛍谷貝塚などの遺跡があり、孝謙天皇の離宮保良宮の造営が伝えられる地でもある。奈良時代には平城京などへの木材運搬をつかさどる石山院が設立され、この石山院が石山寺の前身となった。平安時代に入ると石山寺は真言宗の道場として皇室、貴族、庶民の信仰を集め、「石山詣」が盛んであった。交通の要衝であるため、しばしば合戦場となり、小城砦なども設けられた（但し、織田信長と浄土真宗本願寺勢力との十年にわたる石山合戦（1570～1580）が起こったのは摂津国石山で、別の場所である）。

attributes.title: 浅間

field_history_en.value: It has a majestic appearance emitting plumes of smoke, but it erupted violently sometimes. In the Nihon shoki, first month of the 14th year (685) of Emperor Tenmu’s reign, it is written that “this month ash fell in Shinano and all the trees and plants withered away.” In the year Tenmei 3 (1783), a large eruption claimed many deaths and Onioshidashi and other lava flows were formed. There is also the prefectural-run Asama farm in Naganohara at the foot of the northeastern mountain, and in recent years efforts have been focused on tourism development. In Tsumagoi village situated to the north and northeast, Onioshidashi, which was formed by the lava flow of the Tenmei eruption, remains and northwest of the same village are more than 450 lava tree moulds (a nationally designated natural monument). The Asama-Shirane volcano route, which runs along the northeastern foothills of the mountain, is often used by tourists. Because it is an active volcano, its volcanic smoke was often compared to the emotion of a burning love in waka poetry. On the other hand, there was also a way to derive the word asamashi (miserable) from asama using homophone repetition. The landscape itself is rarely included in poems.

field_history_ja.value: 噴煙をあげつつ雄大な姿をみせているが、ときには激しい噴火をした。『日本書紀』天武天皇一四年（685）一月条に「是月、灰信濃国に零り、草木皆枯」とみえる。天明3年（1783）の大爆発では多数の死者を出し、溶岩流は鬼押出（おにおしだし）などを形成した。北東山麓の長野原町には県営の浅間牧場もあるが、近年は観光開発に力が入れられている。北から北東にかけての嬬恋村に天明の噴火によって形成された溶岩流鬼押出しが残り、北西方（同村）には四五〇以上の溶岩樹型（国指定天然記念物）もある。北東麓を通る浅間白根火山ルートは回遊観光客の利用が多い。活火山であるため、和歌では、その噴煙を燃えた恋の思いにたとえることが多かった。一方、同音反復で「あさま」から「あさまし」を導き出すよみ方もあった。風景が詠まれる場合はまれである。

field_topography_en.value: Mt. Asama is an active complex volcano straddling Shinano Province (now Nagano Prefecture) and Kōzuke Province (now Gunma Prefecture). It is 2568 meters high and is mainly composed of andesite. In Nōin utamakura, it is the utamakura of Shinano Province. It is a typical active volcano of Japan that has repeatedly erupted since the start of recorded history (685 AD). Although it is located at the junction of both the Nasu and Fuji volcanic belts, it is usually classified as belonging to the former.

attributes.title: 安達

field_history_en.value: Adachigahara is mentioned as a famous place topic (meisho-dai) in the Saishō shitennōin shōjiwaka (1207) and Kenpō meisho hyakushu (1215). It became known as an utamakura through Taira no Kanemori’s poem “Is it true what I hear, that a demon has hidden in the black mould in Adachigahara of Michinoku” (78) from the Yamato monogatari (chapter 58). The Nō play Adachigahara (also called Kurozuka) and the jōruri called Ōshū Adachigahara by Chikamatsu Hanji e.a. from the early modern period, tell the story of a medieval ascetic monk, who stayed one night in the house of a demonic old women and after finding a pile of corpses fled pursued by the demon. In waka poetry, there is an early reference to the place in the Kokin wakashū, “If I were to draw the bow of sandalwood of Adachi, the tips would turn towards me. In the same way, you should come close to me, but unnoticed.” (1078) Many of the poems use the metaphor of a bow made from white sandalwood, that is believed to have grown in this region and they have been greatly influenced by the poem “The white sandalwood of Adachinohara in Michinoku; it is you who seems cold hearted” (Shūi wakashū, poet unknown). Later, Adachinohara, which began with the legend of the demon from Kurozuka, seems to have dispelled this uncanny image and became known as a hunting ground, reminiscent of the Mutsu wilderness.

field_history_ja.value: 「安達原」は『最勝四天王院障子和歌』と『建保名所百首』の名所題とされる。『大和物語』58段にいう平兼盛の「みちのくの安達の原の黒塚に鬼こもれりと聞くはまことか」（78）の歌によって歌枕として知られるようになった。中世には山伏が鬼女の老婆の家に宿り、死骸の山を見て逃げ出し、追いかけてきた鬼女を折伏するという内容の謡曲「安達原」（「黒塚」とも）、近世には近松半二らの浄瑠璃「奥州安達原」が作られる。和歌では、早く『古今集』神遊びの歌に採物の歌として「みちのくの安達のま弓わが引かば末さへ寄り来忍び忍びに」（1078）と歌われる。また、「陸奥の安達の原の白まゆみ心こはくも見ゆる君かな」（拾遺集・恋四・読人不知）の影響も大きく、この地に多く生えていたと思われる白木の檀で作った弓すなわち白真弓を比喩にした歌が多い。後に黒塚の鬼伝説からはじまった安達の原も、次第に鬼伝説のイメージを払拭して陸奥の原野をイメージさせ、狩場としてのイメージを付与されてゆくようだ。

field_topography_en.value: The area around the eastern foot of Mt. Adatara in present-day Adachi District, Fukushima Prefecture. It used to be a site for rearing horses and manufacturing bows. It is known for the tale of Kurozuka, which tells of an onibaba that lived in Adachigahara, as well as the Nō song Kurozuka. Its remains extend to the east of Nihonmatsu, Adachi District.

attributes.title: 片野

field_history_en.value: The place name Katano first appears in the Shoku nihongi in the chapter on the second month of Hōki 2 (771) in the “Imperial visit to Katano” and it appears occasionally thereafter. Emperor Kanmu often visited this area for hunting. Since Katano rikyū was completed, it has been used as a hunting ground for members of the imperial palace and falconry was performed there as a prayer for a good omen, therefore, it was also called Katano no mino (imperial field). The place name Kin‘ya still remains in present-day Hirakata City. It became famous in the world of literature under the influence of Narihira’s poem “If there were no cherry blossoms in this world – how tranquil would our hearts be in spring”, composed at the Nagisa Palace in Katano in chapter 82 of the Ise monogatari. In the Horikawa hyakushu section on falconry, five poets composed on Katano. In the Kenpō meisho hyakushu and the Saishō shitennō-in shōjiwaka, Katano appears as a topic. It is also a famous place for cherry blossom viewing.

field_history_ja.value: 「交野」という地名の初見は『続日本紀』宝亀2年（771）二月庚子条の「車駕幸交野」であり、以後散見する。桓武天皇はこの地にしばしば行幸し遊猟を行った。その交野離宮以来、禁裏御料の狩場とされ、日次の贄として鷹狩が行われたため、「交野の御野」ともいう。今も枚方市に禁野という地名が残っている。文学の世界で有名になったのは、『伊勢物語』八二段、交野の渚の院での業平の詠「世の中に絶えて桜なかりせば春の心はのどけからまし」の影響である。『堀河百首』の「鷹狩」題では、五名の歌人が「交野」を詠んでいる。『建保名所百首』および『最勝四天王院障子和歌』では、「交野」が設題された。桜の名所としても有名。

field_topography_en.value: An ancient hunting ground in Kawachi Province (Ōsaka Prefecture). It was also written as 郊野 and 片野 as well as referred to as Todachigahara, Momoegahara and Nagisaokahara. It refers to the entire relatively low hill area within Katano, extending from present-day Katano City in Ōsaka Prefecture to Hirakata City. The geographical scope is as follows: to the east it reaches the low hills of the Ikoma Mountains, which extend north to south; to the west it reaches the Yodo River; to the south the Amano River which originates from the eastern Ikoma-system and as for east and north, it is said to extend to Yamato, Yamashiro and Sakai.

field_topography_ja.value: 河内国（大阪府）の古代の遊猟地。郊野・片野とも書き、鳥立原・百重原・渚岡原の別称もある。同国交野郡内の比較的低い丘陵地帯全域を指し、現在の大阪府交野市から枚方市にかけての一帯をいう。地域的範囲は、南北にのびる生駒山系の低丘陵を東限とし、西は淀川、南は東生駒系を源とする天の川、東・北は大和・山城両国堺までといわれる。

attributes.title: 葛城

field_history_en.value: According to the Jinmu-ki in the Nihon shoki, the place name originates from a tale of imperial troops catching tsuchigumo (a term for renegade local clans) with nets woven from kuzu (arrowroot) and slaying them. Mt. Kongō and Mt. Yamato-Kazuraki are still known as areas for growing and gathering kuzu. The second character 城 is said to be used in Chinese (Tang) fashion with an aesthetic meaning. It is the home of the Kazuraki clan, a powerful family of ancient Yamato, and the birthplace of Emperor Nintoku's empress, Iwanohime. It is the place where shrines such as the one for the god Hitokotonushi, and gods from the Izumo context like Kotoshironushi, Ajisukitakahikone who were venerated by the Yamato court, are located, and it is thought to have originally been the base of a force that opposed the Yamato court. In the Nō play Kazuraki, the name of Mt. Katsuragi is said to have originated from an act of mountain worship that involved tying kuzu vines together to form a shrine. Mt. Katsuragi is an utamakura in numerous poems from the Man’yōshū. It is one of the founding sites of Shugendō, and especially in light of the old and well-known legend of the god Hitokotonushi, the gods Kumeji and Katsuragi were mentioned in poems or in the prefaces to poems in combination with the word “naka (仲, 中)” in a metaphorical way, which became an established format in Heian poetry. On the other hand, combinations with words such as “clouds” and “snow” evoke the image of a high mountain, in particular the highest peak of the mountain range (supposedly Mt. Kongō), capped by white clouds, that was also used as a symbol of a lover who was difficult to reach. Furthermore, building on this connection with clouds, many poems about distant views of cherry blossoms have been composed.

field_history_ja.value: 『日本書紀』「神武紀」によれば、地名は、葛（クズ）の網で土蜘蛛を掩殺したことに由来する。金剛、葛城山中はいまもクズが生え葛根の採集地として知られる。「城」は唐風の美称的意味をもつ用字であるという。古代大和の豪族葛城氏の本拠地、仁徳天皇の皇后磐之媛の出身地である。大和朝廷も一目を置いた一言主の神や、出雲系の事代主・味耜高彦根などの神の社の鎮座する地で、元来は大和朝廷と対立する勢力の根拠地と思われる。謡曲「葛城」には、葛の蔓を結って神籬を立てるという山岳信仰から起こったという葛城山の名の由来について説いている。「葛城山」は歌枕として、『万葉集』から数多く詠まれてきた。修験道の拠点の一つで、特に古くから有名である一言主神の伝説を踏まえ、「久米路の神」「葛城の神」などの語を用いて、多く比喩あるいは序詞的文脈の中で「葛城」を詠み、「なか（仲・中）」に言及する、というのが平安以来の用法の一典型であった。一方、「雲」や「雪」との取り合わせは高山としてのイメージを感じさせ、特に、連山の最高峰高間山（金剛山とされる）が白雲を頂く様子は、容易に手の届きがたい恋の相手の象徴としても用いられた。さらに、雲との結合の発展として、桜の遠望の歌も多く詠まれている。

attributes.field_spot_name_furigana: かつらぎ（古くはかづらき）

field_topography_en.value: An old common name for the area that spans present-day Kita-Katsuragi District, Yamato-Takada City and Gose City in Nara Prefecture. It is also written as 葛木. It is located on the eastern foot of Mt. Kongō. The Katsuragi River flows from south to north parallel to the Soga River, which flows into the Yamato River. Roads such as Tatsutamichi and Ōsakagoe, which connect Yamato Province and Kawachi Province, all crossed through this region. The road to Kii, passing through the southern part of this area was also important. Having a higher elevation than the Yamato Basin, it forms an area called Katsuragi no kuni. It has been an important place since the ancient time as one of the six prefectures of the Yamato court. The old road that runs from north to south at the eastern foot of Mt. Katsuragi has been maintained as Katsuragi no michi, and the Katsuragi-no-michi History Museum has also been built there. In 2004, Taima Town and Shinjō Town in Kita-Katsuragi District merged to form Katsuragi City.

field_topography_ja.value: 今の奈良県北葛城郡・大和高田市・御所市にわたる地域の古代の汎称。「葛木」とも書く。金剛山地の東麓。南から葛城川が北に向かって貫流し、その東側を平行して北流する曾我川として大和川に注ぐ。大和から河内へ越える竜田道や大阪越え、竹の内越えなどの諸道はすべてこの地を通過し、紀伊ヘ越える道もこの地の南部を通過する要地であった。大和平野より高みをなし「葛城の国」と呼ばれる一区画を形成し、古くから重要な意味を持つ地で、大和朝廷の六つの御県（ミアガタ）の一つであった。葛城山東麓を南北に延びる古街道が「葛城の道」として整備され、葛城の道歴史博物館も作られている。なお、2004年に北葛城郡の當麻町と新庄町が合併して、葛城市となっている。

attributes.title: 甲斐

field_history_en.value: During the Heian period many shōen were established and the grandchild of Minamoto no Yorinobu as well as Minamoto no Yoshimitsu, after being successively appointed to Kai, settled in the region. Yoshimitsu’s grandson Nobuyoshi introduced the name Takeda clan and established the Kai-Genji clan based on these shōen. The Takeda clan held the post of military governor during the Kamakura and Muromachi periods and during the Warring States period, when Takeda Shingen suppressed the rebellions of clans and exerted authority over neighbouring regions. However, during the time of his son Katsuyori, the clan was attacked and destroyed by Oda Nobunaga. Because it is located in an important area near Edo, feudal lords of the Tokugawa clan like Yoshinao were stationed there. But in 1724, it became a territory under the direct control of the Shogunate. As an utamakura, Kai appears in the Man’yōshū as Namayomi no Kai no kuni (Volume 3, 319, 322) in a poem about Mt. Fuji. It was often used as an expression connecting the words kai (買ひ) and iki-kayoi-ji (行き交ひ路). As an utamakura, it was featured often in poetic treatises such as the Waka dōmō shō and the Toshiyori zuinō and was used in the form of Kai ga (mi)ne, Kai no kuni, and Kai no kurokoma. Poems featuring the expressions Kai ga ne and Kai no shirane often depict snow-covered mountains.

field_history_ja.value: 平安時代には官牧・荘園が多く置かれ、源頼信の孫・新羅三郎義光が相次いで甲斐に任ぜられて以来土着し、義光の孫の信義が武田氏を称し、国内の荘園を基盤に甲斐源氏を興した。鎌倉・室町時代にも武田氏が守護で、戦国時代、武田信玄のとき、一族や諸氏の反抗を鎮め隣国を合せて威を振るったが、子の勝頼のとき、織田信長に攻められて滅亡した。江戸に近い重要な地にあるので、徳川義直らの親藩大名などが配置されたが、享保九年（1724）幕府直轄地となった。歌枕としての「甲斐」は、古く『万葉集』に「なまよみの甲斐の国」（巻三・319・322）と、富士山を詠む歌に登場する。「買ひ」と「行き交ひ路」を掛けた表現として、隠題のように詠み込まれたことが多かった。歌枕としては、『和歌童蒙書』や『俊頼髄脳』などの歌学書で多く注目され、「甲斐が嶺」や「甲斐の国」、「甲斐の黒駒」などの形で詠まれた。「甲斐が嶺」「甲斐のしらね」では、叙景的な、雪の深い山を詠むことが多い。

field_topography_en.value: It refers to present-day Yamanashi Prefecture, and lays on the Tōkaidō. It is a mountainous region surrounded to the east by Musashi and Sagami Province, to the south and west by Suruga Province and to the north by Shinano Province. Kai City is located on the east bank of the Kamanashi River in central Yamanashi Prefecture and there are remains of the Shingen embankment built by Takeda Shingen. In Kefuki Volume 4, paper, silk woven by hand, lacquer and wax are listed as special products of the region. Grapes, tobacco and the view of Mt. Fuji seen from behind are also famous and there are sacred sites such as Mt. Minobu. Cotton was popular during the Edo period, and today, in addition to growing grapes and other fruits, the electronic industry has developed.

field_topography_ja.value: 現在の山梨県を指す。東海道の一国。東は武蔵、相模、南、西は駿河、北は信濃に囲まれた山国。山梨県中部、釜無川東岸に甲斐市があり、武田信玄が築いた信玄堤の遺構がある。名産として、『毛吹・四』に、甲州判・郡内紬・紙・漆・ろうなどを挙げる。そのほか、ぶどう・たばこや裏から見る富士も名物であり、身延山などの霊場もある。江戸時代には綿花が盛んで、現在はぶどうなど果樹栽培のほか、電子産業も発達。

attributes.title: 佐野

field_history_en.value: The Sano pontoon bridge that once stood here is famous and became an utamakura from classical times. Its name appears in the Makura no sōshi and the Nōin utamakura, and it was chosen as one of the love themes in the Kenpō meisho hyakushu. It was also widely known as the hometown of Sano Genzaemon Tsuneyo through the Nō play Hachigi. In waka poetry, the Sano pontoon bridge was included in poems from Sano Province as early as the Man’yōshū. This pontoon bridge rested on a row of lined-up boats, and the distinctive poetic motive was that it was dismantled, the ships being separated. In the Heian period, words associated with the word “bridge”, such as “to cross (wataru)” and “to erect (kaku)”, were used in poems. They were especially often used in love poems in the form of “to keep yearning for (omoiwataru)”, “to remain in love (koiwataru)” and “to feel drawn to (omoikaku)”.

field_history_ja.value: ここにあった佐野舟橋が有名で、中古以降歌枕となった。『枕草子』と『能因歌枕』にその名が見え、『建保名所百首』では、恋題の一つとして選ばれている。また、佐野源左衛門常世の故地として、謡曲「鉢木」を通して広く知られていた。和歌では、早く『万葉集』に上野国の歌に「佐野舟橋」が詠まれ、「船橋」は船を並べてその上を渡した橋として、その「とりはなす」ことが特色としてとらえられていた。平安時代になると、「渡る」「掛く」などの「橋」の縁語が詠みこまれ、特に「思ひ渡る」「恋ひ渡る」「思ひかく」などの形で恋の歌に詠まれることが多くなった。

field_topography_en.value: An utamakura of Kōzuke Province. It is located on the shore of the Karasu River in what is now Kamisano, Takasaki City, Gunma Prefecture. Along the Karasu River the names of Kamisano and Shimosano remain unchanged. Southeast of the JR Station Takasaki, a little further from present-day Karasu River, is the Funagi no Kannon Monument. The poem “Like the pontoon bridge in Kamisano that is dismantled, my parents disunited us, but how could I be separated from you” from the Man’yōshū is engraved on its surface, and it is said to be a remnant of Sano’s pontoon bridge. There are also legends of love featuring the Karasu River, and the crossing of Sano (Sano no watashi) in the Nō play Hachigi refers to this pontoon bridge. Nearby are the Tokoyo Shrine, which is regarded as the remnant of Sano Genzaemon’s residence that Hōjō Tokiyori (Saimyō-ji nyūdō) has visited, as well as the Teika Shrine, dedicated to Fujiwara no Teika.

field_topography_ja.value: 上野国の歌枕。今の群馬県高崎市上佐野、烏川の沿岸に位置する。烏川沿いに上佐野町・下佐野町の地名が残る。JR高崎駅の南東、今の烏川よりすこし離れた所に「船木の観音の碑」がある。その表面に『万葉集』の「上野佐野の舟橋取り放し親はさくれど我はさかるがへ」の歌が刻され、佐野の舟橋の遺跡といわれる。これと烏川を挟んでの恋愛伝説もあり、また謡曲『鉢木』の佐野の渡も舟橋である。付近に最明寺入道北条時頼ゆかりの佐野源左衛門屋敷の遺跡とされる常世神社と、藤原定家を祀った定家神社がある。

attributes.title: 布留

field_history_en.value: In the book on Emperor Richū in the Nihon shoki, the Isonokami no furu no kami no miya (shrine) is mentioned. Furu is said to be originally the name of a sword enshrined there. In ancient times, the old town of Tenri and the area to the east was called Ishigami, and Furu was a part of that called Isonokami Furu. As an utamakura, it developed and became popular early on and was often used as a symbol of old things. Mt. Furu was also used in poems as a place for cherry blossoms. Moreover, there is a Nō play with the title Furu.

field_history_ja.value: 『日本書紀』履中天皇の条に「石上の振神宮（いそのかみのふるのかみのみや）」とある。「布留」は元来神宮に鎮座する剣の名という。古代は天理市旧市街とその東方一帯を石上といい、布留はその一部だったので、「石上布留」と呼び習わされた。歌枕として、早くから成熟し親しまれていたのであり、古いものの象徴として用いられることが多かった。また「布留の山」は桜の名所としても詠まれた。謡曲にも「布留」という作品がある。

field_topography_en.value: A place name for Tenri City in northern Nara Prefecture, located on the Furu River alluvial fan. It is the location of Isonokami Shrine. Mt. Furu is close by and the Furu river flows from Mt. Ryūō to join Hase River. Near Isonokami Shrine, the Furu archaeological site can be found, which date from the Jōmon to the Kofun periods as well as the Tenri Sankōkan Museum where artifacts excavated from this site are on display.

attributes.title: 木曾

field_history_en.value: The first time Kiso appears officially as a place name is in a passage dated from the 10th of the 12th month, Taihō 2 (702) in the Shoku nihongi where the “opening of the Kiso Mountain Road in Mino Province” is mentioned. In ancient times it belonged to Mino Province, but in the medieval period it was regarded as a part of Shinano Province, which became officially the case in the year Genroku 15 (1702). It is said to be the place where Kiso Yoshinaka raised his army, and there are many historical sites such as the remains of Yoshinaka's residence, Hataage Hachimangū Shrine and Tokuon Temple. In the Middle Ages, the Kiso clan built a residence in the centre of the Kiso Valley, and Kōzen Temple holds the graves of generations of Kiso clan members.

field_history_ja.value: 地名としての木曾が正史に現れるのは『続日本紀』大宝二年（702）十二月十日条に見える「始開美濃国岐蘇山道」が最初である。古代には美濃国に属したが、中世には信濃国の一部と考えられ、元禄十五年（1702）に正式に信濃国に属した。木曽義仲挙兵の地と伝えられ、義仲の居館跡や旗上八幡宮、徳音寺などの伝承遺跡が多い。中世には木曽氏が木曽谷の中心地で居館を築き、興禅寺には木曽氏代々の墓がある。

field_topography_en.value: It was a common name for the entire Kiso district of Shinano Province, but in ancient times it belonged to Mino Province. It is the name of the area in the southwestern part of Kiso in today’s Nagano Prefecture as well as the upper reaches of the Kiso River. Its boundaries are the Kiso mountains to the east, the summit of Mt. Agatazaka to the north and Mt. Norikura and Mt. Mitake (bordering Hida Province) to the west. It is a mountainous, forested area.

attributes.title: 勢田（瀬田・勢多）

field_history_en.value: The place name Seta has been around for a long time. Although the characters 瀬田 (Seta) are also used in the Nihon shoki, in many ancient texts such as the Shoku nihongi and the Engishiki have 勢多 (Seta). Setagō (勢多郷) appears in the Wamyō ruijushō, while other names such as Setatsu (Seta Harbour), Setabashi (Seta Bridge) and Setasō (Seta Lodging House) also appear repeatedly in the literature on this region. Among them, Seta Bridge, which spans the Seta River, was in an important position connecting western and eastern Japan. In waka poetry, it was often called Seta no hashi, Seta no karahashi and Seta no nagahashi. Seta Bridge has long been known as a famous sunset spot and is one of the Eight Views of Ōmi.

field_history_ja.value: 「勢田」という地名は古くから見え、『日本書紀』には「瀬田」の表記も見えるが、『続日本紀』や『延喜式』などの古代の文献資料の多くには「勢多」の字が用いられている。『倭名類聚抄』に「勢多郷」が見えるが、それ以外にも当地域には勢多津・勢多橋・勢多荘などの名称が文献にたびたび出てきている。中でも瀬田川にかかる勢多橋は、西日本と東日本を結ぶ重要な位置にあった。和歌では、「勢多の橋」「勢多の唐橋」「勢多の長橋」と詠まれることが多かった。瀬田唐橋は夕日の名所として大昔から知られており、瀬田の夕照として近江八景の一つとなっている。

field_topography_en.value: It is located in the western part of the Kurita District, Ōmi Province (present-day Seta, Ōtsu City, Shiga Prefecture) and is a common name for a wide area that spans from the southernmost tip of Lake Biwa to the mouth of Seta River. The writing can vary (瀬田, 勢田, 世多). It was known as the most important area in Ōmi throughout the ancient and medieval period. The Ōmi seat of the Governor, the Ichinomiya Takebe Taisha Shrine as well as a harbour, ferry, bridge and post station, the Seta no Karimiya (temporary palace), the Seta private estates (荘園) and Seta kitchen were located here.

attributes.title: 井手

field_history_en.value: It was developed from an early stage as a key point connecting Kyōto and Nara. It became especially famous because Tachibana no Moroe, an influential aristocrat from the Nara period who is said to have compiled the Man’yōshū and was known as “Ide’s Minister to the Left”, had a villa there and enjoyed its elegance. Ide Temple, which is said to have had a close relationship with Tachibana no Moroe, was also built in this area. In addition, the Tama River in Ide, which flows westward into the Kizu River, is one of the Six Jewel Rivers and a famous spot for Japanese kerria and frogs. It is an utamakura in many poems.

field_history_ja.value: 京都と奈良をつなぐ要地として、早くからひらかれていたが、「井手の左大臣」と呼ばれ、『万葉集』の撰者とも伝えられる奈良時代の有力貴族橘諸兄がここに別荘を設け風流を楽しんだため、特に有名になった。橘諸兄とも関わりが深いとされる井手寺もこの地に建立された。また、西流して木津川に注ぐ井手の玉川は六玉川の一つであり、山吹と蛙の名所として知られており、歌枕として多くの和歌に詠まれた。

field_topography_en.value: An utamakura of Yamashiro Province. Ide, Tsuzuki District, is in the southern part of present-day Kyōto Prefecture. It is located on the alluvial fan of the Tama River, which flows into the Kizu River in the Kyōto Basin, and is a key transportation point to Nara. There are historical sites of Tachibana no Moroe, the remnants of Ide temple, the Kawazu-zuka (frog mound), the Ono no Komachi-zuka and others.

field_history_en.value: Miyagino was first mentioned in the poems "The sparsely scattered/ leaves of bush clover weighted/ with the heavy dew/ yearn for winds on Miyagi/ Moor as I long for my love” (Kokinshū, Love 4; English translation by Rodd, Laurel Rasplica; and Henkenius, Mary Catherine (1984): p. 249) and "Oh guardsman remind/ your master to wear his hat – / here on Miyagi/ Moor the dewdrops fall from the/ trees more heavily than rain" (Kokinshū, Azuma uta 1091; English translation ibid, p.372). Since then, it became an utamakura with the attributes bush clover (hagi) and dew (tsuyu). Thus, bush clover was mentioned together with “deer”, dew with “flower” and in furthermore “deer” with “autumn leaves”. The word “miyaki” is sometimes used in poems to refer to the palace, as in the poem “Hearing the wind sigh, burdening with drops of dew all Miyagi Moor, my heart helplessly goes out to the little hagi frond.” (Genji monogatari, Kiritsubo, English translation by Royall Tyler (2001): p.8). In the Nō play “Miyagino”, which isn’t performed anymore, there is a scene where the spirit of the little bush clover appears, performing a song and a dance. In Oku no hosomichi there is the passage “The fields of Miyagi were thick with clover, and I could imagine how lovely they would look in autumn.” (English translation by Keene, Donald (1996): p.71 ), indicating that Bashō associated Miyagino with “bush clover” and “autumn”. On the other hand, Miyagino is thought to be the place where Fujiwara no Yasuhira of Hiraizumi welcomed Minamoto no Yoritomo's army during the Battle of Ōshū in 1189 (Bunji 5).

field_history_ja.value: 「宮木ののもとあらのこはぎつゆをおもみ風をまつごときみをこそまて（古今集・恋四）」「みさぶらひみかさとまうせ宮木ののこの下露は雨にまされり（古今集・東歌1091）」が初見で、以後「萩」「露」を景物とする歌枕となった。そこから派生し、萩の縁で「鹿」、露の縁で「花」、ひいては鹿の縁で「紅葉」が詠まれるようになった。また「宮きのの露吹き結ぶ風の音に小萩がもとを思ひこそやれ」（源氏・桐壺）など、「みやき」の語から宮中にたとえて詠まれることがある。なお、廃曲となった謡曲「宮城野」の舞台で、小萩の精が現われて歌舞を奏する場面がある。『奥の細道』にも「宮城野の萩茂りあひて、秋の気色思ひやらるる」とあり、芭蕉が宮城野から「萩」「秋」を連想していることがわかる。一方、宮城野は文治五年（1189）の奥州合戦で平泉の藤原泰衡が源頼朝軍を迎えた地と考えられている。

field_topography_en.value: It is also called Miyagi nohara (Miyagi plain). It was a plain in the eastern part of Sendai City, Miyagi Prefecture, from which the present name of the prefecture is derived. In former times it was famous for its autumn flowers, especially hagi (bush clovers, Lespedeza), but also ominaeshi (Patrinia scabiosifolia, flower), and suzumushi (cricket, Meloimorpha japonica) are well known. In Yakumo mishō, Miyagino was described as a place in Mutsu Province and in the Shōhō Sendai-jō ezu of the Edo period it was described as a place northeast of Yakushi-dō and to the southeast of Tsutsujigaoka. In the Edo period Miyagino was also called “Ikesuhara (生巣原)”. According to the Kanseki bunrō-shi, the plain is wide and is overgrown with thick grass. It is said that there are more than 100 species of autumn flowers, starting with the famous nishiki hagi (bush clover, Lespedeza thunbergii), which is known since ancient times, it includes ominaeshi (Patrinia scabiosifolia), waremōko (Sanguisorba officinalis), hagi (bush clover, Lespedeza), fujibakama (Eupatorium japonicum), karukaya (general term for various grasses like, Themeda japonica, Cymbopogon tortillis etc.), kikyō (Platycodon grandifloras), and other countless wild plants. Additionally, the birds hibari (Alauda arvensis) and the uzura (Coturnix japonica, Japanese quail) are mentioned in this work to appear often at Miyagino. It was also the hunting ground of the feudal lords. On weekdays pheasant and rabbit hunters, weed cutters and lumberjacks were forbidden to enter without permission. The local people called it thus Ikesuhara (活巣原) from the birds’ nests.

field_topography_ja.value: 宮城野原ともいう。宮城県仙台市の東部にあった原野で、現在の県名もこの原に由来する。古くは秋草、特に萩の名所として有名で、オミナエシやスズムシでも名高い。『八雲御抄』第五に陸奥されており、近世の正保仙台城絵図では薬師堂の北東、榴ヶ岡の南東に宮城野とみえる。なお、近世には生巣原（いけすはら）とも称し、「観蹟聞老志」によれば、平原は広く草は茂り、古来有名な錦萩をはじめ女郎花・吾亦紅・萩・藤袴・刈萱・桔梗ほか名もなき野草など無数の秋花が100種を数え、雲雀・鶉が多い。また藩主の狩場であり、平日は雉や兎をとる人、草刈、樵夫がみだりに入ることを禁じられたため、郷人は活巣原（いけすはら）と呼んだという。

field_history_en.value: In waka poetry the phrase 'the lake of Ōmi (Ōmi no umi)' refers to Lake Biwa. Many of the poems about Ōmi use the pivot word (kakekotoba) "to meet” (au) as in the poem "Today we must part/ although I think we may meet/ again tomorrow/ at Ōmi  my sleeves are dew-/ drenched  for the night has grown late” (Kokinshū, Parting, Ki no Toshisada; English translation by Rodd, Laurel Rasplica; and Henkenius, Mary Catherine (1984): p. 153). In particular, the words mirume (a meeting between man and woman, homophone: seaweed), namida (tears) and “(Ausaka) no seki” (Ausaka barrier) are commonly used in love poems, as in the poems: "I heard that there is no one in Ōmi who cuts seaweed, but how could seaweed not be plucked by fishermen?” (Gosenshū, Love 3, poet unknown) and "Let us hope that the river of tears, that is gushing out, will end  in the sea of Meeting (the sea of Ōmi)." (Gosenshū, Love 5, poet unknown). Ōmi is also used in the form of “Ōmi naru” and “Ōmi no ya” as attribute to place names. From the mid-Heian period onwards, it was not only used in love poems, but also in poems connected with personnel matters and in poems of landscape sceneries.

field_history_ja.value: 和歌で「近江の海」といえば琵琶湖のことをさす。近江を詠んだ歌は「今日別れ明日はあふみと思へども夜やふけぬらむ袖の露けき」（古今集・離別・利貞）のように、「逢ふ」を掛詞にした表現が多い。特に「みるめ刈るかたぞあふみに無しと聞く玉藻をさへや海人はかづかぬ」（後撰集・恋三・読人不知）、「流れいづる涙の川の行く末はつひにあふみの海と頼まむ」（後撰集・恋五・読人不知）のように「見る目」「涙」「（逢坂の）関」などの語を用いて恋の歌に詠み込まれるのが一般的であった。なお「近江なる」「近江のや」という形で地名に冠して用いられることもある。一方、平安時代中期以降は恋歌のみならず、人事に結びつける用法のほか、叙景的な歌にも詠まれるようになった。

field_topography_en.value: Today’s Shiga Prefecture. The place name "afumi (Ōmi)" is a phonetic variant of "aha-umi (淡海)", which derives from the implication that the land was close to the freshwater lake, Biwa. The name "近江 (Ōmi)" with its characters derived from the fact that Lake Biwa was called Ōmi (近江; “close freshwater lake”), while Lake Hamana in Shizuoka was called Tōtōmi (遠江, faraway freshwater lake). Ōmi was one of the major provinces of the Higashiyama Road, established at the time of the Taika Reform (7th century). It is close to Kyōto and is a key point of transportation between Higashiyama, Tōkai and Hokuriku Roads. Since the times Emperor Tenji built the palace Ōmi no miya (between 667-672) in Shiga, it has been of great historical and literary importance. Since the Heian period (794-1185), Ishiyama-dera, Enryaku-ji and Onjō-ji have often been the setting for literary works and the Sarugaku performances of the shrines and temples have been well known. Economically, markets and theatres developed, especially since the end of the Muromachi period, the Ōmi merchants have been active all over Japan. Famous products of this area were Japanese straw hats (sugekasa), rush matting for tatami (tatami omote), mosquito nets (kaya), thin rush matting (goza), bleached fabrics (sarashi nuno), Carassius (funa) and linen (asanuno). In addition, the Eight Views of Ōmi (Ōmi hakkei) illustrates the inherent natural beauty of the area.

field_topography_ja.value: 現在の滋賀県。「あふみ」は「あはふみ（淡海）」が音変化したもので、淡水湖の琵琶湖がある土地という意味に由来した地名である。「近江」という文字は、静岡にある浜名湖を遠江（遠つ淡海）と称したことに対し、琵琶湖を近江（近つ淡海）と称したことによる。大化改新のときに設置された、東山道の大国の一つで、京に近く、東山・東海・北陸道との交通の要衝に当り、天智天皇が志賀に大津宮を営んで（六六七～七二）以来、歴史上はもちろん、文学史的にもはなはだ重要な意味を持つ。平安時代から石山寺・延暦寺・園城寺はしばしば文学の舞台となり、諸社寺の猿楽も知られていた。経済的には市場・座が発達し、ことに室町時代末以来、近江商人が各地に進出した。名物に、菅笠・畳表・蚊帳・蓙・晒布・鮒・麻布などがあり、また、風光明媚で近江八景がその代表とされる。

attributes.title: 老曾（老蘇）

field_history_en.value: In Ryōjin hishō, Oiso is poetically referred to as "Ōmi ni okashiki utamakura" [a beautiful utamakura in Ōmi], and in poetic treatises such as Nōin utamakura and Waka shogaku-shō, Oiso is also referred to as a utamakura for Ōmi. As in the poem “Let it be a memory of the journey to the east, the voice of the cuckoo in the middle of the night in the woods of Oiso ” (Goshūishū, book three: summer, Ōe no Kin’yori) the hototogisu (a cuckoo) is often mentioned. There are also poems where the character 老 from 老蘇 (Oiso) is used as a kakekotoba for (the aging) lyrical I as in the poem “As I regard my changing reflection in the mirror, I am lamenting at the forest of Oiso.“ (Kin’yōshū, book nine: Miscellaneous I, Fujiwara no Morokata). In connection with “old” (老) the words „year, age“ and „frost” (which implies grey hair) and in connection with “forest” words such as “undergrowth”, “withered leaves” „tree / lament” are used.

field_topography_en.value: Higashi-Oiso and Nishi-Oiso in Azuchi-chō, Ōmihachiman City, is located in the centre of Shiga Prefecture. In the Edo period (1603-1868), the area was a post town on the Nakasendō highway linking Nihonbashi (Edo) and Sanjō-Ōhashi (Kyōto). It is also a famous place for the hototogisu (a cuckoo, Cuculus poliocephalus) and in the forest there is the Oiso (Ōiso) Shrine, a shikinai-sha (a shrine which is enregistered in the Engishiki from the early 10th century). According to the Oiso-jinja hongi, the "Oiso Forest" in Higashi Oiso, a historic site, is said to have been planted by Ishibe Ōmuraji during the reign of Emperor Kōrei. He planted Japanese cedar, pine, and Japanese cypress trees in a slough, resulting in a large forest.

attributes.title: 越

field_history_en.value: Koshi first appears in the Nihonshoki as Koshi-no-shima, in the myth about the birth of the land. After the Taika Reforms, Koshi was established as a new political unit under the Yamato administration, encompassing the entire Hokuriku region. In the Nihonshoki, the name Echizen first appears in the entry for the 21st day of the 9th month of the 6th year of Empress Jitō's reign (692). This suggests that the division of Koshi Province into the three provinces of Echizen, Etchū, and Echigo occurred in the late 7th century, not long before this date. In the Man’yōshū shinazakaru, meaning a remote place beyond many mountains, is used as a makurakotoba for Koshi. Due to the climate of Hokuriku, it is known as a region of deep snow and a region where spring comes late. Additionally, because of mountains like Shirayama, that are covered with snow even in the summer, snow is often a theme in poems. It is also known as a place from where wild geese fly away in spring and return to in autumn and poems often combine geese with the seasons.

field_history_ja.value: 越の地名は、『日本書紀』の国生み神話に「越洲（こしのしま）」とあるのが初見。大化改新の後、北陸地方一帯を包含する越国が大和政権の新たな政治支配の単位として設置された。『日本書紀』持統天皇6年（692）九月癸丑（21日）条に越前の国名が初見して、これをあまりさかのぼらない七世紀末に越国から越前・越中・越後三国の分立したことがうかがわれる。『万葉集』には、幾山坂越えて隔たった僻遠の地を意味する「しなざかる」という言葉を「越」の枕詞として使用された歌がある。北陸の風土性から、雪深い地、春の到来が遅い地とされており、また、白山など夏でも雪がある高山があるため、雪が詠みこまれることが多い。また、雁が春に飛び立つ地、秋に飛んで来る地として知られ、雁と季節の組み合わせで詠まれることがある。

field_topography_en.value: A general term for the Hokuriku region before the implementation of the ancient provincial administrative system. Koshi (越) was the term used by the Yamato government and had multiple other spellings, for example 高志 or 古志. It refers to the area stretching from Kyōto along the coast of the Sea of Japan to present-day Niigata. It was divided into Echizen, Etchū, and Echigo and later further divided into Noto and Kaga. This corresponds to the present-day prefectures of Fukui, Ishikawa, Toyama, and Niigata. It is also known as Koshi-no-kuni, Koshi-no-michi, and Hokurikudō.

attributes.title: 筑紫

field_history_en.value: Tsukushi has been in contact with the culture of the continent since ancient times. It was divided into the two provinces Chikuzen and Chikugo before the second year of Monmu Tennō (698). There are various opinions about the origin of the name Tsukushi, but the theory that it resembles the shape of a bird, the tsukudori (木兎鳥), found in the Shaku nihongi, was popular among renga poets. Since the Dazaifu, the administration of Chikuzen Province, was established as a guard against invasions from the Korean Peninsula, it appeared in many poems, from the Man’yōshū onwards. For example, the expression kokorozukushi (心づくし), meaning “to yearn for”, was often used as a wordplay (kakekotoba) in poems about separation and love. This was due to the fact that Tsukushi Province had the image of a distant land. It was sometimes also mentioned along other utamakura such as Iki-no-matsubara, Somekawa, and Ōnoyama. The contemporary local pronunciation is Chikushi.

field_history_ja.value: 大陸文化との接点として古くから開けた土地だが、文武2年（698）以前に筑前・筑後の二国に分割された。筑紫の由来は諸説あるが、『釈日本紀』などに見える木兎鳥（つくどり）に形が似るという説は連歌師の間で広く用いられた。朝鮮半島からの外敵の侵入に備えて大宰府が置かれたため、『万葉集』以来多くの和歌に詠まれた。例えば、「思い乱れる」という意味の「心づくし」に掛けて詠まれたり、その後も離別の歌や恋の歌に詠まれたりすることが多かった。それは、筑紫国が僻遠の地というイメージが強く意識されたためである。また、生の松原・染川・大野山など、他の歌枕とともに詠まれることもあった。なお、現在当地ではチクシと発音する。

attributes.title: 箱根

field_history_en.value: Mount Hakone has been an important centre of transportation and a place of mountain worship since ancient times. It was mentioned in the Man'yōshū, but gradually, poems stopped describing the scenery of Mount Hakone. Instead, they used wordplays (kakekotoba) with hako (箱, box) and related words such as futa (蓋, lid; 二, two), mi (身, body; 三, three), and aku (開, open; 明, bright), and often prefixed the word tamakushige (玉くしげ, pearly) to hako as a makurakotoba. Minamoto no Sanetomo, who visited Hakone several times as shōgun of the Kamakura bakufu, contributed poems to the Kinkai wakashū such as, "The cuckoo of Mount Hakone (that beautiful comb box) sings facing it every morning." In the early modern period, the Tōkaidō Hakone-hachiri route was opened (Odawara – Hakone – Mishima), and in the 4th year of Genna (1618), the post station Hakone was established on the shores of Lake Ashi. The following year, the Hakone checkpoint (sekisho) was set up adjacent to Hakone-juku. Mount Hakone had a number of hot springs since ancient times, and in the early modern period, these hot springs became known as the Seven Hot Springs of Hakone and became bustling spots.

field_history_ja.value: 箱根山は古くから交通の要地で山岳信仰の中心であったため、古く『万葉集』にも詠まれたが、徐々に箱根山の景色を詠むことはなくなり、「箱」と掛詞にして「ふた（蓋・二）」「み（身・三）」「あく（開・明）」などの縁語を用いたり、「箱」に掛かる枕詞「たまくしげ」を冠して詠まれることが多かった。鎌倉幕府の将軍として何回か訪れていた源実朝は『金槐和歌集』に「たまくしげ箱根の山の郭公むかふの里に朝な朝な鳴く」などの和歌を残している。近世に入ると東海道箱根八里が開かれ、元和四年（1618）には芦ノ湖畔に箱根宿が、翌年には箱根宿の隣接地に箱根関所が設置された。箱根山中の各地には古くから温泉が涌出していたが、近世になるとこれら温泉は箱根七湯と呼ばれて賑わった。

field_topography_en.value: An utamakura of Sagami Province. It corresponds to the mountainous area in the southwestern part of present-day Kanagawa Prefecture and is a complex volcano that spans both Sagami and Suruga Province. Lake Ashi can be found at the summit. The mountain path is famous for its steepness, and the route over the mountain has changed over time.

attributes.title: 有磯海

field_history_en.value: Ōtomo no Yakamochi, who resided in Fushiki as the governor of Etchū (present-day Toyama Prefecture), contributed the following poem to the Man'yōshū, [hearing that his brother had died in the capital] "If I had known this would happen, I would have shown you the waves on the rough shore of Koshi (Koshi no umi no ariso).” Later generations interpreted this as a place name, turning it into an utamakura. Additionally, there is a poem in the Man'yōshū that goes, "Like the vine that stretches over the great cape of Ariso, will I continue to yearn not knowing where it leads?" (author unknown). Although originally unrelated to Etchū, due to the influence of this poem, Arisoumi came to be seen as a famous place for kuzu/kazura (vines). A verse on Arisoumi also appears in Bashō's Oku no hosomichi.

field_history_ja.value: 越中（今の富山県）の国司として伏木に居住した大伴家持が『万葉集』に「かからむとかねて知りせば越の海の荒磯の波も見せましものを」と詠み、後世これが地名と解釈され、歌枕となった。また、『万葉集』の「大崎の有磯のわたり延ふ葛の行くへもなくや恋ひ渡りなむ」(作者未詳)という歌は、元来越中とは無関係の作だったが、この歌の影響により、有磯海が「葛」の名所と捉えられもした。芭蕉の『奥の細道』にも有磯海の句が残されている。

attributes.title: 白山

field_history_en.value: The earliest example of Shirayama as an utamakura is found in the Man’yōshū (Azuma-uta), “Lying down in a thin gown on Shirayama, I cannot sleep in the mountain wind, but how fortunate to have a coat from my loved one.” In the Nōin utamakura, it refers to Kaga Province, but many books on poetry, such as the Waka shogakushō classify it as belonging to Echizen Province. In the context of shugendō (Yamabushi-sect), Shirayama in Echizen Province is emphasized. In waka poetry it is common to see Koshi no Shirayama and Koshiji naruShirayama in combination with snow since the Kokinshū. Since the Gosen wakashū, it suggests an image of snow that does not melt throughout the year. Snow can also be applied metaphorically to represent old age or lamentation over bad fortune. The reason for designating as an utamakura of Echizen lies not only in the fact that Kaga Province once belonged to Echizen Province, but also in the historical dispute between Kaga and Echizen over rights such as the construction of shrines and the collection of fees from worshippers along the Zenjōdō route. This dispute intensified in the medieval period, and in the eighth year of Kanbun (1668), it became a territory under direct control of the bakufu. In the fifth year of Meiji (1872), it was returned to Nomi District, Kaga Province (present-day Ishikawa District).

field_history_ja.value: 『万葉集』の「栲衾之良山風の寝なへども児ろがおそきのあろこそ良しも」（東歌）の「之良山」が最も古い例。『能因歌枕』では加賀国だが、『和歌初学抄』など多くの歌学書は越前国に分類する。修験道関係でも越前国の白山を強調する場合も多く、和歌では『古今集』以来、「越の白山」「越路なる白山」など、雪が詠まれることが多く、その雪は『後撰集』によって年を越しても消えないというイメージができた。雪の景物であるため老身になぞらえたり、不遇沈淪の身を訴嘆したりと応用された例もある。越前の歌枕とするのは、加賀国が昔、越前国に属したこと以外に、山頂の社殿などの造営権、登拝からの参銭徴収権をめぐって加賀・越前の両馬場（禅定道の拠点）が争ったことによる。その争論は中世以後激化し、寛文8年（1668）には天領となり、明治5年（1872）に加賀国能美郡（現在は石川郡）に復帰した。

field_topography_en.value: The name for a volcano whose three main peaks rise above the borders of Kaga (now Ishikawa Prefecture) and Hida (now the northern part of Gifu Prefecture), and whose branches extend from Echizen (Fukui Prefecture) to Mino (southern part of Gifu Prefecture) in a series of peaks in the south. Today pronounced as Hakusan. Its highest peak is Gozenmine at 2702 meters. Shirayama Shrine and Shirayama-hime Shrine are located there, and it has been a place of worship since ancient times. During the Edo period, Shirayama, Fujisan, and Tateyama were regarded as Japan’s three famous and sacred mountains. The name Shirayama is said to have originated from its particularly conspicuous white appearance throughout the year. Rivers that flow from Shirayama include the Tedori River in Ishikawa Prefecture, the Kuzuryū River in Fukui Prefecture, and the Nagara River in Gifu Prefecture.

field_topography_ja.value: 主峰をなす三峰が加賀国（今の石川県）、飛騨国（今の岐阜県北部）の国境にそびえ、支峰が南に連なって越前国（今の福井県）から美濃国（今の岐阜県南部）にまたがる火山の総称。最高峰は御前嶺の2070メートル。白山神社・白山比咩神社奥院があり、古くから信仰の対象とされ、江戸時代には富士山・立山とともに日本三名山・三霊山に数えられた。一年を通して白い山容が特に目立つことから、白山の名が生じたものと伝えられる。白山から流れ出る川は、石川県の手取川、福井県の九頭竜川、岐阜県の長良川などがある。

field_history_en.value: The poem from the ninth section of the Ise monogatari, “At the foot of Mount Utsu in Suruga, whether in dreams or waking, I cannot meet you.” influenced many poems in the Shinkokinshū and Utsu no yama was often used to contrast dreams and reality. Additionally, following the ninth section of the Ise monogatari which reads, “The path I am to enter is dark and narrow, with vines growing thickly…”, many poems in the Shinkokinshū used vines in the context of Utsu no yama. This location is mentioned in works such as the Kaidōki, the Tōkan kikō, and the Izayoi nikki based on actual experience. From the medieval to the early modern period, the specialty of the mountain pass was the tōdango (a type of sweet rice cake), which is well-known through Morikawa Kyoriku’s haiku “Even the tōdago have become small – autumn wind is blowing.”

field_history_ja.value: 『伊勢物語』九段の歌「駿河なるうつの山べのうつつにも夢にも人にあはぬなりけり」によって、その後、『新古今集』では「夢」と「うつつ（現）」を対照させて詠むことが多くなった。また、『伊勢物語』九段の本文「わが入らむとする道はいと暗う細きに、蔦かへでは茂り…」によって、その後、『新古今集』では「蔦」とともに詠まれることも多かった。実際にこの地を通過して詠まれたのは『海道記』や『東関紀行』、『十六夜日記』にある。中世から近世にかけて峠の名物は十団子で、許六の「十団子も小粒になりぬ秋の風」でよく知られている。

attributes.title: 清見（潟、が関）

field_history_en.value: Due to the mountains being so close to the sea, the Barrier of Kiyomi was set up here. The coastline from here to Miho no saki was referred to as Kiyomigata. The Man’yōshū contains the poem, “As I gaze upon the sea from the coast of Kiyomi at Miho Bay in Iohara, I am free from worldly thoughts” (Taguchi no Masuhito). Kiyomi ga seki and Kiyomigata became common motifs in poetry from the late Heian period onwards, and they are also mentioned in works like the Makura no sōshi and the Sarashina nikki. Additionally, there is a theory that the Seikenji, located near Kiyomi ga seki, was the temple of the barrier. However, according to the Kaidōki, by the Kamakura period, Kiyomi Barrier had already lost its function.

field_history_ja.value: 山が海に迫り隘路でもあったために清見が関が作られ、そこから三保の崎へかけての海岸を清見潟と言っていた。古くは『万葉集』に「蘆原の清見の崎の三保の浦のゆたけき見つつ物思ひもなし」（田口益人）と見え、「清見が関」と「清見潟」は平安時代後期から多く詠まれるようになった。『枕草子』や『更級日記』にも「清見が関」の存在が窺われ、この清見関付近にある清見寺は清見が関の関寺ではないかという説もあるが、『海道記』に拠ると、鎌倉時代には既に清見が関の機能は失われていた。

field_topography_en.value: An utamakura of Suruga Province. It refers to the coastline, more precisely to the bay between Kiyomi no saki and Miho no saki, near the Seiken-ji in Okitsu, Shimizu Ward, Shizuoka City, Shizuoka Prefecture. During the Heian period, the Kiyomi Barrier stood near this location. Settlements developed along the long and narrow coastline stretching from east to west, because the mountains of Ihara press against the sea. Many reefs hide below the surface of the water. Moreover, the spot offers a view of the pine forest of Miho (Miho no matsubara) to the south across the bay, and Mount Fuji can also be seen to the east, making it a place of scenic beauty.

attributes.title: 田子の浦

field_history_en.value: Through the Shoku nihongi it is known that Tago no ura was a place where gold was mined. One famous poem in the Man’yōshū by Yamabe no Akahito reads, “As I part from Tago no ura and look up, it appears that snow has fallen pure white on the high peak of Mount Fuji.” In the Hyakunin isshu, however, the same poem says “In Tago no ura” (Tago no ura ni), and consequently Tago no ura itself became known as a scenic spot for viewing Mount Fuji. However, there are various theories about its exact location. In the Sarashina nikki it says that people passed through Tago no ura on their way from Kazusa Province to Heiankyō. But by the medieval period, it seems that Tago no ura came to refer to the coastline around the port of Yoshiwara (near the Tago no ura port in today’s Fuji City). Furthermore, it seems to differ as well in the Genpei jōsuiki, the Tōkan kikō, and also in the Izayoi nikki.

field_history_ja.value: 『続日本紀』から、田子の浦は黄金が採掘された場所であることがわかる。有名な歌は『万葉集』の「田子の浦ゆうち出でて見ればま白にそ富士の高嶺に雪は降りける」（山部赤人）だが、『百人一首』では「田子の浦に」の形になったことで、富士山を望める名勝となった。しかし、その場所は諸説あり、『更級日記』では、上総国から京都へ上る途中に田子の浦を通ったとしているが、中世になると、吉原湊（現富士市の田子の浦港付近）周辺の海岸を指すようになったらしい。また、『源平盛衰記』、『東関紀行』、『十六夜日記』でもそれぞれ異なる。

attributes.title: 鈴鹿（川、山）

field_history_en.value: Many poems about Mount Suzuka were composed in the context of crossing the Suzuka Barrier. This barrier was established during the Taika Reforms as a security checkpoint, and in times of national importance, messengers were dispatched to this checkpoint. Even after its abolition in 789 (Enryaku 8), the dispatch of the messengers continued ceremonially. According to the Azuma kagami, it was re-established as a checkpoint in the medieval period. A representative poem is found in the Shūishū, which reads, “If I live on in this world, I will once again cross Mount Suzuka – will the past become the present” (by Saigū no nyōgo Kishi). The poems often allude to the ringing of bells (suzu). The Konjaku monogatari and the Hōgen monogatari describe it as a place inhabited by mountain bandits, indicating that it was a difficult pass to traverse despite the checkpoint. In the Edo period, it became one of the lodgings along the Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō.

field_topography_en.value: An utamakura from Ise Province. Although it is located on the border with Ōmi Province, it belongs to Suzuka City in Mie Prefecture. Suzuka-no-seki, located at the southern end, was a strategically important checkpoint for crossing between the Tōkaidō and Ise via the Iga Pass since ancient times. Fuwa-no-seki in Mino, Arachi-no-seki in Echizen and Suzuka-no-seki were referred to as the Three Barriers (sanseki). Bandits also frequently appeared in the area, making it one of the dangerous sections on the Tōkaidō.

attributes.title: 鳴門（阿波）

field_history_en.value: In ancient times, it was called Awa no mito (Awa's water gate or doorway), Awato, and Awa no to, and later came to be known as Naruto (in the spellings 鳴門, 鳴戸 and 鳴渡) as well. It was mentioned in the Nihon shoki and the Man’yōshū as a place with strong tidal currents, but this perception became less prominent in the Heian period. In the Tosa nikki, it was mentioned as a place where pirates appear. It is listed as utamakura in Yakumo mishō, as Naruto no ura (Bay of Naruto), and in the Godaishū utamakura, as Naruto, and subsequently, it was incorporated into numerous poems. In the Taiheiki, the spellings 鳴戸 and 鳴渡 are used, indicating that from the Kamakura period on, Naruto became firmly established as its name. Later, in the first year of Kōan (1361), due to the Nankai earthquake the sea in Naniwa overflowed and a sudden rip current occurred at Naruto. In Awa shi (Topography of Awa) it is also recorded, that the Naruto tide had dried up.

field_history_ja.value: 古くは「あはのみと」（阿波の水門・粟門）、「あはと」、「阿波の戸」とも称され、のち鳴門・鳴戸・鳴渡とも呼ばれた。『日本書紀』や『万葉集』では潮の流れの激しい場所として詠まれるが、平安時代にはその認識は希薄になる。『土佐日記』では海賊が出没する場所として知られる。『八雲御抄』には「なるとのうら」、『五代集歌枕』には「なると」を歌枕としてあげ、その後、多数の歌に詠みこまれた。『太平記』では「鳴戸」「鳴渡」という表記が見えることから、鎌倉期以降に「なると」の名称が定着したと考えられる。また、康安元年（1361）には南海地震によって難波の海があふれ、「鳴戸」で急に潮が引き陸となったことも書かれており、『阿波志』にも鳴門潮が涸れたと記されている。

attributes.title: 玉島（玉島川）

field_history_en.value: It can be found in the poetic treatises Godaishū utamakura and Yakumo mishō. Eleven poems, compiled under the title “Idling at the Matsuura River” in the Man’yōshū, became the foundations of subsequent waka expressions. Sometimes referred to as Tamashima no ura (Bay of Tamashima), it is speculated that in ancient times, this area was reached by the sea. According to the Hizen Fudoki, the Kojiki and the Nihon shoki, there is a tale of Empress Jingū fishing for ayu (sweetfish) in the Tamashima River. Since then, it is said that the women of this country always fished for ayu in the forth month, and even if men tried, they couldn’t catch any. Until the early Meiji period, following the story of the empress, only women were allowed to fish for sweetfish.

attributes.title: 玉津島

field_history_en.value: The poem “When the tide fills the bay of Waka, the lagoons disappear, and a crane cries out as it heads for the reedy shore.” (Yamabe no Akahito) from the Man’yōshū cannot be said to directly describe Tamatsushima. However, the poem had a significant role in forming utamakura, coining associated expressions like “kata wo nami” (as lagoons disappear) in the third line. Additionally, due to associations with Wakanoura, Sotoori-hime came to be worshiped as the deity of poetry in Tamatsushima Shrine, completing the trio of waka deities along with the deities of Sumiyoshi and Kakinomoto (or Kitano) Shrine. The fact that it was not only often mentioned in poems, but also included in officially selected or privately compiled anthologies, in diaries of monks etc. is obviously due to its proximity to the Kumano and Kōya pilgrimage routes, the famous site of Fukiage Beach to the north of Wakanoura, and the increase in pilgrimages leading to many people stopping by.

field_history_ja.value: 『万葉集』の「若の浦に潮満ち来れば潟をなみ葦辺をさして鶴鳴き渡る」（山部赤人）は、玉津島そのものを詠んだと断言できないものの、第三句からは地名の「片男波」が派生するなど、歌枕の形成には大きな役割を果たした。また、和歌浦からの連想で玉津島神社には和歌の神として衣通姫も併祀され、住吉・柿本（または北野）両社とともに和歌三神を形成していった。そのため多く歌に詠まれたが、勅撰・私撰を問わず僧侶の日記などにも詠まれたのは、熊野・高野参詣路に近く、和歌浦の北には名勝吹上浜もあって、参詣の盛行により立ち寄る人々が多かったことも影響したと考えられる。

field_topography_en.value: An utamakura of Kii Province. In the past, the area around Tamatsushima Shrine was submerged in the sea, and several present-day hills were islands. Tamatsushima is thought to refer to either a part or the entirety of this area. Nowadays, they are no longer islands but are connected to the land, forming Mount Tengu and Mount Imose behind Tamatsushima Shrine. The deity of Tamatsushima Shrine was revered as a deity of poetry.

field_topography_ja.value: 紀伊国の歌枕。かつて玉津島神社周辺は海中にあって、今あるいくつかの丘陵地も島として点在していた。玉津島はその中の一部または全体の呼称と思われる。現在では、島ではなくなり、地続きとなっており、玉津島神社の背後の奠供山と妹背山となっている。玉津島神社は和歌の神として尊ばれた。

attributes.title: 衣川

field_history_en.value: The name Koromogawa (Koromo River) is said to originate from the Koromo Falls upstream, based on legends according to which Kōbō-daishi (Kūkai) washed his robes (koromo) here, or celestial beings descended to dry their celestial robes at the Gorin Valley on Mount Takahino. The earliest mention in poetry can be found in the Kokin waka rokujō, in the poem “I have trusted the name close to my heart, and now I cross over thinking that it is Koromogawa of Michinoku.” After its establishment as an utamakura, poems about Koromo no seki were included in the Gosen wakashū. Koromo no seki also appears in military chronicles such as the Mutsu waki and the Azuma kagami. According to the Kokon chomonjū it is said that during the Former Nine Years’ War (Zenkunen War, 1052-1063), Minamoto no Yoshi’ie and Abe no Sadatō composed renga while battling at Koromogawa. In the Gikeiki, it is said that when Minamoto no Yoshitsune committed suicide, his retainer Benkei passed away standing in the currents of Koromogawa.

field_history_ja.value: 衣川の名称は上流にある衣滝に由来すると言われ、衣滝で弘法大師が衣をすすいだためという説、高檜能山の五輪谷上に天人が降りて天の羽衣を乾かしたためという説がある。和歌での初出は『古今和歌六帖』の「身にちかきなをぞ頼みしみちのくの衣の川とみてや渡らん」で、歌枕としての成立後に『後撰集』に衣関を詠んだ歌が収められた。衣関については『陸奥話記』や『吾妻鏡』など軍記物語にも登場する。『古今著聞集』では、前九年の役で源義家と安倍貞任が衣川で戦い連歌を詠んだと伝えられており、『義経記』では、源義経が自害した時、従者の弁慶は衣川の中の瀬で立往生したという。

field_topography_en.value: An utamakura of Mutsu Province, which corresponds to Hiraizumi in present-day Iwate Prefecture. The name of the temple precincts of Chūson-ji is called Kōzan, indicating that there was indeed a barrier in this area. The river flows right next to Chūson-ji and through the northern part of Hiraizumi before it joins with the Kitakami River. The name also refers to this region. Among the many utamakura of Mutsu, it is located at the northernmost point. As such it was the frontline in battles against the Emishi. Originally, Tagajō (in Shiogama City, Miyagi Prefecture) was the northernmost point, but the by moving the centre of military administration to Isawa Castle (northwest of Mizusawa City, Iwate Prefecture), the control was expanded to this region.

field_topography_ja.value: 陸奥国の歌枕。今の岩手県平泉。中尊寺の山号を関山ということから見ても、このあたりに関のあったことは確かで、中尊寺のすぐ傍を流れる川。平泉北部を流れ、北上川に入る。また、その辺の地名を指す。歌枕の多い陸奥でも最北端に位置する。つまり、対蝦夷作戦の最前線である。もともとは多賀城（宮城県塩釜市）が最北端であったが、胆沢丈（岩手県水沢市の西北）を鎮守府としてここまでの支配の範囲を広げたのである。

attributes.title: 筑波山

field_history_en.value: In the entry to Hitachi Fudoki, only Nyotai-san is mentioned as the place where young men and women from various provinces in the Kantō region gathered dancing and singing (utagaki). The fact that such courtship events were held on Mount Tsukuba indicates that this mountain was considered a sacred place. From the Man’yōshū we know that it was a mountain for overlooking the land (kunimi), and it also appeared in the Azuma-uta and the songs of frontier guards. Perhaps because both a goddess and a god are enshrined there, it was often used as a symbol of love. From the Heian period to the medieval period, it also signified wishing for the favour of one's lord. Because the question-and-answer style of poems, like the poems of Yamato Takeru found in the Kojiki and the Nihon shoki, were considered the origin of renga, popular in the medieval period, they came to be known as "The way of Tsukuba."

field_history_ja.value: 『常陸国風土記』では、女体山のみに関東諸国の男女が集い遊ぶと記している。筑波山で歌垣が行なわれたことは、この山が聖なる境界の場であることを示している。また、『万葉集』によれば、国見をする山であったことがわかり、他にも東歌や防人の歌にも詠まれた。女神と男神が祀られているためか、恋の表象として詠まれることが多かったが、平安時代から中世にかけて、主君の恩寵を願う歌として詠まれた。『古事記』や『日本書紀』に見られる日本武尊の歌謡を含む片歌の問答が連歌の起源とされたため、中世に盛行した連歌が「筑波の道」と呼ばれた。

field_topography_en.value: An utamakura in Hitachi Province. It is a mountain located on the border of present-day Tsukuba City, Sakuragawa City, and Ishioka City in Ibaraki Prefecture. The mountain's summit has two peaks, Nyotai-san in the east and Nantai-san in the west, each of which enshrines a goddess and a god, respectively. Because it can be seen from anywhere in the Kantō Plain, it became a symbol of longing for people since the ancient times and attracted many pilgrims.

field_history_en.value: There are three cases in which the term Futami is used: 1. when it refers to Harima Province (Futamichō, Akashi City, Hyōgo Prefecture), 2. when it refers to Tajima Province (Futami in Kinosaki District, Hyōgo Prefecture), and 3. when it refers to Ise Province. For example, in the Godaishū utamakura, it is referred to as being in Harima Province, but in the Waka shogakushō and the Waka iroha, it is referred to as being in Ise Province. Often, it is unclear which of the three locations is being referred to. However, since the Shinkokin wakashū, when it comes to composing poems, it has mainly been associated with Ise Province, perhaps due to its connection with the Ise devotion.

field_topography_en.value: An utamakura of Ise Province. It is located on the coast of Ise Bay in Futami Town, Ise City, in the central eastern part of Mie Prefecture. It is a beach about 4 kilometres long with white sand and green pines, east of Imaisshiki at the mouth of the Isuzu River. At its eastern end is Futami-okitama Shrine, in front of which lay the famous Wedded Rocks. Historically, it has been a place for purification through bathing, and even today, visitors to the Grand Shrine of Ise partake in purification rituals here.

attributes.title: 箱崎

field_history_en.value: Since ancient times, it has been called Hakozaki no tsu (harbour). In the late Heian period, it became a centre for trade with the Song Dynasty along with Hakata, quickly absorbing continental culture. In the Kamakura period, defences were built here to repel the Mongol invasions, making it a historic battlefield. In the medieval period, there was an oil guild associated with Hakozaki Shrine, and Korean traders also resided there, leading to prosperity through commerce and trade. In the early modern period, it was divided into Hakozaki Village and Hakozaki Bay. It also became a post station town on the road extending east from Hakata and inns for the use by feudal lords (honjin) were installed. There is a Nō piece titled Hakozaki. Additionally, Hakozaki Shrine, one of Japan’s Three Great Hachiman Shrines, is located there, and the nearby pine grove has been renowned as a scenic spot since ancient times. Consequently, in waka poetry, the pines, that are said to date back to the age of the gods, are often venerated. There are also poems reflecting on one's own aging in relation to the long-lived pines, and some use associated words (engo) such as hako (box) and futa (lid), playing on the word futatsu (two).

field_history_ja.value: 古来、箱崎の津と呼ばれる。平安時代後期には、博多と並んで日宋貿易の拠点となり、大陸文化の早く流入した所である。鎌倉時代には元寇防塁が築かれ、元寇の古戦場でもある。中世には、筥崎宮に属する油座があり、また朝鮮貿易商人が居住するなど、商業や貿易で栄えた。近世には箱崎村と箱崎浦に分かれた。博多から東にのびる街道の宿場町ともなり、藩主の本陣も置かれた。謡曲では「箱崎」という曲がある。また、日本三大八幡の一つ、筥崎八幡宮があり、そのあたりの松原は、古来、景勝地として名高かった。したがって、和歌では、神代から伝わるという松を、祝意を込めて詠むことが多い。また、長寿の松に寄せて自らの老いを詠んだもの、「箱」の縁語、「蓋（ふた）」を「二つ（ふたつ）」の意に掛けて用いたものがある。

field_topography_en.value: An utamakura of Chikuzen Province. Currently located in the Hakozaki district of the Higashi Ward in Fukuoka City. It is situated on the left bank of the lower reaches of the Umi River, facing Hakata Bay. In ancient times, it was also written as 筥崎. It is the site of Kyūshū University and Hakozaki Shrine, which enshrines Emperor Ōjin.

attributes.title: 鎌倉

field_history_en.value: In the Nijikkanpon wamyō ruijushō, Kamakura appears as the name of a village in the Kamakura District. The Man’yōshū also mentions Kamakura yama and Kamakura no mikoshi no saki, indicating that the origins of this word lie far in the past. According to legend, Fujiwara no Kamatari went on a pilgrimage to Kashima in Hitachi, to fulfil a long-cherished wish, and he had a revelatory dream in the village (post station) of Yui. On waking, he buried his sickle (kama) in Ōkura Matsugaoka. This is said to be the origin of the name Kamakura. From the Heian period, Kamakura was an important base for the Minamoto clan, and its members such as Minamoto no Yoriyoshi and Minamoto no Yoshi’ie, and later Minamoto no Yoshitomo, and they had the Tsurugaoka hachimangū built there. In the year Kenkyū 3 (1192), when Minamoto no Yoritomo established the bakufu, Kamakura became the political centre, mentioned alongside Kyōto, and flourished as a representative medieval city of the eastern provinces. Its centre was the Tsurugaoka hachiman Shrine, enshrining Kiyomizu Hachiman. From there, along Wakamiya Road, samurai came and went and as a consequence more and more houses were built. In the mountains, temples such as the Kenchō-ji and Engaku-ji, were established as the Five Mountains in Kamakura (Kamakura gozan) and their flourishing was depicted in works such as the Tōkan kikō and Kaidōki. Kamakura deteriorated with the end of the Muromachi period. Since the early modern period, it has become a touristic town visited by pilgrims to Tsurugaoka hachimangū and Enoshima Benten, as well as by literati and artists visiting its picturesque spots.

field_history_ja.value: 『二十巻本和名類聚抄』の鎌倉郡の郷名に「鎌倉」の名が見え、『万葉集』に「可麻久良夜麻」「可麻久良の見越の埼）」などあり、その名称の由来は古い。藤原鎌足が宿願のため、常陸の鹿島ヘ詣でた折、由比の里で霊夢あり、持っていた鎌を大蔵松が岡に埋めたことよりこの名が起るという伝説がある。平安時代から鎌倉は源頼義・源義家、その後は源義朝と源氏の重要な根拠地であり、鶴岡八幡宮も建てられる。建久3年（1192）、源頼朝が幕府を開いてからは政治の中心となり、京・鎌倉と併称され、東国の代表的な中世都市として繁栄した。その中心は清水八幡を勧請した鶴岡八幡宮と、そこから南へ海岸に向かって走る若宮大路で、武人が往来し谷々には人家が並び、山内の建長寺・円覚寺はじめ鎌倉五山が建立され、その繁栄のさまは『東関紀行』『海道記』などに描かれている。室町末期には衰微した。近世以降は鶴岡八幡・江島弁天の参詣者や、景勝地を訪れる文人墨客による観光都市となる。

field_topography_en.value: An utamakura of Sagami Province, which corresponds to the present-day city in the southeastern part of Kanagawa Prefecture. To the south, it faces Sagami Bay and is surrounded by hills and valleys on three sides, making it a natural fortress. Originally it appeared as the name of a district and village. However, during the Kamakura period, the area centred around Tsurugaoka-hachiman Shrine served as the seat of the bakufu and was called Kamakura, a name that persisted into later times. It corresponds to the central part of present-day Kamakura City. The area is rich in historical, religious and cultural sites, including the site of the former bakufu, Tsurugaoka-hachiman Shrine, Kenchō Temple, Engaku Temple, the Great Buddha of Hase, and Hase Kannon. Today it is known as a high-end residential area, as well as a destination for sightseeing and beach activities.

field_topography_ja.value: 相模国の歌枕。現在神奈川県南東部の市。南は相模湾に面し、三方は丘陵や谷が多く、天然の要塞とされる。古くは郡名・郷名として現れるが、鎌倉時代には幕府所在地として鶴岡八幡宮を中心とした一帯を鎌倉と称し、それが後世に及んだ。現在の鎌倉市の中心部にあたる。幕府跡・鶴岡八幡宮・建長寺・円覚寺・長谷の大仏・長谷観音などの史跡・社寺や文化財が多い。また、今日では高級住宅地として有名であり、行楽地、海水浴場としても知られる。
